results.text:
Read text file `.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md`.
1|---
2|name: muse-round
3|description: Run one round of the Muse agent on the MobileMoE-S kernels as a swarm. Explorers map the code and measurements into a shared analysis; then competing builders write and grade fused Metal kernels for the top inefficiencies. From round 2 on, the round starts from the previous rounds' results and must beat their best attempts. Both phases are tracked in shared documents.
4|---
5|
6|# One round of the Muse agent: a swarm explores, then builds
7|
8|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed on main and tagged `muse-code-era` before the first Muse Code session; each later version is committed before the round that uses it. [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
9|
10|**Skill version 8.** This file, the role cards and tracking.md are versioned together; [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) lists every version. Each round records the version it ran (see *Versions* in tracking.md).
11|
12|You are the **lead** of a Muse Code session in your own worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. The first prompt names the Meta model you run as, the name your commit subjects start with, and the co-author line every commit ends with. `claude/muse-agent-brief.md` fixes the task, the slots, the tools and limits, the grader command and the pass criteria (G1, G2). Four ADRs change it in five ways:
13|
14|1. **Harness** ([ADR 0006](../../../claude/adr/0006-muse-spark-in-muse-code.md)). You are a Muse Code session, not a Claude Code one. Muse Code adds no trailer, so you write the first prompt's co-author line on every commit yourself (see *Commits*).
15|2. **No attempt limit and no stop rule** (ADR 0006). The brief's *When a slot stops* no longer applies: you decide when a slot is done. Every graded attempt is committed, so the history shows every try.
16|3. **A swarm** ([ADR 0007](../../../claude/adr/0007-muse-spark-swarm.md)). Helpers explore and build; you coordinate and commit.
17|4. **Files** (ADR 0007, [ADR 0009](../../../claude/adr/0009-rounds-build-on-each-other.md)). Each round writes in its own **round folder**: round 1 at the top of `muse-spark/`, round N from 2 on in `muse-spark/round-<N>/`. It holds `exploration/` and `implementation/`, the round's shared documents, which replace `strategy.md`; `kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<M>/`; and `summary.md`. tracking.md writes it `<round>/`.
18|5. **Rounds build on each other** (ADR 0009). A finished round's files are frozen: read them and cite them, and the hooks refuse any change to them. From round 2 on, a slot may have a **baseline**: the best attempt so far that passes the current G2 and that Claude's G3 accepted: against the unchanged model and the compiled reference, faster in one phase, decode or prefill, and slower in neither ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A new attempt must beat it in the same grader run. A slot without one has a **starting point** instead: an earlier attempt to build from, which Claude's measurement names, with what kept it from being a baseline.
19|
20|The rest of the brief stands. The goal: kernels that make whole requests faster. In the grader they pass G1 and G2 and have `beats_compiled` true, faster in one phase, decode or prefill, and slower in neither (ADR 0011), and where the slot has a baseline `beats_baseline` true too, because they remove a cause you can name. Then the **ready check**, the same G3 Claude runs after the round, run by you inside it, must pass them before they are `ready` ([ADR 0013](../../../claude/adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)). A faster decode step bought with a slower prefill is no improvement, and a claim no one measured is no result. An attempt built for decode sizes may hand prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference with `max_rows` (the brief's launch spec). The Muse agent was Muse Spark in round 1 and Muse Wonder in round 2 ([ADR 0008](../../../claude/adr/0008-muse-wonder.md)), and is Muse Spark's contributor model again from round 3 ([ADR 0012](../../../claude/adr/0012-muse-spark-contributor-unattended.md)); the first prompt names the model you run as, and documents from earlier rounds say the model of their round. No one approves your tool calls during the round, so the rules here are yours to keep.
21|
22|## The swarm
23|
24|| Role | Name | Task | Card |
25||---|---|---|---|
26|| **Lead** (you) | | Start the helpers, keep the two READMEs, settle clashes, commit | this file |
27|| **Explorer** | `explorer-<territory>` | Map one territory into entries, and find where it loses time | [explorer.md](explorer.md) |
28|| **Verifier** | `verifier` | Check every inefficiency against its sources | [verifier.md](verifier.md) |
29|| **Builder** | `builder-<n>-<letter>` | Write and grade one solution for one hypothesis: one attempt | [builder.md](builder.md) |
30|| **Boundary agent** | `boundary-<n>` | Write what a hypothesis's solution must keep identical, and check passing attempts against it | [boundary.md](boundary.md) |
31|| **Checker** | `checker-<n>`, `checker-final` | Check every speed claim against the file it cites: a hypothesis's before it closes, and the round's final claims | [checker.md](checker.md) |
32|
33|You don't explore, build or grade yourself; the one GPU job you run is the ready check (step 4). Start each helper with a prompt of this shape:
34|
35|> You are `<name>`, a `<role>` in round `<N>`'s swarm; this round writes in `<round folder>`. Read `.agents/skills/muse-round/<card>` and `.agents/skills/muse-round/tracking.md`, then: `<task>`.
36|
37|[tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the shared documents (the two phase folders, their READMEs, entries and logs) and the rules every agent keeps. Read it before starting anyone. Up to 12 agents run at once, you included.
38|
39|**A checkpoint** is what you do each time a helper returns, and whenever the log shows something to settle:
40|1. **Read the log.** Read the phase log since your last checkpoint.
41|2. **Settle clashes.** When two entries describe one cause, keep the fuller one and set the other's status to `superseded by <entry>`. When two helpers work on one item, redirect one of them (`subagent_send_message`). Log what you decided.
42|3. **Refresh the tracker.** Update the phase README's tracker table, and raise the version of each hypothesis entry that changed.
43|4. **Raise the version.** Raise the phase README to its next version, and add its line to `## Versions`, naming the entries that changed and their versions (see *Versions* in tracking.md).
44|5. **Commit** the phase folder, plus any attempt that came back, as that version (see *Commits*).
45|
46|## The round
47|
48|### 0. Find where you are
49|
50|- Run `git log --oneline main -1`, then `git tag --list -n1 'muse-round-*'`, which lists the finished rounds. **This round** is one more than the highest; with none, it is round 1. Its folder is `muse-spark/round-<N>/` (round 1: `muse-spark/`).
51|- `git log --oneline --grep '^Muse ' muse-code-era..HEAD` lists the Muse agent's commits of every round.
52|- **From round 2 on,** read Claude's measurement of the previous round, `claude/findings/muse-round-<N-1>.md`. It has the G3 results and names each slot's baseline or starting point. If it is missing, stop and reply "Claude's measurement of round <N-1> is missing": this round builds on it.
53|- If this round's folder already exists, a session stopped partway: carry on from its READMEs' last versions.
54|- Read the brief.
55|
56|**Done** when you can name the round number and its folder, and from round 2 on each slot's baseline or starting point and the latest G3 results.
57|
58|### 1. The starting point (from round 2 on)
59|
60|This is the round's plan, built on what the earlier rounds learned. Read:
61|- the previous rounds' final exploration and implementation READMEs and `summary.md`;
62|- the `notes.md` of each baseline or starting-point attempt;
63|- Claude's measurement.
64|
65|Then write the opening of this round's `exploration/README.md` (set up as in step 2.1), a section **Starting point**:
66|- **Per slot:**
67|  - the baseline, or the starting point where there is none, and its piece timing;
68|  - its G3 effect, and how that compares with what was predicted, with the reason where Claude's measurement gives one;
69|  - what keeps a starting point from passing G2, and where the attempt still spends its time.
70|- **What is left:**
71|  - the confirmed inefficiencies not yet built or not fully removed, ranked by predicted saving against the baselines, or the reference where a slot has none;
72|  - the slots not yet tried, for example `routing+combine`;
73|  - the recommendations outside the slots.
74|- **Refuted claims,** which no one chases again.
75|- **Territories** this round opens (step 2.2), each with the line of this section that reopens it.
76|
77|Commit it as exploration v1. **Done** when every slot has its baseline or starting point and every territory has its reason.
78|
79|### 2. Exploration
80|
81|1. **Set up the folder.** Write `<round>/exploration/README.md` with a heading, its version line (v1, with skill version 8), the tracker (one row per territory) and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`.
82|2. **Start the explorers and the verifier,** all at once.
83|   - **Round 1** starts with these territories:
84|
85|     | Territory | Covers |
86|     |---|---|
87|     | `model` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py`: the decoder layer, `MoE.__call__` and everything around the slots |
88|     | `switch-layers` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/switch_layers.py`: the routed experts' path, `gather_qmm`, the sort from 16 rows |
89|     | `quantized-kernels` | `quantized.h` and `quantized_utils.h` in `.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/`: the `affine_gather_*` kernels behind `gather_qmm` |
90|     | `other-kernels` | the other Metal kernels in the same folder that the routing and combine slots launch: sort, softmax, reductions, elementwise, copies |
91|     | `vllm-metal` | `third_party/vllm-metal/vllm_metal/`: how the engine runs a decode step and a prefill chunk around the model |
92|     | `grader` | `bench/grader/`: the slot interface, what G1, G2 and the piece timing measure, and so the boundary every solution keeps |
93|     | `findings` | `claude/findings/` and `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/` |
94|     | `runs` | `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/`, `2026-10-29-baseline/` and `2026-10-30-micro/` |
95|
96|   - **From round 2 on,** the starting point lists the territories:
97|     - `baseline-<slot>` for each slot: its baseline's kernels and `spec.json`, which are now the code in the slot, or its starting point's. Map them with the checklist, and find where they still lose time and, for a starting point, why it fails G2;
98|     - `g3`: Claude's measurement of the previous round, where the end-to-end change differs from the piece timing, and why;
99|     - of round 1's territories, only those the starting point reopens. An explorer starts from that territory's earlier entries and writes only what is new.
100|3. **Refocus as costs show up.** When an entry shows that one file holds most of a territory's cost, split it off as a territory of its own, with its own explorer. Merge or close a territory that turns out to hold nothing, and add one when an inefficiency points somewhere no one covers. Log each change and update the tracker.
101|4. **Checkpoint** each time a helper returns.
102|
103|**Done** when every territory entry is `done`, the verifier has returned, and every inefficiency is `confirmed`, `refuted` or `superseded`.
104|
105|### 3. The analysis
106|
107|Write the final `<round>/exploration/README.md`. It is the round's report on the code, for this round's builders and for future improvements:
108|
109|- **Tracker:** the final table.
110|- **Starting point** (from round 2 on), as written in step 1, with any correction exploration made.
111|- **Context:** the decode step and the prefill, the MoE block and its slots, and what the measurements say about where the time goes in each.
112|- **Territory map:** how the territories feed each other. For each territory: what it receives, what it passes on, and its measured cost.
113|- **Inefficiencies, ranked:**
114|  - the confirmed ones inside the slots, ranked by predicted saving as a share of the decode step, averaged over 1, 8 and 32 rows, or of the prefill chunk, averaged over 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows; from round 2 on, the saving is against the baseline where the slot has one;
115|  - each with what removing it does to the other phase, and whether a hand-off (`max_rows`) keeps that phase unchanged;
116|  - each with its cost, kind and entry;
117|  - Claude's findings marked as Claude's, earlier rounds' entries linked as theirs, and this round's own reading marked as yours.
118|- **Recommendations:** the confirmed inefficiencies outside the slots, with their evidence. They're for surucuonur's team.
119|- **Refuted claims,** in one line each, so no one chases them again.
120|- **Files read:** links to each territory entry's list.
121|
122|Commit it. **Done** when every ranked item links a confirmed entry and every number in the README has its source.
123|
124|### 4. Implementation
125|
126|Take the ranked inefficiencies in order, at most two at a time, in different slots so their attempts never touch. Write `<round>/implementation/README.md` with a heading, its version line, the tracker and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`. For each hypothesis:
127|
128|1. **Open the hypothesis.** Write `<round>/implementation/hyp-<n>-<slug>.md`, with status `boundary`, the inefficiency, the slot and, from round 2 on, the slot's baseline folder or `none`. Add its tracker row and log it.
129|2. **Draw its boundary.** Start `boundary-<n>` to write the boundary, and wait for it.
130|3. **Compete.**
131|   - Set the status to `building`.
132|   - Start 2 or 3 builders, `builder-<n>-a`, `-b` and `-c`. Give each a different direction drawn from the analysis: for example, fusing kernels, reading each weight byte once, or a different threadgroup shape. From round 2 on, a direction may start from the baseline's or starting point's kernels, or from scratch.
133|4. **Collect.** Each time a builder returns:
134|   - checkpoint, committing its attempt folder with the hypothesis entry, the README and the log;
135|   - if the attempt passed G2, start `boundary-<n>` to check it.
136|5. **Harden.**
137|   - Pick the best attempt: it passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, has `beats_compiled` true and, where the slot has a baseline, `beats_baseline`, and it is the fastest across the six sizes.
138|   - Set the status to `hardening`, and start a builder for that attempt's next single change.
139|   - Repeat while the attempt still has a cause you can name and remove.
140|   - **Change approach after three alike failures.** Keep the hypothesis entry's failure ledger at each collect: every graded attempt that lost, the size or phase it lost at, and its named cause. When three attempts have lost at the same phase for the same cause, the next one changes approach (another kernel structure, parallelisation or dataflow, not a tuning), and its `notes.md` says "approach change: from X to Y"; or you log why not. A cause renamed without a measurement that refutes the old one is the same cause.
141|6. **Close.**
142|   - **`candidate`:** the best attempt passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, has `beats_compiled` true and, where the slot has a baseline, `beats_baseline` true, and you can name no further change worth making. Write the **Decision**: the attempt, why it is best, and the change in whole requests you predict, labelled a prediction. Then start `checker-<n>` on the entry; the hypothesis is a candidate once its **Checks** section says `pass`.
143|   - **`dropped`:** say why. A slot whose hypotheses are all dropped keeps its baseline, or the reference where it has none.
144|
145|Then open the next-ranked inefficiency.
146|
147|**The ready check** ([ADR 0013](../../../claude/adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)). Once no hypothesis is building or hardening and at least one is a `candidate`, run it yourself, over every candidate in one call:
148|
149|```bash
150|.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_ready.py <round>/checks/ready-<k> <slot>=<attempt folder> [<slot>=<attempt folder> ...]
151|```
152|
153|It times the candidates in vLLM exactly as Claude's G3 will after the round, each alone and, with more than one, all together, then audits its own log and writes `ready-verdict.json`. It takes about 10 to 15 minutes per slot, more for an attempt with a slow prefill, and waits its turn for the GPU. Commit its folder at the next checkpoint.
154|- **Exit 0 or 1: a verdict, and it stands.** A candidate whose `muse-<slot>` passes becomes `ready`; one that fails goes back to `hardening` with the failure in its ledger, or to `dropped`. Cite the file either way. With more than one candidate, submitting them together needs `muse-all` to pass; if some pass alone and `muse-all` fails, a second check may take only those.
155|- **Exit 2: no verdict.** The run stopped or broke the protocol; run it again in a new folder.
156|- **At most two ready checks per round.**
157|
158|**Done** when no confirmed inefficiency is left that you judge will pay, and every candidate has a ready-check verdict. Write why in the implementation README.
159|
160|### 5. Finish
161|
162|1. **The implementation README:** the final tracker, one paragraph per hypothesis, and a **Ready to test** section. It names the attempt per slot that goes to Claude's G3: a `ready` attempt, the baseline kept, or the reference. For the `ready` ones it shows the ready check's measured change in the four workloads (the decode step, the prompt time and the whole request, against the unchanged model and the compiled reference), citing `ready-verdict.json`, with your earlier prediction beside it, labelled PREDICTION, and the **Unverified** list. Nothing else in it is an end-to-end number.
163|2. **The exploration README:** add *What building taught*, the analysis corrected by what the attempts showed.
164|3. **`<round>/summary.md`:** a `## Round N` section with:
165|   - the model, the skill version this round ran, and the final versions of both READMEs;
166|   - the final attempt per slot;
167|   - the number of graded attempts per slot, this round and over all rounds;
168|   - the ready check's measured change, citing its file;
169|   - what you'd try next;
170|   - your recommendations outside the slots.
171|4. **Check, commit, reply.** Start `checker-final` on *Ready to test* and the summary, and fix what it finds until it signs `pass`. Then commit, and reply with this round's commits and the words "Round N finished".
172|
173|## Your own rules
174|
175|- **Writes:**
176|  - you write the two READMEs, the hypothesis entries' status blocks and decisions, and `summary.md`;
177|  - every helper writes only what its card names;
178|  - all of it stays in this round's folder.
179|- **Claude's G3 after the round is the authority;** your ready check is the same measurement, made earlier. vLLM runs only through the ready check.
180|- **The rules every agent keeps** are in tracking.md.
181|
182|## Commits
183|
184|You are the only agent that commits. Commit only on `muse-agent`.
185|- **What to add:** this round's phase folders that exist so far (only `exploration` until implementation starts) and the attempt folders that came back. An attempt another builder is still writing waits for its own commit. An entry that is mid-edit is committed as it stands, and finished in a later commit.
186|- **The message:**
187|  - every subject starts with the name the first prompt gives you, then a colon;
188|  - a checkpoint's subject is `<name>: <phase> v<N>: <what changed>`, the version it records;
189|  - every message ends with the first prompt's co-author line, exactly.
190|
191|For example, in round 2 as Muse Wonder:
192|
193|```bash
194|git add muse-spark/round-2/exploration muse-spark/round-2/implementation muse-spark/round-2/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<M>
195|git commit -m "Muse Wonder: implementation v4: experts attempt 3 graded, beats baseline" \
196|  -m "Co-Authored-By: Muse Wonder (Meta Model API) <muse-wonder@meta-model-api.invalid>"
197|```
198|
199|Use no other co-author. The hooks refuse a commit without a Muse agent's co-author, a commit outside `muse-spark/`, a change to a finished round's files, a new file outside this round's folder, and any merge. Push, merge, rebase, tags, git config and hook skipping stay with surucuonur.

results.text:
Read text file `.agents/skills/muse-round/tracking.md`.
1|# The swarm's shared documents, and the rules every agent keeps
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Part of the [muse-round skill](SKILL.md). [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|Every agent of the round reads this file. The documents below are how the swarm shares what it knows and how surucuonur follows the round while it runs, so keep them current as you work, not at the end.
6|
7|## The round folder and its two phase folders
8|
9|`<round>/` is this round's folder: `muse-spark/round-<N>/` from round 2 on (round 1's is `muse-spark/` itself). The lead's prompt names it.
10|
11|| Folder | Phase | Holds |
12||---|---|---|
13|| `<round>/exploration/` | Exploration | the analysis: `README.md`, territory and inefficiency entries, `log.md` |
14|| `<round>/implementation/` | Implementation | the report: `README.md`, hypothesis entries, `log.md` |
15|
16|Kernels go in `<round>/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>/`, numbered from 1 in each round; the grader reads any attempt folder it is given.
17|
18|**Earlier rounds' folders are frozen.** Read them and cite them by path; write what you add in this round's entries. The hooks refuse a change to any file a finished round left.
19|
20|Each folder has three kinds of document:
21|
22|- **`README.md`.** The phase's document. Only the lead writes it, refreshing it and raising its version at every checkpoint. It opens with its version line and the tracker table below.
23|- **Entries.** One file per territory, inefficiency or hypothesis. The owner keeps it current, and other agents append notes.
24|- **`log.md`.** One line per event, from every agent, appended only.
25|
26|## Versions
27|
28|Every shared document carries a version number, so a reader knows which version they're looking at, and git holds every version.
29|
30|**Phase versions.** Each README opens with its version line:
31|
32|```markdown
33|**Version:** v5 · 2026-11-04T09:40Z · skill version 8
34|```
35|
36|- **Who raises it:** the lead, at every checkpoint, and each version is exactly one commit.
37|- **The commit:** its subject names the version, `<name>: exploration v5: <what changed>`, where `<name>` is the Muse agent's name from the lead's first prompt. `git log --grep 'exploration v5:'` finds it, and `git diff` between two such commits shows what changed.
38|- **The changelog:** the README ends with `## Versions`, one line per version, newest first, naming the entries that changed and their new versions:
39|
40|```markdown
41|- v5 · 2026-11-04T09:40Z · split quantized-kernels in two · changed: territory-quantized-kernels v4, ineff-quantized-kernels-2 v2
42|```
43|
44|**Entry versions.** Each entry's status block has a `Version` line, starting at 1:
45|- **Territory and inefficiency entries:** the owner raises it with every change to its own text. The verifier raises it when it writes the verdict.
46|- **Hypothesis entries:** the lead raises it at each checkpoint where the entry changed, builders' and the boundary agent's sections included.
47|- **Notes:** a note under `## From other agents` leaves the version alone. The owner raises it when folding the note in.
48|
49|**Times.** Every time you write, in a version line, a status block, a tracker row, a note or a log line, is the output of `date -u +%FT%TZ` run at that moment. Never estimate or round one.
50|
51|## The README trackers
52|
53|Exploration, `exploration/README.md`:
54|
55|| Territory | Agent | Status | Inefficiencies | Updated |
56||---|---|---|---|---|
57|| `quantized-kernels` | `explorer-quantized-kernels` | exploring | `ineff-quantized-kernels-1` (confirmed), `-2` (open) | 2026-11-04 09:40Z |
58|
59|Implementation, `implementation/README.md`:
60|
61|| Hypothesis | Slot | Builders | Attempts: G1, G2, µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (compiled) | Status |
62||---|---|---|---|---|
63|| `hyp-1-fused-gather` | `experts` | `builder-1-a`, `builder-1-b` | 3: pass, pass, 41 / 55 / 180 (48 / 70 / 260) | hardening |
64|
65|From round 2 on, where the slot has a baseline, the attempts column also gives its time from the same run, and whether `beats_baseline` is true.
66|
67|## Entries
68|
69|Each entry opens with a status block that its owner keeps current:
70|
71|```markdown
72|- **Owner:** explorer-quantized-kernels
73|- **Status:** exploring
74|- **Version:** 3
75|- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T09:40Z
76|- **Next:** read the 32-row dispatch of affine_gather_qmm
77|```
78|
79|Entries are named so that two agents never pick the same name:
80|- `<round>/exploration/territory-<territory>.md`
81|- `<round>/exploration/ineff-<territory>-<n>.md`, numbered by the explorer of that territory
82|- `<round>/implementation/hyp-<n>-<slug>.md`, numbered by the lead
83|
84|**Another agent's entry:** append under its `## From other agents` heading, starting with your name and the time. The owner's text stays as written, so two agents never overwrite each other. The owner reads these notes and folds in what holds.
85|
86|### Territory entry
87|
88|1. Status block (statuses: `exploring`, `done`).
89|2. **What it does** in the decode step, in a few lines.
90|3. **The checklist** below, filled in for each piece of code or table in the territory.
91|4. **Relations:** which territories feed it and which it feeds, with the data passed.
92|5. **Inefficiencies:** links to the entries this territory raised.
93|6. **Files read**, and what each one gave.
94|
95|### Inefficiency entry
96|
97|1. Status block. The statuses are `open`, `confirmed`, `refuted` and `superseded by <entry>`; only the verifier sets `confirmed` or `refuted`.
98|2. **Slot:** `routing`, `combine`, `experts`, or `outside the slots`.
99|3. **What happens:** what the code does, and where (file and lines).

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write faster MobileMoE-S kernels, for decoding and prompt processing
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|A request goes through two phases: **prompt processing** (the prefill), which runs its whole prompt through the model, and **decoding**, one step per generated token. An improvement must hold in both: faster in one, and no slower in the other ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A kernel that speeds up the decode step but slows the prefill is not an improvement.
12|
13|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
14|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
15|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
16|
17|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
18|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
19|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
20|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
21|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
22|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
23|
24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
95|
96|## Tools and limits
97|
98|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.

100|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
101|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.

180|## How each attempt is judged
181|
182|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.
183|
184|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
185|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
186|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
187|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
188|
189|   At every size:
190|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
191|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
192|
193|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
194|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
195|3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
196|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
197|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
198|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
199|
200|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
201|
202|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).
203|
204|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
205|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
206|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
207|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same` or `slower`); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.
208|
209|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
210|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
211|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
212|- **Per phase:** decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) are each `faster` when every size is, `slower` when any size is, and `not slower` otherwise.
213|- **`beats_compiled`** is true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
214|
215|It is a guide; the ready check in the round, and Claude's G3 after it, decide.
216|
217|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, or after 5 attempts. Name your final attempt per slot in `muse-spark/summary.md`; it goes to the end-to-end and G3 checks, which surucuonur's team runs after merging your branch.

97|A decode step produces one token per request. On plain MLX with 128-token prompts the bare step takes 4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (Claude: `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md`, via round 1); in vLLM the unchanged step Claude re-measured for round 1 takes 5.370 / 14.363 / 29.851 ms (`claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` §3). A step is 867 kernels at 1 row, 987 at 32 rows, far below both hardware limits (whole-step 24–41 GB/s against 200 GB/s peak, ≤9% of peak compute), so it is overhead-bound throughout. Each tiny kernel costs ~6.81 µs end to end in the whole-step accounting, but the piece harness prices kernels differently (see *Territory map*): a fused kernel's floor is ~17 µs per layer when barrier-free and ~24 µs with barriers/serial tails, while the reference's kernels cost ~3–4.5 µs each when pipelined 20 deep. Round 2 ranks by the chained piece timing (each layer's call waits for the previous through the grader's `link` kernel), which matches the model's real dependency; the old independent timing is retained only as history.

Per layer it launches: routing, 12 kernels (router cast+matmul+sigmoid, bias add, negate, argpartition, gather, weight norm); the routed experts, 7 kernels at 1 row (3 products + activation + 3 off-chain index ranges) and 13 from 16 rows (6 sort/unsort glue kernels); combine, 5 kernels (cast, multiply, sum, cast, add with the shared expert); plus the shared expert, 4 kernels. The three slots mirror this split: `routing` (240 kernels/step), `experts` (140–260/step), `combine` (100/step). At 1 row, routing costs 1.02 ms and combine 0.61 ms — together 1.63 ms of the 4.75 ms step (34%), more than the routed experts' 0.92 ms. At 32 rows the experts cost 14.67 ms of 28.19 ms (52%) while routing falls to 1.68 ms (6%) and combine to 0.33 ms (1%). The experts read 908 MB at 32 rows against 443 MB for the distinct experts — half the bytes are repeat reads, and even so the path runs at only 62 GB/s (31% of peak), so most of it is kernel efficiency, not bytes. Those costs are Claude's knock-outs and counters; the mechanisms are the swarm's readings, round 1's carried forward where they still hold and this round's where the starting points changed the code in the slot.

158|The analysis corrected by what the attempts showed (see `../implementation/README.md`):
159|
160|1. **Scalar sums reproduce MMA rounding — the round's central surprise.** Exploration held that the steel regimes' 8-product hardware accumulation could not be reproduced by scalar reordering (`ineff-baseline-routing-1`). Routing attempt-2 disproved it at decode sizes and attempt-3 at all six: serial scalar sums over the same partition/K order are bit-identical to `simdgroup_float8x8` accumulation on this GPU, including the 8-partition (127-row) and single-accumulator (>768) groupings. The same held for experts prefill: attempt-1's serial BK=32 scalar path matched `gather_qmm_rhs` bit for bit, as did attempt-2's MMA-tile form. Future exact kernels should try scalar first — it is simpler and, once staged, faster.
161|2. **Unstaged scalar is latency-bound; staging is the fix, not MMA.** Routing attempt-3 (scalar, device loads) ran 300 µs/layer at 8/32 rows on uncoalesced loads and threadgroup bank conflicts; attempt-4 (same sums, coalesced `float4` staging, padded `x`) runs 69–73 µs and beats compiled everywhere. 162|3. **Experts 1-row latency is a plateau, not a packing problem.** Six G2-exact attempts spanning 4 to 144 threadgroups per call, 128–512 threads per group, fused and split, interleaved and parallel-stored, all chain at 92–110 µs/layer at 1 row against compiled 73–87. Width, group count, interleave and store parallelism each moved 8/32 rows (best 510 µs at 32 rows, attempt-7) and none moved 1 row by more than ~12 µs. The remainder is the per-block serial K chains plus chained fixed cost; a fused exact kernel may need to stop fusing (reference-shaped separate products) to win at 1 row — untested, since every attempt kept at most two kernels.
163|4. **Chained floors replace independent floors.** Combine's ~17 µs independent floor is ~32–40 µs chained; routing's compiled bar is 56–91 µs chained against 30–49 independent. Every builder prediction anchored on the independent basis missed by +80–150% in the same direction, candidates and compiled alike. Predict only on the chained basis; within-run vs-compiled remains the valid comparison (1-row baselines still shift 73–87 µs for experts across runs).
164|5. **Contraction suppression needs volatile, not `precise`.** The literal `precise float` qualifier does not compile under MLX 0.32.4's header; `volatile` thread-local round-trips reproduce the reference's per-op roundings exactly (differ 0 over 49.6M graded combine elements) in both combine organizations. The residual is toolchain dependence — re-grade after any MLX/macOS change (boundary-3).

1|# Attempt 1 — builder-3-a, direction (a): thread-per-output + precise stepwise sum
2|
3|First attempt in this direction (round 2, `hyp-3-combine-exact`, slot
4|`combine`, baseline `none`). Builds on the starting point
5|`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1` (`block-0.metal:12-25`,
6|`spec.json`: grid `rows*768`, threadgroup [256,1,1], no threadgroup
7|memory). The starting point is not a baseline: under round 2's bit-exact
8|G2 it fails at five of six sizes on FMA contraction alone (decode
9|0 / 2 / 2 differ, prefill 6 / 50 / 130; `ineff-baseline-combine-1`,
10|`territory-baseline-combine.md` checklist D), so it counts as the attempt
11|this one changes.
12|
13|## What changed
14|
15|Only the arithmetic. Indexing, grid, threadgroup, inputs/outputs and the
16|final line `bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase]` are verbatim from the starting
17|point. The single-expression sum
18|
19|```metal
20|float acc = float(y0)*w0 + float(y1)*w1 + float(y2)*w2 + float(y3)*w3;
21|```
22|
23|which the compiler FP-contracts into FMAs (each product kept unrounded
24|into its add), becomes seven fma-free stepwise ops with explicit
25|rounding barriers:
26|
27|```metal
28|volatile float p0 = float(y[ybase]) * weights[wbase];        // rounded to f32
29|volatile float p1 = float(y[ybase+768u]) * weights[wbase+1u];
30|volatile float p2 = float(y[ybase+1536u]) * weights[wbase+2u];
31|volatile float p3 = float(y[ybase+2304u]) * weights[wbase+3u];
32|volatile float s01 = p0 + p1;                                // rounded to f32
33|volatile float s012 = s01 + p2;                              // rounded to f32
34|volatile float acc = s012 + p3;                              // rounded to f32
35|out[sbase] = bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase];                    // verbatim
36|```
37|
38|Each `volatile` store materialises its f32 value, so no product can stay
39|unrounded into the next add and no add can be fused with a later mul;
40|the fold is exactly `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3` with a rounding after every add,
41|then one bfloat16 round and the single-rounding bfloat16 `+ shared`,
42|matching the reference's separate kernels (`binary_g` multiply,
43|`col_reduce_small` sum, `copy_v`, `binary_vv`; `slots.py:51-52`,
44|Boundary steps 1–5). No reassociation, no `fma`, no threadgroup memory.
45|
46|Note on spelling: the literal `precise float` qualifier does not compile
47|under MLX 0.32.4 (`metal::precise` is a function namespace in the MLX
48|header, e.g. `metal::precise::exp`; a leading `precise` is parsed as
49|that namespace and rejected). Volatile stepwise barriers are the
50|"explicit rounding barriers" the hypothesis design names as the
51|alternative to `metal::precise` operations, with the same semantics:
52|every mul rounds once to f32, every add rounds once to f32. Probes
53|outside the grader (random [512,4,768] inputs vs the eager MLX
54|reference, 3 × 393,216 elements) gave differ 3–4 for the starting
55|point's contracted expression and differ 0 for this kernel.

190|## Verdict
191|
192|G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0

197|merged down loop's per-block order and the parallel stores are
198|bit-exact, and the `rows >= 60` scalar `qmm_accum` branch is
199|untouched. The 512-thread launch now compiles: sharing one
200|kernel-scope `q[32]` between gate/up's second accumulator and
201|down's second block restores the pipeline's threadgroup budget
202|that attempt-6's three distinct arrays exceeded (512 > 448).

212|at 1 row and 798.2 → 792.7 at 32 rows between runs, so treat
213|cross-run deltas as indicative): 93.8 vs 92.1 at 1 row
214|(**+1.8%**), 160.1 vs 162.0 at 8 rows (**−1.2%**), 510.1 vs
215|534.8 at 32 rows (**−4.6%**). Effective bandwidth on pair
216|bytes: 23.6 / 110.5 / 138.8 GB/s (attempt-5: 24.0 / 109.2 /
217|132.3). The down interleave therefore helps where group
218|parallelism already hides load latency (32 rows, +4.9% GB/s,

220|8 rows, but it does not move the latency-bound 1-row size.

222|## Miss analysis (prediction 85 / 156 / 540, measured 93.8 / 160.1 / 510.1)
223|
224|Misses are +10.4% / +2.6% / −5.5% — all inside the 20% bar, so
225|no formal miss, but the size pattern was inverted versus the
226|prediction (saving predicted largest at 1 row, actually largest
227|at 32 rows) and that needs explaining:
228|
229|1. **The compilation fix worked exactly as predicted, the
230|   latency saving did not.** G1 passes at 512 threads with the
231|   same 3,840 B of threadgroup memory, confirming attempt-6's
232|   failure was the third distinct accumulator array, not
233|   threadgroup memory or the merged loop itself: two distinct
234|   arrays (`p`, shared `q`) fit, three do not. That part of the
235|   prediction (pure rename, identical bits) is confirmed by
236|   G2's differ 0 at all six sizes.
237|2. **At 1 row the down waves were not a third of the layer's
238|   latency in the way the arithmetic assumed.** The prediction
239|   priced the down phase at ≈ 30 µs and the merged step at
240|   1.3× a single-block step. Measured 93.8 ≈ attempt-5's 92.1
241|   says the merged step costs closer to 2× at this size: with
242|   only 4 threadgroups (one per pair) on 16 cores, the down
243|   phase's latency was already hidden *across* simdgroups —
244|   attempt-5's wave 0 runs 16 blocks concurrently per group,
245|   attempt-7 runs 12 simdgroups each serially merging two
246|   blocks, so concurrent in-flight loads per group fall
247|   (48 vs 64 simdgroup-block chains per call at 1 row) while
248|   each chain's step doubles its loads. The gate/up precedent
249|   hid ≈ 20% because gate and up *share* the `tg_x[k]` read and
250|   both blocks' loads were previously fully sequential phases;
251|   down's two blocks share only `tg_h[k]` and already overlapped
252|   across the 16-simdgroup wave. The remaining ≈ 19 µs gap to
253|   compiled (93.8 vs 74.8) is therefore still the `tg_x` load,
254|   silu, the two barriers and the chained launch/link cost —
255|   none of which this change touches.
256|3. **At 32 rows the merged loop pays for a different reason.**
257|   One wave instead of two removes a wave-quantization tail
258|   (wave 1 ran 8 of 16 simdgroups) on every pair and halves the
259|   down loop's barrier-free step count, which at 128 groups
260|   shows up as throughput: 138.8 vs 132.3 GB/s. The predicted
261|   +5 µs register tax did not appear (measured −24.7 µs vs
262|   attempt-5 cross-run) — consistent with the shared `q`: peak
263|   live accumulators never exceed gate/up's 64 floats, so there
264|   is no new spill, and claim 2's cross-simdgroup overlap loss
265|   is hidden by group parallelism at this size.
266|
267|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: a merged pair helps only
268|where the two blocks were previously *phases* (gate then up,
269|fully sequential, shared activation read); where the blocks
270|already ran as concurrent simdgroups in one wave (down's 24
271|blocks), merging trades cross-simdgroup parallelism for
272|in-step parallelism and is latency-neutral at 4 groups — the
273|1-row remainder is fixed cost and the serial gate/up chain,
274|not the down wave count. Register headroom at 512 threads is
275|exactly two 32-float accumulators; a third distinct array,
276|however short-lived, fails G1.
277|
278|## Next change
279|
280|Leave the down interleave in (it is the best 32-row time and
281|G2-exact) and attack the actual 1-row remainder named above:
282|the `tg_x` load + silu + barrier chain and the chained fixed
283|cost. Concretely, overlap the down product's first K steps with
284|the silu tail (down blocks whose `tg_h` slice is already
285|written) or narrow the silu barrier to a simdgroup-local one —
286|but any such change must keep the full-bfloat16 silu bits and
287|every accumulation order, and must not add a third accumulator
288|array (this attempt's G1 lesson).

1|# Explorer
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Part of the [muse-round skill](SKILL.md). [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are `explorer-<territory>`, one of the swarm's explorers. You map one **territory** of the code or the measurements, and you find where it loses time. The lead's prompt names your territory and its paths. [tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the documents you write and the rules you keep.
6|
7|First read:
8|- the brief, `claude/muse-agent-brief.md`: *The task*, *The slots* and *How each attempt is judged*;
9|- `claude/GLOSSARY.md`;
10|- the exploration README's tracker, so you know who covers what, and from round 2 on its **Starting point**;
11|- from round 2 on, the earlier rounds' entries for your territory. They are frozen: cite them by path, and write only what is new.
12|
13|## Steps
14|
15|1. **Open your entry.** Write `<round>/exploration/territory-<territory>.md` with its status block (`exploring`), and log that you started.
16|2. **Map the territory.** For each piece of code or table in it, fill in the checklist in your entry, with a source for every line.
17|   - Follow a call or a buffer into a neighbouring territory as far as you need to understand your own piece. Leave what you learn there as a note in that territory's entry. The swarm sees the whole system only when each explorer sees the edges of its own territory.
18|3. **Post inefficiencies.** Each time you find time lost, write an inefficiency entry with its cost arithmetic and predicted saving, and log it. Examples:
19|   - kernels that could be one;
20|   - weight bytes read more than once;
21|   - threads left idle;
22|   - work repeated across layers or rows.
23|4. **Adapt.** After every post, follow *Adapting to the others' work* in tracking.md. Narrow in on the part of your territory where the measured cost is; when the cause lies in another territory, put a note in that territory's entry instead of exploring it yourself.
24|5. **Answer notes.** Read the notes under `## From other agents` in your entries, and fold in what holds.
25|
26|**Done** when every piece of code or table in your territory has its checklist filled with sources, every inefficiency you found has an entry, and every note on your entries is answered. Then set your entry to `done`, log it, and return the names of your entries with one line each.
27|
28|## Sources outside the worktree
29|
30|MLX's C++ code, which picks the kernel and its threadgroup sizes for each op, isn't installed; only the Metal headers are. If web fetch works, read it at the installed version (`.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; print(mx.__version__)"`) in `github.com/ml-explore/mlx`, and cite the URL with the tag and lines.
31|
32|## What you write
33|
34|Your territory entry, your inefficiency entries, notes in other entries, and log lines.

1|# Verifier
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Part of the [muse-round skill](SKILL.md). [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are `verifier`. The implementation phase builds only on inefficiencies you confirmed, so every claim an inefficiency rests on is checked against its source before anyone builds on it. [tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the documents and the rules.
6|
7|## Steps
8|
9|Repeat until done:
10|
11|1. **Find open entries:** `grep -l 'Status:\*\* open' <round>/exploration/ineff-*.md`.
12|2. **Check each claim** the cost and the predicted saving rest on:
13|   - open the cited file at the cited lines;
14|   - find the cited table row;
15|   - redo the arithmetic.
16|3. **Write the entry's `Verdict` section.** Mark each claim `confirmed`, `wrong` (with what is right, and its source) or `no source`.
17|4. **Set the status:**
18|   - `confirmed` when every claim the cost and the saving rest on holds;
19|   - otherwise `refuted`, with the reason in one line.
20|   
21|   Raise the block's `Version`, update its `Updated` line, and log the verdict. The `Verdict` section and these status-block lines are the only text you change in another agent's entry.
22|5. **Re-check on reply.** When an owner answers your verdict under `## From other agents` with a correction, check it again.
23|6. **Report duplicates to the lead.** When two entries describe the same cause, log `duplicate: <entry> and <entry>` for the lead to settle.
24|
25|**Done** when every explorer has logged that it finished and no inefficiency entry is `open`. Return how many entries you confirmed and refuted, and the refuted ones with their reasons.
26|
27|## What you write
28|
29|The `Verdict` section and status of inefficiency entries, and log lines.

1|# Builder
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Part of the [muse-round skill](SKILL.md). [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are `builder-<n>-<letter>`. You write one solution for one hypothesis and grade it. That is one attempt. The lead's prompt names the hypothesis entry and your direction. Other builders take other directions on the same hypothesis, so keep to yours. [tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the documents and the rules.
6|
7|First read:
8|- the hypothesis entry, its **Boundary** above all;
9|- the inefficiency and territory entries it links;
10|- in the brief, `claude/muse-agent-brief.md`: your slot, *Tools and limits*, *Your files* (the attempt layout and launch spec) and *How each attempt is judged*;
11|- the `notes.md` of the slot's earlier attempts: this round's in `<round>/kernels/<slot-folder>/`, and earlier rounds', the baseline's or starting point's above all.
12|
13|**One grader run is one attempt.** After a run, any change, even a one-line fix, is a new attempt with its own number, built by copying the files you keep. Scratch kernels and timing experiments that aren't attempts go in `probes/` inside your attempt folder and are never graded. You return after one attempt; the brief's *When a slot stops* rule no longer applies, and the lead decides what comes next.
14|
15|## Steps
16|
17|1. **Claim an attempt number.**
18|   - N is one more than the highest `attempt-<N>` in this round's slot folder, or 1. Run `mkdir -p <round>/kernels/<slot-folder>` once, then `mkdir <round>/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>`.
19|   - If it fails, another builder took N: try N+1.
20|   - Log the claim.
21|2. **Write the attempt** in the brief's layout, plus a `notes.md` that says:
22|   - what changed since the attempt it builds on (the baseline counts), or that it is the first in your direction; from round 2 on, a starting point that fails G2 counts too;
23|   - which inefficiency it removes, and how;
24|   - the predicted µs per layer at the six sizes, decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows), with the arithmetic; from round 2 on, against the baseline's where the slot has one;
25|   - with `max_rows`, the row count and why: the sizes above it run the compiled reference;
26|   - what the attempt leaves unmeasured, for the hypothesis entry's **Unverified** list.
27|   
28|   Make one main change, the simplest kernel that removes the cause, and stay inside the boundary.
29|3. **Grade it** with the brief's grader command, once, keeping its verdict in the attempt folder: add `--out <attempt folder>/grade.json`. When the hypothesis entry names a baseline, add `--baseline <baseline folder>`; for `routing+combine`, `--baseline routing=<folder> --baseline combine=<folder>`. It times your attempt, the compiled reference and any baseline in paired repeats at the six sizes. At each size your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs and `slower` when it loses 22. `beats_compiled` and `beats_baseline` are true when one phase is `faster` at every size and neither phase is `slower` at any. The grader may print "waiting for the GPU" while another run has it; keep waiting. A run itself takes under 3 minutes once it starts, for an attempt about as fast as the reference; one much slower at the prefill sizes takes longer (round 2's experts attempt-7: 5 minutes). The grader prints only when it finishes; stop a run only after 15 minutes, and record it.
30|4. **Record the verdict** in `notes.md` and in your section of the hypothesis entry, citing `grade.json`: G1; G2 at each size, decode and prefill, with the first difference; your timings at each size next to the original's, the compiled reference's and any baseline's, with the verdicts, `phases_vs_compiled`, `beats_compiled` and, with a baseline, `beats_baseline`. Log it.
31|5. **Learn.** If the attempt failed, or its time missed your prediction by more than 20%, find out why. Write the answer in `notes.md`, and add it to the inefficiency entry as a note.
32|
33|**Done** when the attempt is graded, recorded and any miss is explained. Return the attempt folder, its verdict, and the one change you would make next.
34|
35|## What you write
36|
37|Your attempt folder, your section of the hypothesis entry, notes in other entries, and log lines.

1|# Boundary agent
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Part of the [muse-round skill](SKILL.md). [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are `boundary-<n>`, the boundary agent of hypothesis `<n>`. A solution replaces one slot, and everything before and after it in the decode step must work exactly as before. You write down that **boundary**, and later check attempts against it. The lead's prompt names your task: *write the boundary* or *check an attempt*. [tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the documents and the rules.
6|
7|## Task: write the boundary
8|
9|Write the hypothesis entry's **Boundary** section, with a source for each line:
10|- **Inputs and outputs:** the slot's inputs and outputs with names, shapes at 1, 8 and 32 rows of a decode step and at the prefill's 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows, dtypes and layouts. Sources: the brief's slot section and `bench/grader/slots.py`.
11|- **Before and after:** what runs just before and after the slot in `MoE.__call__` (`third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py`), and what each neighbour expects.
12|- **What must stay identical:** every output, bit for bit (the brief's G2): the rounding points and the order of each sum, the tie rule for the 4th and 5th expert, and the order of the 4 pairs. Where the reference's MLX kernel changes with the row count, say at which count and how its rounding changes.
13|- **What the grader checks, and what it can't see.** The *can't see* part is the start of the hypothesis's **Unverified** list. G1 and G2 run 1, 8 and 32 rows of a decode step and 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows of a prefill, but a decode step can have any row count from 1 to 32, a prefill chunk others again, and other inputs.
14|- **The GPU limits:** at most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory.
15|
16|Use the checklist in tracking.md for each neighbour. From round 2 on, an earlier round's hypothesis entry may already hold the slot's boundary: cite it, check each line still holds for the baseline or starting point and for the current G2, and write only what changed. Log it, and return when the section is complete.
17|
18|## Task: check an attempt
19|
20|The lead sends you each attempt that passed G2. Check it against the boundary for what the grader can't see:
21|- row counts other than those G2 tests: any decode count up to 32, and prefill chunks of other sizes, on each side of 60 rows;
22|- reads of threadgroup memory that was never written;
23|- use of threadgroup memory close to the limit;
24|- results that depend on thread timing;
25|- any assumption about the captured inputs that real inputs may break;
26|- with `max_rows`: that every decode step, up to 32 rows, stays at or below it, and, for experts, on which side of MLX's own switch at 60 rows the hand-off sits.
27|
28|Append the result to the entry's **Boundary checks**: `pass`, or each defect with the file and line. Log it and return.
29|

{"content":"# Exploration: round 3 — analysis

## Starting point

Round 3 builds on rounds 1 (`muse-spark/`, frozen, tagged `muse-round-1`) and 2 (`muse-spark/round-2/`, frozen, tagged `muse-round-2`) as measured independently by Claude in `claude/findings/muse-round-2.md` (2026-11-04, on `main` after merging round 2 at `4033cae`). Round 2 ran skill version 5 as Muse Wonder. The judgment changed for round 3 ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)): an improvement must hold in both phases, decode and prefill — faster in one, slower in neither — against the unchanged model and the compiled reference, in the piece timing (`beats_compiled`) and in G3, where no whole request may be slower. A slot's baseline is its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true, and passes G3; anything else that passes G2 is a starting point. **No slot has a baseline.** A new attempt must pass G1 and G2 (bit-exact at 1, 8, 32 and 127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) and beat the compiled reference in the chained two-phase timing; there is no `--baseline` to pass. Inside the round, the lead's ready check (`bench/grader/check_ready.py`, [ADR 0013](../../../claude/adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)) times every candidate exactly as Claude's G3 will, and only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`.

Round 2's final attempts, their piece timings and G3 effects are summarised per slot. Piece timings are Claude's re-grade on main with the two-phase grader (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-*.json`), chained µs per layer as reference / compiled / candidate. G3 is the vLLM decode-step change against the unchanged model (median of 3 shuffled repeats, `console-vllm.txt`) plus the whole-request throughput change at 1×128, 8×128, 32×128 and 32×1,024 (prompt-time multiple in brackets, `results/runs/2026-11-04-engine-comparison/`). Round 2's own prediction was decode-only (piece basis × 20 layers plus compiled G3 offsets); both are quoted so the gap can be seen.

### Per slot

#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7`

- **What it is.** One fused per-pair kernel (512 threads per (row, expert-slot) pair, `rows*4` threadgroups): interleaved gate/up plus interleaved down in a merged K loop, intermediates in threadgroup memory (3,840 B), full-bfloat16 silu-mul. Per-block numerics replicate MLX's `affine_gather_qvm` bitwise at decode sizes; a `rows >= 60` branch runs a scalar `qmm_accum` (bfloat16-rounded dequant, contiguous `BK=32` order) to match `gather_qmm_rhs` at prefill sizes. See `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/notes.md` and `muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-1-experts-exact.md`.
- **Piece timing** (`grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`). Decode: 84.0 / 78.6 / **92.1** at 1 row (slower), 239.3 / 235.5 / **162.8** at 8 rows, 806.5 / 797.8 / **515.3** at 32 rows. Prefill: 963.4 / 960.8 / **15220.0** at 127 rows (15.8× compiled), 3979.3 / 4306.0 / **119154.4** at 1,016 rows (27.7×), 7359.8 / 11998.9 / **240681.1** at 2,048 rows (20.1×). `beats_compiled` false: decode `slower` (the 1-row size), prefill `slower` (every size).
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Round 2 dropped this attempt and predicted nothing for it; Claude timed it anyway. Per decode step in vLLM: +0.29 ms (+5.4%) with 1 request, −1.22 ms (−8.4%) with 8, −5.35 ms (−17.5%) with 32. Over whole requests (with routing attempt-4): throughput −10.0% / −37.5% / −48.0% / −82.5%, with prompt processing 6.63× / 14.50× / 12.50× / 13.09× slower than the unchanged engine. The fastest exact decode step measured (routing + experts: −20% with 32 requests in plain MLX) is the slowest whole request.
  - **Reason (measured).** The scalar prefill branch copies `gather_qmm_rhs`'s rounding but not its speed: every prompt chunk here has at least 128 rows, so it always runs that branch. At 1 row the fused designs plateau at 92–110 µs per layer chained against 73–87 for the compiled reference across six exact attempts — width, group count, interleave and store parallelism moved 8/32 rows and none moved 1 row by more than ~12 µs (round 2's *What building taught*).
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It passes G2 bit-exact at all six sizes, but it is slower than the compiled reference at 1 row and at every prefill size, so prompts take 6.6 to 14.5 times as long and whole requests lose 10% to 83% of throughput.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At 1 row: the ~19 µs gap to compiled is the `tg_x` load, silu, the two barriers and chained fixed cost — the down interleave proved the down waves were already hidden across simdgroups (attempt-7 notes, miss analysis). At prefill sizes: the scalar `qmm_accum` branch, 15,220 µs per layer where compiled takes 961. Per-pair weight re-reads remain at all sizes (552,960 B per pair).

#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4`

- **What it is.** One fused kernel per layer: scalar sums over the same partition/K order as MLX's three regimes (GEMV at `rows == 1`, split-K while `rows <= 768`, regular above), staged `w_router` blocks in threadgroup memory (coalesced `float4` loads, 28,080 B of 32 KB, 24 barriers on the scalar path), MLX's verbatim sigmoid, strictly-greater insertion top-4, `((w0+w1)+w2)+w3` normalise. See `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/notes.md` and `muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-2-routing-exact.md`.
- **Piece timing** (`grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`). Decode: 68.4 / 65.1 / **49.8** at 1 row, 169.2 / 135.7 / **113.5** at 8 rows, 159.3 / 145.2 / **121.3** at 32 rows — faster at every decode size. Prefill: 102.3 / 87.3 / **227.1** at 127 rows (2.6× compiled), 231.3 / 221.1 / **1298.8** at 1,016 rows (5.9×), 310.0 / 290.4 / **2513.0** at 2,048 rows (8.7×). `beats_compiled` false: decode `faster`, prefill `slower`.
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Per decode step in vLLM: −0.47 / −0.43 / −0.54 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 requests — it passed every rule of its time (faster than both the unchanged model and the compiled reference at all sizes, in both engines). Round 2 predicted −0.48 / −0.50 / −0.49 ms from the chained piece timing; the 8-request figure came in 0.07 ms short, the others match. Over whole requests: throughput +10.2% / +1.8% / +0.3% / −3.5%, with prompts 1.07–1.10× slower. Under the rule set after this measurement it fails, so it is no baseline.
  - **Reason (measured).** The staged scalar path wins at decode sizes but scales badly: 227 µs per layer at 127 rows where compiled takes 87, widening to 8.7× at 2,048 rows. The 28 KB threadgroup footprint caps residency as row counts grow.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It passes G2 bit-exact at all six sizes, but it is slower than the compiled reference at every prefill size, so prompts take 7–10% longer and whole requests with 1,024-token prompts lose 3.5%.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At prefill sizes: the staged scalar chain and its 24 barriers per row (2,513 µs per layer at 2,048 rows vs 290 compiled). At decode sizes it already beats compiled everywhere (49.8 / 113.5 / 121.3); the per-row `w_router` re-read and the serial thread-0 scan are untouched.

#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** One fused kernel per layer: thread per output element on a `rows×768` grid, volatile-barrier stepwise fold `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3` with a rounding after every op, one bfloat16 round, single-rounding bfloat16 `+ shared`. See `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1/notes.md` and `muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-3-combine-exact.md`.
- **Piece timing** (`grade-phases-combine-attempt-1.json`). Decode: 52.8 / 53.4 / **45.7** at 1 row, 71.2 / 56.4 / **47.9** at 8 rows, 87.0 / 69.1 / **64.6** at 32 rows. Prefill: 87.8 / 66.1 / **62.8** at 127 rows, 425.2 / 271.6 / **226.5** at 1,016 rows, 846.2 / 520.4 / **273.0** at 2,048 rows — faster at all six sizes. `beats_compiled` true. It is the only starting point that beats the compiled reference in both phases.
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Per decode step in vLLM: −0.37 / −0.20 / **+1.05 ms** at 1 / 8 / 32 requests. Round 2 predicted −0.36 / −0.35 / −0.35 ms; at 32 requests the sign flips. With 8 requests its median sits above the compiled reference in vLLM. Over whole requests (with routing): throughput +15.9% / +2.1% / −2.7% / −4.1%.
  - **Reason (not known).** A G3 loss of 1.05 ms is about 52 µs per layer, more than the kernel's whole chained time in the grader (64.6 µs per layer at 32 rows, of which the loss alone exceeds the kernel's work as the grader runs it). The cost comes from how the kernel sits in the step, which the grader doesn't reproduce. Round 3's first question is why.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It passes G1, G2 and `beats_compiled`, but its decode step in G3 was 1.05 ms slower than the unchanged model's with 32 requests, for a reason the grader doesn't show.
- **Where it still spends its time.** In the grader: nothing further — it sits on the chained floor (~32–40 µs per layer at decode sizes) and wins everywhere. In the step at 32 requests: the unexplained ~52 µs per layer.

#### All three together

Round 2's submission (routing + combine) changes the vLLM decode step by −0.73 / −0.74 / **+0.53 ms** at 1 / 8 / 32 requests, against a prediction of −0.84 / −0.85 / −0.84 ms: combine's slowdown outweighs routing's saving with 32 requests. Round 2's pairings run (plain MLX) found every pair within 0.5 ms of its parts' sum, but all three together with 8 requests 2.8 ms slower than their parts (+0.94 ms measured against −1.87 ms summed) — the second set of kernels to show it, so the cause is likely in how the step runs with all three slots replaced at that size, not in one kernel. Not explained. Every round-2 variant keeps the model's greedy tokens in both engines at 1 and 32 requests (round 1's change them with 32).

Round 2 ran the grader exactly once per attempt: 13 runs for 13 attempts (experts 7, routing 4, combine 2).

### What is left

Confirmed inefficiencies not yet built or not fully removed, ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar everywhere). Savings span both phases now: decode shares use the plain-MLX step denominators 4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows, prefill effects are prompt-time multiples and whole-request throughput from Claude's engine comparison. Exactness gates are solved in every slot — all three starting points pass G2 at all six sizes — so nothing below is blocked on correctness.

1. **Experts prefill path 15–28× slower than compiled.** The slot's scalar `qmm_accum` branch takes 15,220 / 119,154 / 240,681 µs per layer where compiled takes 961 / 4,306 / 11,999, and prompt processing runs 6.6 to 14.5 times slower, costing 10% to 83% of whole-request throughput. Removing it — a fast exact prefill branch, or a `max_rows` hand-off that keeps prefill-sized inputs on the compiled reference (Claude checked the hand-off bit-exact on a copy with `max_rows` 59, `results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`) — recovers the whole loss while keeping the 8/32-row decode wins (−1.22 / −5.35 ms per step). This is Claude's question 4 for round 3 (prefill half).
2. **Experts 1-row decode latency.** The starting point chains at 92.1 µs per layer against 78.6 for compiled (+13.5; G3 +0.29 ms with 1 request), the last size where it loses. Six exact fused packings plateaued at 92–110 µs; round 2's summary suggests copying the reference's unfused structure exactly for small row counts. Worth up to ~0.3 ms per step at 1 request plus unlocking `beats_compiled` on the decode phase. Claude's question 1.
3. **Routing prefill 2.6/5.9/8.7× slower than compiled.** 227 / 1,299 / 2,513 µs per layer against 87 / 221 / 290; prompts take 7–10% longer and 1,024-token-prompt requests lose 3.5% throughput. Same two outs as experts: a prefill branch that scales, or `max_rows`. Decode already wins everywhere, so the hand-off alone banks the slot if the decode win survives composition. Claude's question 4 (prefill half).
4. **Why combine attempt-1 costs ~1 ms in the step with 32 requests and not in the grader.** The chained piece timing has it faster (64.6 vs 69.1 µs per layer); G3 has it 1.05 ms slower per step. No hypothesis can bank combine until the mechanism is found — it may be a property of the kernel (grid shape, cache behaviour) or of the step around it. Claude's question 2.
5. **Why all three slots replaced at once lose 2.8 ms with 8 requests.** Every pair adds up; all three together miss by 2.8 ms in plain MLX (round 2 pairs run), repeating round 1's shape. Until it is understood, per-slot piece wins may not compose into a G3 win. Claude's question 3. Carried as a constraint on every hypothesis; the ready check measures each candidate alone and all together, so round 3 sees composition inside the round.
6. **Experts per-pair weight re-reads persist** (round 2 `ineff-baseline-experts-3`, confirmed): 908 MB read vs 443 MB distinct at 32 rows, floor 2.33 ms per step at 32 rows, 0 banked — grouped designs lost in both rounds on duty-cycle ceilings. Banks only if a grouped design holds the chained rate on distinct bytes.
7. **Routing `w_router` re-read per row** (round 2 `ineff-baseline-routing-4`, confirmed): excess floor 0 / 0.13 / 0.57 ms per step; round 1's tiled-sharing attempt was slower everywhere, and attempt-4 already wins in spite of it. Upper bound only.
8. **Prefill-only reference waste, now judged** (round 2 `ineff-quantized-kernels-1`, `-2`, confirmed): BM=16 padded tiles waste 47.1 / 15.3 / 5.2% of issued row-work at 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows, and `gather_mm_offsets` is recomputed 3× per layer (≤0.26 ms per chunk forward). Round 2 ranked these at 0 µs of decode time; under two-phase judgment they are prompt-time savings a fast prefill branch takes for free.

**Slots not yet tried.** `routing+combine` (brief: both slots, each with its own kernels, in one candidate; the grader tests each part on its own and the combine part receives the reference routing weights). Neither round has graded one `routing-combine` folder. It remains available; since the parts are graded independently it is packaging unless a shared design emerges.

**Recommendations outside the slots** stand as written in `muse-spark/round-2/summary.md` and round 2's exploration README *Recommendations*; Claude's measurement did not test them. In brief: attention K/V re-read per query head (up to ~2 ms at 32 rows); split-K partial traffic from 14 rows (≈2.4 ms upper bound at 32 rows, unmeasured); 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers + copies (−0.21 ms measured at 8 rows, `squeeze(0)` fix); ~2 ms engine CPU per 1-row step (≈0.5 ms of Python fixes); prefill tile waste and redundant `gather_mm_offsets` in MLX's `gather_qmm_rhs` (time-to-first-token only — now prompt time, item 8 above). They are for surucuonur's team; no hypothesis targets them.

### Refuted claims

No one chases these again.

- `ineff-runs-3` (round 1, refuted): the micro sorted/unsorted gaps measure per-pair vs grouped kernel choice on identically ordered pairs, not pair order — sorting serving's pairs at 8 rows cannot yield 1.3 ms, and the 32-row gap was never collected.
