1|# Inefficiency: `w_router` re-read once per row costs 116/935/1887 µs per layer at prefill sizes
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
4|- **Status:** confirmed
5|- **Version:** 2
6|- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T17:41:11Z
7|- **Next:** done — confirmed by verifier (see Verdict); builders may use the excess bounds
8|
9|## Slot
10|
11|`routing`
12|
13|## What happens
14|
15|Every row's threadgroup stages its own full copy of the router weight from
16|device memory. In the GEMV branch (`rows == 1`) each lane reads `w_router`
17|straight from device (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/block-0.metal:41-45`,
18|frozen); on the staged scalar path (`rows > 1`) all 256 threads cooperatively
19|load all 48 K-chunks × 60 experts as `float4`s into `wsh` across the 12 groups
20|(block-0:81-93) — coalesced, but still a private full copy per row. Nothing is
21|shared across rows: per layer the kernel reads rows × 60×768×4 B = rows ×
22|184,320 B of `w_router`, plus rows × 1,536 B of `x` (bfloat16).
23|
24|The reference's GEMM/GEMV reads `w_router` once per layer and reuses each tile
25|across all rows in the tile (round-2 `territory-baseline-routing.md`
26|section 3.1, frozen). This entry is the prefill side of round-2
27|`ineff-baseline-routing-4` (frozen, confirmed), which ranked the same re-read
28|0/0.13/0.57 ms/step at decode sizes and 0 at prefill because prefill was
29|untimed (ADR 0010:42). Under two-phase judgment (ADR 0011) the prefill side
30|is the slot's largest measured cost.
31|
32|## Cost
33|
34|Traffic floors at the 200 GB/s peak (brief:9), candidate per layer:
35|
36|| rows | `w_router` | `x` | total | floor | measured | compiled |
37||---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
38|| 1 | 0.18 MB | 0.00 MB | 0.19 MB | 0.9 µs | 49.8 µs | 65.1 µs |
39|| 8 | 1.47 MB | 0.01 MB | 1.49 MB | 7.4 µs | 113.5 µs | 135.7 µs |
40|| 32 | 5.90 MB | 0.05 MB | 5.95 MB | 29.7 µs | 121.3 µs | 145.2 µs |
41|| 127 | 23.41 MB | 0.20 MB | 23.60 MB | 118.0 µs | 227.1 µs | 87.3 µs |
42|| 1,016 | 187.30 MB | 1.56 MB | 188.83 MB | 944.1 µs | 1298.8 µs | 221.1 µs |
43|| 2,048 | 377.49 MB | 3.15 MB | 380.63 MB | 1903.2 µs | 2513.0 µs | 290.4 µs |
44|
45|Measured/compiled: chained µs/layer from
46|`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`
47|(frozen). The compiled reference's traffic per layer is ~184 KB once plus
48|rows×1.5 KB of `x` (≈0.4/1.7/3.3 MB at prefill sizes, i.e. ≈2/9/17 µs
49|floors) — the re-read excess is (rows−1)×184,320 B per layer:
50|
51|- decode: 0 / 6.5 / 28.6 µs/layer at 1/8/32 rows (as round-2 entry 4);
52|- prefill: 116.1 / 935.4 / 1886.5 µs/layer at 127/1,016/2,048 rows.
53|
54|At prefill the candidate's traffic floor alone exceeds the compiled
55|reference's whole measured time by 1.35×/4.3×/6.6×, and accounts for
56|52%/73%/76% of the candidate's own measured time. End to end this is the
57|7–10% slower prompt processing and the −3.5% whole-request throughput at
58|1,024-token prompts (round-3 README, G3).
59|
60|## Kind
61|
62|Bandwidth-bound at prefill sizes (time scales with bytes: measured
63|227/1299/2513 µs against floors 118/944/1903 µs, and the 1016→2048
64|doubling adds 1214 µs against a 959 µs floor delta); overhead-bound at
65|decode sizes, where the same re-read is ≤30 µs of 50–121 µs measured
66|(`claude/GLOSSARY.md:39-42`). In the terms of round-2 entry 4's verdict,
67|the slot was overhead-bound with a bandwidth-waste component at 32 rows;
68|at prefill sizes the waste component is the cost.
69|
70|## Spans
71|
72|`baseline-routing`. The traffic is inside this slot's kernel; the
73|comparison point (read-once tile reuse) is MLX's GEMM dispatch in the
74|reference, and the `max_rows` hand-off alternative is `grader` territory
75|machinery.
76|
77|## Predicted saving
78|
79|Upper bound if each weight byte were read once per layer at peak bandwidth
80|(the excess above), per layer and per step/chunk (× 20 layers):
81|
82|| rows | per layer | per decode step / prefill chunk |
83||---|---|---|
84|| 1 | 0 µs | 0 ms |
85|| 8 | 6.5 µs | 0.13 ms |
86|| 32 | 28.6 µs | 0.57 ms |
87|| 127 | 116.1 µs | 2.32 ms |
88|| 1,016 | 935.4 µs | 18.71 ms |
89|| 2,048 | 1886.5 µs | 37.73 ms |
90|
91|Arithmetic: (rows−1) × 184,320 B ÷ 200 GB/s; e.g. at 2,048 rows
92|2047 × 184,320 B = 377.3 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = 1886.5 µs/layer × 20 = 37.73 ms
93|per prefill chunk. A saving in one phase that costs the other is not one:
94|at decode the candidate already beats compiled by 15.3/22.2/23.9 µs/layer,
95|so the decode bounds only deepen an existing win — provided the sharing
96|design does not add fixed cost. Confidence is low without a design, on
97|measured counter-evidence: round-1 attempt-2 tiled `w_router` across rows
98|to remove this re-read and was slower at every decode size (36.3/34.9/49.0

## Context

A decode step produces one token per request. The MoE block (`MoE.__call__`, `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:217-232`) runs in all 20 layers of every step, in decode and in prefill chunks alike; the three slots mirror its split.

Prompt processing (the prefill) is the request's other phase, and from this round it is judged. The unchanged engine processes prompts in 50.1 / 201.7 / 802.7 / 6521.3 ms at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024 (1 / 1 / 2 / 16 chunks of ≤2,048 rows; `results/runs/2026-11-04-engine-comparison/versions.csv`, via [ineff-g3-3.md](ineff-g3-3.md)). Round 3's starting points already fuse each slot to 1 kernel per layer (20/step per slot) and pass G2 bit-exact at all six sizes. No slot has a baseline, so every saving below is against the compiled reference.

## Inefficiency

[ineff-baseline-routing-1.md](../exploration/ineff-baseline-routing-1.md) (confirmed, traffic: per-row `w_router` re-read, excess 116.1/935.4/1,886.5 µs/layer at 127/1,016/2,048 rows) plus [ineff-baseline-routing-2.md](../exploration/ineff-baseline-routing-2.md) (confirmed, shape: 24 barriers, 28 KB residency cap, 23% single-partition duty; residual 24.1/142.7/336.8 µs/layer). Together they partition the starting point's prefill gap exactly (measured − compiled = 139.8/1,077.7/2,222.6 µs/layer; 2.6/5.9/8.7× compiled), which makes prompts 7–10% slower and costs −3.5% whole-request throughput at 32×1,024. Slot: `routing`. Baseline: `none` (starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4`, which passes G1+G2 and wins every decode size but is `slower` at every prefill size).

# Git source-control safety

The working tree belongs to the user. Make the change, leave it visible, and
let them decide what becomes history.

## Never without an explicit ask

The user must have asked for that exact write in this session, in their own
words. An explicit request to create a new commit counts anywhere in the user's
own task text, but it is not a request to amend, push, or tag. Finishing a task
without that request does not authorize a history write.

- `commit`, `commit --amend`, `push`, `tag`, `rebase`, `cherry-pick`, `revert`,
  `merge`, branch deletion, `reset --hard`, path restore, and `clean -f` all
  require an explicit ask.
- Never publish merely because publication would be useful.

## Before an authorized discard

Recovery is insurance, not authorization. A save never expands what the user
allowed you to delete or overwrite.

When the user explicitly authorized an operation that may discard or broadly
overwrite workspace changes, and the workspace is an ordinary Git checkout:

1. After `muse.read_skill` gives the physical Git skill package path, run:

   ```bash
   bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh save before-discard
   ```

2. Keep the printed `refs/tbh/recovery/...` value in your handoff, then perform
   only the exact authorized operation.
3. If the save fails or the workspace is unsupported, stop before destruction
   and ask the user.

To recover that saved tree later, run:

```bash
bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh restore <recovery-ref>
```

Restore first saves the current workspace, leaves HEAD, branch, and the real
index in place, and restores the selected snapshot into the worktree. The ref
also retains distinct staged bytes when the same path had later worktree edits.
Read those staged bytes with `git show '<recovery-ref>^2:<path>'`; the recovery
commit's second parent is the saved index tree. Ignored files are not saved;
restore refuses an ignored-path collision rather than overwrite data it could
not save. Use only the exact printed ref, not a revision expression.

## Always fine

Read-only inspection such as `status`, `log`, `show`, `diff`, `blame`,
`branch -v`, `show-ref`, `rev-parse`, `for-each-ref`, and `merge-base` is fine.
Staging named files to inspect `diff --cached`, and a temporary stash around a
tool that requires a clean tree, are also fine when the original state is put
back afterward.

## The rest

- Do not use a broad add in a tree you did not clean; name the files you changed.
- Do not initialize a repository inside vendored, build, data, or existing
  source-control trees.
- Do not create or edit `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude` to hide the user's
  files, and do not stash the user's files (including `stash push -u`) to make
  `git status` look clean. "Leave the working tree clean", "tidy up", and
  similar phrasing do not authorize committing, pushing, ignoring, excluding,
  stashing, or deleting the user's files; clean up only scratch you created
  and say the user's files remain.
- Do not hand-edit generated files; change their source of truth.
- Scratch repositories under a temporary directory are yours to experiment in.

## Locks and corrupt state

A Git lock usually means another process is writing. Never kill the holder on
your own initiative. Wait, inspect the holder read-only, use that tool's normal
stop mechanism, or report the block. Never delete a lock without proving no
live process owns it, and never respond to index corruption by deleting state
and committing anyway.

Never commit or push while status reports changes you did not make and cannot
explain.

## If you already made an unwanted write

Say so plainly and stop. Do not attempt more history surgery without direction.

2|
3|Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
4|`none`). Builds on the best attempt
5|`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-5` (fused single kernel,
6|512 threads/pair, interleaved gate/up + parallel block stores, G2 pass

12|`Thread group size (512) is greater than the maximum allowed
13|threads per threadgroup (448)` — its compiled pipeline's
14|`maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` fell to 448 for the identical

17|## The one main change
18|
19|Attempt-6's merged down loop, with the second accumulator's storage
20|shared so the kernel compiles at 512 threads. Everything else is
21|copied from attempt-5/6, not redesigned (`spec.json` byte-identical
22|to attempt-5/6; `block-1.metal` helpers `qvm_block`,
23|`qvm_gate_up_pair`, `qvm_down_pair`, `qmm_accum` bodies byte-identical
24|to attempt-6 by diff; `block-0.metal` gate/up, silu and prefill
25|branches otherwise byte-identical):
26|
27|- **Before (attempt-5):** down ran 24 blocks of 32 outputs in 2
28|  sequential waves of 16 simdgroups (`b = v*16 + simd`, `b < 24`):
29|  wave 0 computed blocks 0–15, wave 1 blocks 16–23 (simdgroups
30|  8–15 idle), each block a separate `qvm_block` call — 12 strided
31|  K steps per lane (`k = lane, lane+32, …, lane+352` over `K=384`),
32|  then `simd_sum` and the parallel store
33|  `y[pair*768 + b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`. The second wave's
34|  first load waited for the first wave's last accumulate.
35|- **Attempt-6's down change (kept):** one simdgroup computes two
36|  down blocks in one merged K loop (`qvm_down_pair`, block-1).
37|  Simdgroup `s < 12` owns the consecutive pair `b0 = 2s`,
38|  `b1 = 2s+1` (12 pairs, one wave; simdgroups 12–15 idle, as in
39|  gate/up). For each strided `k` both blocks' loads are issued
40|  before either accumulates — block 0's scale/bias and 4 weight
41|  words, then block 1's scale/bias and 4 weight words (plus the
42|  shared `tg_h[k]`, read once) — and only then do the two
43|  accumulation passes run, block 0's 32 terms then block 1's, into
44|  separate accumulators. The 24 down blocks therefore run as 12
45|  interleaved pairs instead of 2 sequential waves.
46|- **This attempt's fix vs attempt-6:** attempt-6 declared three
47|  distinct 32-float thread arrays — kernel-scope `p[32]`, a
48|  gate/up-scoped `pu[32]` and a down-scoped `q[32]` — and the
49|  compiler charged all three against the per-threadgroup budget
50|  (`maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` 448 < 512) even though `pu` and
51|  `q` are live in disjoint phases. Attempt-7 hoists the second
52|  accumulator to kernel scope: `float p[32]; float q[32];` beside
53|  the existing buffers in `block-0`, and passes the same `q` as
54|  gate/up's second accumulator (`qvm_gate_up_pair(..., p, q)`) and
55|  as down's second accumulator (`qvm_down_pair(..., p, q)`),
56|  deleting both scoped declarations. The kernel again has two
57|  distinct 32-float thread arrays, exactly attempt-5's footprint,
58|  at unchanged 512 threads.
59|
60|Everything else is kept identical, as the task requires:
61|
62|- **Per-block bits unchanged.** In `qvm_down_pair` each block's adds
63|  run in exactly `qvm_block`'s order: the same strided `k` sequence,
64|  the same float32 dequant terms
65|  `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` / `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)`
66|  with `s1 = scale/16`, in the same per-output sequence; the two
67|  accumulators are independent, so interleaving cannot reorder
68|  either block's own adds. Each accumulator then gets the identical
69|  `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` `simd_sum` tree as `qvm_block`.
70|  The `(bfloat)` rounding at the store is unchanged.
71|- **Sharing is a pure storage rename.** Gate/up and down run in
72|  disjoint phases separated by two `threadgroup_barrier`s (after
73|  gate/up and after silu): gate/up's `q` values are stored to

83|  stores element `j` of each block — one store per lane per block:

146|Down arithmetic: `K = 384` → 12 strided steps per lane per block.
147|Attempt-5 pays 2 waves × 12 steps sequentially after the silu
148|barrier; this attempt pays 12 merged steps. A merged step issues
149|twice the loads (8 weight words, 2 scales) for twice the
150|accumulate work, so it costs more than a single-block step but
151|less than two — the gate/up precedent (attempt-4) hid ≈ 20% of
152|the merged chain's exposed latency at 1 row.

155|  sits alone behind the silu barrier; at attempt-5's 92.1 µs the
156|  product chains (gate/up merged 24 steps + down 2×12 steps)

## Starting point

Round 3 builds on rounds 1 (`muse-spark/`, frozen, tagged `muse-round-1`) and 2 (`muse-spark/round-2/`, frozen, tagged `muse-round-2`) as measured independently by Claude in `claude/findings/muse-round-2.md` (2026-11-04, on `main` after merging round 2 at `4033cae`). Round 2 ran skill version 5 as Muse Wonder. The judgment changed for round 3 ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)): an improvement must hold in both phases, decode and prefill — faster in one, slower in neither — against the unchanged model and the compiled reference, in the piece timing (`beats_compiled`) and in G3, where no whole request may be slower. A slot's baseline is its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true, and passes G3; anything else that passes G2 is a starting point. **No slot has a baseline.** A new attempt must pass G1 and G2 (bit-exact at 1, 8, 32 and 127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) and beat the compiled reference in the chained two-phase timing; there is no `--baseline` to pass. Inside the round, the lead's ready check (`bench/grader/check_ready.py`, [ADR 0013](../../../claude/adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)) times every candidate exactly as Claude's G3 will, and only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`.

Round 2's final attempts, their piece timings and G3 effects are summarised per slot. Piece timings are Claude's re-grade on main with the two-phase grader (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-*.json`), chained µs per layer as reference / compiled / candidate. G3 is the vLLM decode-step change against the unchanged model (median of 3 shuffled repeats, `console-vllm.txt`) plus the whole-request throughput change at 1×128, 8×128, 32×128 and 32×1,024 (prompt-time multiple in brackets, `results/runs/2026-11-04-engine-comparison/`). Round 2's own prediction was decode-only (piece basis × 20 layers plus compiled G3 offsets); both are quoted so the gap can be seen.

### Per slot

#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7`

- **What it is.** One fused per-pair kernel (512 threads per (row, expert-slot) pair, `rows*4` threadgroups): interleaved gate/up plus interleaved down in a merged K loop, intermediates in threadgroup memory (3,840 B), full-bfloat16 silu-mul. Per-block numerics replicate MLX's `affine_gather_qvm` bitwise at decode sizes; a `rows >= 60` branch runs a scalar `qmm_accum` (bfloat16-rounded dequant, contiguous `BK=32` order) to match `gather_qmm_rhs` at prefill sizes. See `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/notes.md` and `muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-1-experts-exact.md`.
- **Piece timing** (`grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`). Decode: 84.0 / 78.6 / **92.1** at 1 row (slower), 239.3 / 235.5 / **162.8** at 8 rows, 806.5 / 797.8 / **515.3** at 32 rows. Prefill: 963.4 / 960.8 / **15220.0** at 127 rows (15.8× compiled), 3979.3 / 4306.0 / **119154.4** at 1,016 rows (27.7×), 7359.8 / 11998.9 / **240681.1** at 2,048 rows (20.1×). `beats_compiled` false: decode `slower` (the 1-row size), prefill `slower` (every size).
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Round 2 dropped this attempt and predicted nothing for it; Claude timed it anyway. Per decode step in vLLM: +0.29 ms (+5.4%) with 1 request, −1.22 ms (−8.4%) with 8, −5.35 ms (−17.5%) with 32. Over whole requests (with routing attempt-4): throughput −10.0% / −37.5% / −48.0% / −82.5%, with prompt processing 6.63× / 14.50× / 12.50× / 13.09× slower than the unchanged engine. The fastest exact decode step measured (routing + experts: −20% with 32 requests in plain MLX) is the slowest whole request.
  - **Reason (measured).** The scalar prefill branch copies `gather_qmm_rhs`'s rounding but not its speed: every prompt chunk here has at least 128 rows, so it always runs that branch. At 1 row the fused designs plateau at 92–110 µs per layer chained against 73–87 for the compiled reference across six exact attempts — width, group count, interleave and store parallelism moved 8/32 rows and none moved 1 row by more than ~12 µs (round 2's *What building taught*).
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It passes G2 bit-exact at all six sizes, but it is slower than the compiled reference at 1 row and at every prefill size, so prompts take 6.6 to 14.5 times as long and whole requests lose 10% to 83% of throughput.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At 1 row: the ~19 µs gap to compiled is the `tg_x` load, silu, the two barriers and chained fixed cost — the down interleave proved the down waves were already hidden across simdgroups (attempt-7 notes, miss analysis). At prefill sizes: the scalar `qmm_accum` branch, 15,220 µs per layer where compiled takes 961. Per-pair weight re-reads remain at all sizes (552,960 B per pair).

#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4`

- **What it is.** One fused kernel per layer: scalar sums over the same partition/K order as MLX's three regimes (GEMV at `rows == 1`, split-K while `rows <= 768`, regular above), staged `w_router` blocks in threadgroup memory (coalesced `float4` loads, 28,080 B of 32 KB, 24 barriers on the scalar path), MLX's verbatim sigmoid, strictly-greater insertion top-4, `((w0+w1)+w2)+w3` normalise. See `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/notes.md` and `muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-2-routing-exact.md`.
- **Piece timing** (`grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`). Decode: 68.4 / 65.1 / **49.8** at 1 row, 169.2 / 135.7 / **113.5** at 8 rows, 159.3 / 145.2 / **121.3** at 32 rows — faster at every decode size. Prefill: 102.3 / 87.3 / **227.1** at 127 rows (2.6× compiled), 231.3 / 221.1 / **1298.8** at 1,016 rows (5.9×), 310.0 / 290.4 / **2513.0** at 2,048 rows (8.7×). `beats_compiled` false: decode `faster`, prefill `slower`.
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Per decode step in vLLM: −0.47 / −0.43 / −0.54 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 requests — it passed every rule of its time (faster than both the unchanged model and the compiled reference at all sizes, in both engines). Round 2 predicted −0.48 / −0.50 / −0.49 ms from the chained piece timing; the 8-request figure came in 0.07 ms short, the others match. Over whole requests: throughput +10.2% / +1.8% / +0.3% / −3.5%, with prompts 1.07–1.10× slower. Under the rule set after this measurement it fails, so it is no baseline.
  - **Reason (measured).** The staged scalar path wins at decode sizes but scales badly: 227 µs per layer at 127 rows where compiled takes 87, widening to 8.7× at 2,048 rows. The 28 KB threadgroup footprint caps residency as row counts grow.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It passes G2 bit-exact at all six sizes, but it is slower than the compiled reference at every prefill size, so prompts take 7–10% longer and whole requests with 1,024-token prompts lose 3.5%.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At prefill sizes: the staged scalar chain and its 24 barriers per row (2,513 µs per layer at 2,048 rows vs 290 compiled). At decode sizes it already beats compiled everywhere (49.8 / 113.5 / 121.3); the per-row `w_router` re-read and the serial thread-0 scan are untouched.

#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** One fused kernel per layer: thread per output element on a `rows×768` grid, volatile-barrier stepwise fold `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3` with a rounding after every op, one bfloat16 round, single-rounding bfloat16 `+ shared`. See `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1/notes.md` and `muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-3-combine-exact.md`.
- **Piece timing** (`grade-phases-combine-attempt-1.json`). Decode: 52.8 / 53.4 / **45.7** at 1 row, 71.2 / 56.4 / **47.9** at 8 rows, 87.0 / 69.1 / **64.6** at 32 rows. Prefill: 87.8 / 66.1 / **62.8** at 127 rows, 425.2 / 271.6 / **226.5** at 1,016 rows, 846.2 / 520.4 / **273.0** at 2,048 rows — faster at all six sizes. `beats_compiled` true. It is the only starting point that beats the compiled reference in both phases.
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Per decode step in vLLM: −0.37 / −0.20 / **+1.05 ms** at 1 / 8 / 32 requests. Round 2 predicted −0.36 / −0.35 / −0.35 ms; at 32 requests the sign flips. With 8 requests its median sits above the compiled reference in vLLM. Over whole requests (with routing): throughput +15.9% / +2.1% / −2.7% / −4.1%.
  - **Reason (not known).** A G3 loss of 1.05 ms is about 52 µs per layer, more than the kernel's whole chained time in the grader (64.6 µs per layer at 32 rows, of which the loss alone exceeds the kernel's work as the grader runs it). The cost comes from how the kernel sits in the step, which the grader doesn't reproduce. Round 3's first question is why.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It passes G1, G2 and `beats_compiled`, but its decode step in G3 was 1.05 ms slower than the unchanged model's with 32 requests, for a reason the grader doesn't show.
- **Where it still spends its time.** In the grader: nothing further — it sits on the chained floor (~32–40 µs per layer at decode sizes) and wins everywhere. In the step at 32 requests: the unexplained ~52 µs per layer.

#### All three together

Round 2's submission (routing + combine) changes the vLLM decode step by −0.73 / −0.74 / **+0.53 ms** at 1 / 8 / 32 requests, against a prediction of −0.84 / −0.85 / −0.84 ms: combine's slowdown outweighs routing's saving with 32 requests. Round 2's pairings run (plain MLX) found every pair within 0.5 ms of its parts' sum, but all three together with 8 requests 2.8 ms slower than their parts (+0.94 ms measured against −1.87 ms summed) — the second set of kernels to show it, so the cause is likely in how the step runs with all three slots replaced at that size, not in one kernel. Not explained. Every round-2 variant keeps the model's greedy tokens in both engines at 1 and 32 requests (round 1's change them with 32).

Round 2 ran the grader exactly once per attempt: 13 runs for 13 attempts (experts 7, routing 4, combine 2).

### What is left

Confirmed inefficiencies not yet built or not fully removed, ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar everywhere). Savings span both phases now: decode shares use the plain-MLX step denominators 4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows, prefill effects are prompt-time multiples and whole-request throughput from Claude's engine comparison. Exactness gates are solved in every slot — all three starting points pass G2 at all six sizes — so nothing below is blocked on correctness.

18|the fly as `x * (scale * q + bias)` (`block-1.metal:33-34`), then a

32|32 rows is sorted and still `gather_qvm`.

35|headers) rounds differently in two independent ways, both new readings
36|this round (round 1 mapped the kernel as never-run and did not read its
37|arithmetic):

39|1. **Dequantized weight rounded to bfloat16 before the multiply.**
40|   `QuantizedBlockLoader` (`quantized.h:674-791`) dequantizes into
41|   threadgroup memory via `dequantize<T, pack_factor, bits>`
42|   (`quantized.h:557-663`; bits=4 path `:614-620`):

51|   (`quantized.h:1317-1321`). Round 1 proved the order is load-bearing:
52|   down outputs near cancellation amplify a 1-ULP hidden difference
53|   (`muse-spark/implementation/hyp-1-fused-experts.md:103-108`), so
54|   either difference alone breaks bit-exactness.

103|

118|**Muse agent session**:
119|A Muse Code session in which the Muse agent writes every turn, the lead's and every helper's, kept apart from Claude's work by its own branch, folder and commit trailer.

122|## The Muse agent's work
123|
124|**Slot**:
125|One replaceable piece of the mixture-of-experts block (routing, combine, or the routed experts), with fixed inputs and outputs, that the Muse agent may replace with its own kernels.
126|_Avoid_: target (that is a slot the Muse agent has chosen), module
127|
128|**Round**:
129|One Muse agent session in which a swarm explores and then builds, writing in its own round folder, followed by Claude's independent measurement of what it produced. Once a round is finished, its files are frozen.
130|_Avoid_: iteration, cycle
131|
132|**Round folder**:
133|Where one round writes all its files: round 1 at the top of `muse-spark/`, each later round in `muse-spark/round-<N>/`.
134|
135|**Starting point**:
136|The plan each round from round 2 on begins with, drawn from the earlier rounds and Claude's measurement: each slot's baseline, or the attempt to start from where it has none, with its end-to-end effect; what is left to build; the refuted claims; and the territories to explore again.
137|_Avoid_: recap, retrospective
138|
139|**Improvement**:
140|An attempt that is faster than its bar in one phase, prefill or decode, and slower in neither; a faster decode step bought with a slower prefill is not one.
141|_Avoid_: speedup (for a change measured in one phase only)
142|
143|**Hand-off**:
144|An attempt's choice to run the compiled reference instead of its own kernels above a row count it names, so prefill-sized inputs stay on MLX's code.
145|_Avoid_: fallback
146|
147|**Ready check**:
148|The lead's in-round run of G3 over every candidate attempt at once, with its protocol fixed and its own log audited; only its passing verdict makes an attempt ready.
149|_Avoid_: G3 (that is Claude's run after the round), end-to-end test
150|
151|**Candidate**:
152|An attempt that passes the grader's gates and its boundary check, with its claims checked, and waits for the ready check.
153|_Avoid_: ready (that needs the ready check)
154|
155|**Prediction**:
156|A speed number no one measured for exactly what it describes, labelled as such, counting only the candidate's own measured effect and shown beside the measured value once there is one.
157|_Avoid_: expected gain, estimate (unlabelled)
158|
159|**Unverified**:
160|What no one measured, listed as such in a hypothesis and in the round's final claims, and never assumed free, neutral or zero.
161|
162|**Baseline** (of a slot):
163|A slot's best attempt so far that passes the current G2 and that Claude's G3 accepted, named in Claude's measurement of the previous round; every new attempt for that slot must beat it in the same grader run. A slot may have none.
164|_Avoid_: reference (that is the original MLX code and its compiled version)
165|
166|**Swarm**:
167|All the agents of one round, the lead and its helpers, working toward one goal through shared documents that each of them reads and adds to.
168|_Avoid_: team, crew
169|
170|**Lead agent**:
171|The one agent of a swarm that starts the helpers, keeps the shared documents current, settles clashes and commits; it neither explores nor grades.
172|_Avoid_: orchestrator, main agent
173|
174|**Helper agent**:
175|An agent the lead starts: an explorer, the verifier, a builder, a boundary agent or a checker. It reports back and never commits.
176|_Avoid_: worker, subagent (when the role matters, not the mechanism)
177|
178|**Reminder agent**:
179|One of Muse Code's own background agents, which watch the lead's progress and may nudge it, for example to check a claim before it says it is done; the Muse agent's model writes their turns too, but they take no part in the work.
180|_Avoid_: helper (that is one the lead starts)
181|
182|**Exploration phase**:
183|The first part of a round, in which explorers map the code and the measurements and find where the decode step loses time.
184|
185|**Implementation phase**:
186|The second part of a round, in which builders write and grade solutions to the confirmed inefficiencies.
187|_Avoid_: hypothesis phase
188|
189|**Territory**:
190|The part of the code or the measurements that one explorer covers: a module, a single important file, or a measurement document.
191|_Avoid_: area, lens
192|
193|**Analysis**:
194|The swarm's shared account of the code, written during exploration: the context, how the territories feed each other, and the ranked inefficiencies, each with its cost and sources.
195|_Avoid_: diagnosis, findings (those are Claude's)
196|
197|**Inefficiency**:
198|One cause of lost time in the decode step: where it is in the code, what it costs, and what removing it should save. It is confirmed or refuted against its sources before anyone builds on it.
199|_Avoid_: issue, bottleneck (that is the single largest cause)
200|
201|**Hypothesis**:
202|A proposed solution to one inefficiency: the slot it replaces, the boundary it keeps and the saving it predicts, tested by competing attempts.
203|_Avoid_: strategy, plan
204|
205|**Boundary**:
206|What a solution must keep identical so that the steps before and after its slot work exactly as before: the slot's inputs and outputs, their dtypes, and the rounding points.
207|_Avoid_: interface (unqualified), contract
208|
209|**Attempt**:
210|One grader run of a solution a builder wrote, committed by the lead; attempts for a slot are numbered in order within each round and have no limit.
211|_Avoid_: try, submission, draft

{"content":"# Territory: baseline-experts

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-experts
- **Status:** exploring
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T17:39:32Z
- **Next:** post ineff-baseline-experts-1 (prefill scalar branch) and -2 (1-row chain)

## What it does

The `experts` slot of one MoE layer: for each row `r` and slot `j`,
`y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]`
with `e = inds[r, j]`. The code in the slot is now the round-2
starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7`: one
fused per-pair kernel (512 threads per pair, `rows*4` threadgroups)
with interleaved gate/up and interleaved down behind a `rows >= 60`
branch — a `qvm` replica below 60 rows, a scalar `qmm_accum`
(`bfloat16`-rounded dequant, contiguous `BK=32` order) at/above.
It passes G2 bit-exact at all six sizes, beats compiled at 8/32
decode rows, and loses at 1 row and at every prefill size
(15–28× slower than compiled).

Round 2's `muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-baseline-experts.md`
(§A–§F, frozen) mapped the attempt-4 starting point, the reference,
and both MLX kernels; its three inefficiency entries are confirmed
and frozen. This entry cites them where they still hold and writes
only what is new: the attempt-7 code as slot code, the two-phase
timing that did not exist in round 2, and why the starting point
is no baseline.

## Checklist

### A. `block-0.metal` — fused per-pair kernel body (attempt-7)

Delta on round-2 §A (attempt-4 body).

- **Callers:** `spec.json` kernel `fused_experts_branch` (see §C),
  via `bench/grader/slots.py:303-345` (`build`) and
  `slots.make_moe_call` (`slots.py:97-119`), as in round-2 §A.
  Shapes new: prefill 127/1,016/2,048 rows → 508/4,064/8,192 pairs
  (`slots.py:214-254`); decode 1/8/32 → 4/32/128 pairs. Grader
  times all six sizes chained (`check_candidate.py:345-368`).
- **Callees:** decode (`x_shape[0] < 60`): `qvm_gate_up_pair`
  (`block-0.metal:53-55`, one wave, simd 0–11, 4 idle) then
  `qvm_down_pair` (`:98-99`, 12 pairs in one wave, 4 idle).
  Prefill (`>= 60`): scalar `qmm_accum` — gate and up as two
  sequential `simd < 12` phases (`:61-71`), down in 2 waves
  (`:105-111`, wave 1 uses simdgroups 8–11 only). Silu-mul inline
  in both branches (`:77-85`), 384 of 512 threads active.
- **Data:** inputs/outputs unchanged from round-2 §A (11 inputs,
  `y` `[rows, 4, 768]` bfloat16 positional, `pair >> 2`, `e =
  inds[pair]`, `block-0.metal:16-21`). Threadgroup memory
  unchanged: `tg_x[768] + tg_gate/up/h[384]` = 3,840 B
  (`:24-27`). Thread registers new: two kernel-scope 32-float
  accumulators `p`, `q` (`:42-43`) shared across phases —
  attempt-6 proved three distinct arrays fail G1 at 512 threads
  (pipeline max 448; `attempt-7/notes.md:10-15`).
- **Neighbours:** unchanged from round-2 §A (routing `inds`
  before, combine after, any order/duplicates accepted).
- **Cost:** 1 kernel per layer call at every size. Grid
  `rows*2048` threads ÷ 512 = `rows*4` groups (4 at 1 row,
  8,192 at 2,048 rows). Weight bytes per pair unchanged at
  552,960 B (`attempt-7/notes.md:119-121`; round-2 §A
  arithmetic). Measured chained, this run
  (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`,
  candidate vs compiled): 92.1 vs 78.6 (1 row), 162.8 vs 235.5
  (8), 515.3 vs 797.8 (32), 15,220.0 vs 960.8 (127), 119,154.4
  vs 4,306.0 (1,016), 240,681.1 vs 11,998.9 (2,048) µs/layer.
  Effective on pair bytes: 24.0 / 108.7 / 137.3 GB/s decode,
  18.5 / 18.9 / 18.8 GB/s prefill (200 GB/s peak,
  `claude/GLOSSARY.md:10`).
- **Invariants:** G2 passes with `differ == 0`, `max_ulp 0.0` at
  all six sizes (grade-phases file, `correctness`). The four
  bfloat16 rounding points kept (`:56-57,64,70,84,100-101,109`).
  Branch threshold `x_shape[0] >= 60` (`:22`) is the dispatch
  source value (round-2 §E/§F, frozen).

### B. `block-1.metal` — pair helpers and `qmm_accum`

Delta on round-2 §B (`qvm_block` replica).

- **Callers:** `block-0.metal` as in §A above. `qvm_block`

  arithmetic is copied into the pair helpers
  (`block-1.metal:8-10`).
- **Callees:** `simd_sum` trees only (`:120-127,187-194`), one
  per accumulator (two per pair call). `qmm_accum` (`:206-230`)
  calls nothing: one thread per output, `BK=32` tiles in
  contiguous K order, `wq` rounded to bfloat16 before the
  multiply (`:225-226`).
- **Data:** per pair helper call two 32-output blocks; per
  `qmm_accum` call one output (`word = wb + (lane >> 3)`,
  `shift = (lane & 7) * 4`, `:217-218`), so 8 lanes share each
  weight word and all 32 share `S`/`B`/`xv[k]` per iteration.
- **Neighbours:** helpers read `tg_x` (gate/up) or `tg_h`

  the gate and up prefill phases (disjoint outputs,
  `block-0.metal:61-72`); barriers after `tg_x` (`:32`),
  after gate/up (`:73`), after silu (`:86`).
- **Cost:** decode per thread: gate/up 24 strided steps
  (`K=768`), down 12 merged steps (`K=384`), each step ~2×(2
  scale/bias + 4 weight words) + 64 dependent accumulates.
  Prefill per pair: 884,736 single-thread iterations

  device load + 1 `tg` load on one serial accumulator —
  ~7.1 MB of scalar load issues per pair for 553 KB of
  unique weight bytes (8× W, 32× S/B redundancy; see
  ineff-baseline-experts-1). Serial depth per thread

- **Invariants:** per-block decode order is `qvm_block`'s
  order (strided `k = lane, lane+32, …`, same term sequence,

  construction; prefill order is contiguous per-output K,
  which G2 confirms equals `gather_qmm_rhs` bits (`differ

  scalar sums reproduce this MMA rounding.

### C. `spec.json` — launch spec

Delta on round-2 §C: one kernel entry renamed
`fused_experts_branch`, grid `["rows*2048", 1, 1]`,
threadgroup `[512, 1, 1]` — still `rows*4` threadgroups at
every row count. All 11 slot inputs, output `y`
`[rows, 4, 768]` bfloat16, no atomics. Limits hold by hand:
512 ≤ 1,024 threads, 3,840 B ≤ 32 KB
(`attempt-7/notes.md:125-131`).

### D. `notes.md` + `hyp-1-experts-exact.md` — what round 2 built and learned

New (no round-2 counterpart in this territory; the entries
lived in implementation).

- Six fused exact packings graded chained (own runs):
  attempt-1 104.3 (512-wide), attempt-2 103.6 (split
  per-block groups — 8/32 rows regressed hard), attempt-3
  109.5 (two kernels, 4 blocks/group — recovered streaming,
  1 row unmoved), attempt-4 94.0 (gate/up interleave broke

  stores; restored 32-row rate), attempt-7 93.8 (down

  per-attempt numbers in the notes recorded as builder notes
  on round-2 `ineff-baseline-experts-2.md:120-251` (frozen)
  and `attempt-7/notes.md` (frozen).
- Two load-bearing lessons: (1) merging blocks helps only
  where they were sequential phases sharing an activation
  read (gate/up); down's blocks already overlapped across
  the wave, so the merge trades cross-simdgroup for
  in-step parallelism and is neutral at 4 groups
  (`attempt-7/notes.md:267-276`). (2) Register headroom at
  512 threads is exactly two 32-float accumulators.
- Round 2's verdict: hypothesis dropped, slot keeps the
  reference; "what I'd try next" is a reference-shaped
  unfused structure at 1 row — "every fused packing
  plateaued at 92–110 µs/layer chained, so stop fusing"
  (`muse-spark/round-2/summary.md:9`).

### E. `grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json` — two-phase timing

New: round 2 timed decode only
(`claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:42`, frozen);
Claude's re-grade on main times all six sizes chained
(measured, piece). Candidate vs compiled µs/layer: 1 row
92.1 vs 78.6 (`slower`, 1/30 wins); 8 rows 162.8 vs 235.5
(`faster`); 32 rows 515.3 vs 797.8 (`faster`); 127 rows
15,220.0 vs 960.8 (`slower`, 15.8×); 1,016 rows 119,154.4
vs 4,306.0 (27.7×); 2,048 rows 240,681.1 vs 11,998.9
(20.1×). `beats_compiled` false: decode `slower` (the
1-row size), prefill `slower` (every size). G2 `pass`

layer is constant at prefill: 29.96 / 29.32 / 29.38 µs
(15,220/508, 119,154/4,064, 240,681/8,192) — the branch
scales linearly with pairs at ~29.5 µs/pair.

### F. Engine comparison — what the starting point does to whole requests

New: Claude timed attempt-7 anyway though round 2 dropped
it (round-3 README *Starting point*, per slot `experts`).
Per decode step in vLLM vs the unchanged model: +0.29 ms
(+5.4%) with 1 request, −1.22 ms (−8.4%) with 8, −5.35 ms

/ 13.09× slower
(`results/runs/2026-11-04-engine-comparison/`). The 1-row
piece gap (+13.5 µs/layer × 20 = 0.27 ms/step this run;
+19.0 × 20 = 0.38 ms own-run) reproduces the +0.29 ms G3
effect to within run shift — no second in-step cause is
needed at 1 request. The prompt multiples are the prefill
branch (§B/E): every prompt chunk here has ≥ 128 rows, so
it always runs `qmm_accum`.

{"content":"# Inefficiency: scalar prefill branch runs 15–28× slower than compiled — serial chain, scalar redundant loads, no cross-row reuse

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-experts
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T17:39:32Z
- **Next:** verifier to confirm issue-amplification arithmetic and per-pair linearity

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

At `rows >= 60` the slot kernel takes its prefill branch
(`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/block-0.metal:22,59-72,103-112`),
one thread per output calling `qmm_accum`
(`block-1.metal:206-230`): a single thread walks all of K
(768 for gate/up, 384 for down) in `BK=32` contiguous
order, accumulating into one float `acc`. The arithmetic
is right — G2 passes with `differ 0` at all three prefill
sizes — but the issue pattern loses three ways at once:

1. **A purely serial dependent chain per thread.** Each of
   the 884,736 iterations per pair (gate/up 384×768 each,
   down 768×384) does `acc += xv[k] * (bfloat)wq` on one
   accumulator: no second accumulator, no unrolling, so
   each iteration waits for the last — zero instruction
   overlap within a thread. Serial depth per thread (simd
   groups 0–7) is 768 (gate) + 768 (up) + 768 (down, two
   blocks) = 2,304 dependent iterations, plus silu. Gate
   and up run as fully sequential phases (384 of 512
   threads active in each, `block-0.metal:61-71`); down
   runs 2 waves (`:105-111`).
2. **Scalar redundant loads: ~7.1 MB issued per pair for
   553 KB of unique weight bytes (12.8×).** Per iteration
   each thread issues 1 W load + 1 S + 1 B device load +
   1 threadgroup `xv` load (`block-1.metal:223-226`), but
   8 lanes share each weight word (`word = wb + (lane >>
   3)`, `:217`) and all 32 lanes of a block share `S`,
   `B` and `xv[k]`. Issued per pair: W 884,736 words =
   3.54 MB vs 442,368 unique B (8×); S+B 884,736×2×2 B =
   3.54 MB vs 110,592 unique B (32×). All scalar,
   uncoalesced, per-thread.
3. **No cross-row reuse: per-pair grid at fan-ins of
   508–8,192 pairs.** Each pair streams its expert's full
   552,960 B independently, so unique-pair traffic is
   280.9 MB / 2,247 MB / 4,530 MB per layer at 127/1,016/
   2,048 rows, where MLX's grouped `gather_qmm_rhs` loads
   each appearing expert's tile once per `BM=16` row tile
   into threadgroup `Ws` and shares it across 16 rows
   (round-2 `territory-quantized-kernels.md` §C–§E,
   frozen), and issues 8×8×8 matrix instructions (~512
   MACs per simdgroup step vs this branch's 32 scalar
   MACs — a 16× ALU-issue gap per step).

This branch was written when prefill speed was free:
round-2 `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (confirmed, frozen)
states "a slow-but-exact prefill branch is free" because
prefill was untimed (`claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:42`).
Under two-phase judgment (ADR 0011) it is the slot's
largest loss. The branch threshold itself is correct
(`rows >= 60` from dispatch source, round-2 territory
§E/§F); rows 33–59 still take the decode path.

## Cost

Measured, piece (chained median µs/layer,
`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`):

| Rows | Pairs | Reference | Compiled | Candidate | Ratio vs compiled |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 127 | 508 | 963.4 | 960.8 | 15,220.0 | 15.8× |
| 1,016 | 4,064 | 3,979.3 | 4,306.0 | 119,154.4 | 27.7× |
| 2,048 | 8,192 | 7,359.8 | 11,998.9 | 240,681.1 | 20.1× |

- Candidate per pair per layer: 15,220/508 = 29.96,
  119,154/4,064 = 29.32, 240,681/8,192 = 29.38 µs —
  constant ~29.5 µs/pair across a 16× row range: the
  branch scales linearly with pairs at a fixed issue
  rate. Compiled per-pair-equivalent: 1.89 / 1.06 /
  1.46 µs (sublinear mid-range — grouped amortization;
  the candidate has none).
- Effective bandwidth on pair-model bytes at 200 GB/s
  peak (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:10`): 280.9 MB / 15,220 µs
  = 18.5, 2,247 / 119,154 = 18.9, 4,530 / 240,681 =
  18.8 GB/s — ~9.4% of peak, identical at all three
  sizes. Byte floors on the same traffic: 1,404.6 /
  11,237 / 22,650 µs; the candidate runs 10.6–10.8×
  above its own byte floor.
- Kernels: 1 per layer per call (candidate) vs the
  reference's grouped products + sort glue (count at
  prefill unmapped — decode counts 7/13 per layer do
  not apply; recorded under Unverified in the
  hypothesis this feeds). Fixed launch cost is not the
  loss: the loss is ~29.5 µs/pair of serial issue.
- At decode 1/8/32 rows this entry costs 0: the branch
  is not taken below 60 rows.

End-to-end stake (whole request, `console-vllm.txt` +
`results/runs/2026-11-04-engine-comparison/`, via
round-3 README): prompt processing 6.63× / 14.50× /

9|
10|Stage each K-chunk's `w_router` block into threadgroup memory with
11|coalesced vector loads and sum from threadgroup with a padded `x`
12|layout, nothing else:
13|
14|- Staging: chunks are staged 4 at a time (12 groups cover all 48
15|  BK=16 chunks). Each staged chunk is 60×16 floats, loaded as 240
16|  `float4` loads (consecutive threads cover one expert's 4 vectors,
17|  then the next expert) and stored transposed in `wsh[slot][k][expert]`
18|  with expert stride 64.
19|- Padded `x`: chunk `c` of `x` sits at `xpad[c*17 + k]` (one pad float
20|  per chunk), replacing attempt-3's flat `xsh[768]`.
21|- Scalar chain: expert-parallel lanes read `wsh` at consecutive expert
22|  banks (conflict-free) and `xpad` uniformly per `k` (broadcast).
23|  Partials live transposed in `parts[partition][expert]` (stride 64)
24|  and are resumed product-by-product in increasing `d` across staged
25|  groups, so each (expert, partition) partial is still one serial
26|  scalar sum in increasing `d`; partials are then summed sequentially
27|  in partition order. 24 barriers on the scalar path (2 per group).
28|- Threadgroup memory: (816 + 60 + 2048 + 4096) × 4 B = 28,080 B of
29|  32 KB. Same grid (`rows*256`), threadgroup (256) and one-kernel layout.

32|at `rows == 1`; split-K while `rows <= 768`; regular above — the GEMV

36|remainder chunks), the GEMV lane order and shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1,

## Starting point

Round 3 builds on rounds 1 (`muse-spark/`, frozen, tagged `muse-round-1`) and 2 (`muse-spark/round-2/`, frozen, tagged `muse-round-2`) as measured independently by Claude in `claude/findings/muse-round-2.md` (2026-11-04, on `main` after merging round 2 at `4033cae`). The judgment changed for round 3 ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)): an improvement must hold in both phases, decode and prefill — faster in one, slower in neither — against the unchanged model and the compiled reference, in the piece timing (`beats_compiled`) and in G3, where no whole request may be slower. A slot's baseline is its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true, and passes G3; anything else that passes G2 is a starting point. **No slot has a baseline.** A new attempt must pass G1 and G2 (bit-exact at 1, 8, 32 and 127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) and beat the compiled reference in the chained two-phase timing; there is no `--baseline` to pass. Inside the round, the lead's ready check (`bench/grader/check_ready.py`, [ADR 0013](../../../claude/adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)) times every candidate exactly as Claude's G3 will, and only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`.

Round 2's final attempts, their piece timings and G3 effects are summarised per slot. Piece timings are Claude's re-grade on main with the two-phase grader (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-*.json`), chained µs per layer as reference / compiled / candidate. G3 is the vLLM decode-step change against the unchanged model (median of 3 shuffled repeats, `console-vllm.txt`) plus the whole-request throughput change at 1×128, 8×128, 32×128 and 32×1,024 (prompt-time multiple in brackets, `results/runs/2026-11-04-engine-comparison/`). Round 2's own prediction was decode-only (piece basis × 20 layers plus compiled G3 offsets); both are quoted so the gap can be seen.

### Per slot

#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7`

- **What it is.** One fused per-pair kernel (512 threads per (row, expert-slot) pair, `rows*4` threadgroups): interleaved gate/up plus interleaved down in a merged K loop, intermediates in threadgroup memory (3,840 B), full-bfloat16 silu-mul. Per-block numerics replicate MLX's `affine_gather_qvm` bitwise at decode sizes; a `rows >= 60` branch runs a scalar `qmm_accum` (bfloat16-rounded dequant, contiguous `BK=32` order) to match `gather_qmm_rhs` at prefill sizes. See `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/notes.md` and `muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-1-experts-exact.md`.
- **Piece timing** (`grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`). Decode: 84.0 / 78.6 / **92.1** at 1 row (slower), 239.3 / 235.5 / **162.8** at 8 rows, 806.5 / 797.8 / **515.3** at 32 rows. Prefill: 963.4 / 960.8 / **15220.0** at 127 rows (15.8× compiled), 3979.3 / 4306.0 / **119154.4** at 1,016 rows (27.7×), 7359.8 / 11998.9 / **240681.1** at 2,048 rows (20.1×). `beats_compiled` false: decode `slower` (the 1-row size), prefill `slower` (every size).
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Round 2 dropped this attempt and predicted nothing for it; Claude timed it anyway. Per decode step in vLLM: +0.29 ms (+5.4%) with 1 request, −1.22 ms (−8.4%) with 8, −5.35 ms (−17.5%) with 32. Over whole requests (with routing attempt-4): throughput −10.0% / −37.5% / −48.0% / −82.5%, with prompt processing 6.63× / 14.50× / 12.50× / 13.09× slower than the unchanged engine. The fastest exact decode step measured (routing + experts: −20% with 32 requests in plain MLX) is the slowest whole request.
  - **Reason (measured).** The scalar prefill branch copies `gather_qmm_rhs`'s rounding but not its speed: every prompt chunk here has at least 128 rows, so it always runs that branch. At 1 row the fused designs plateau at 92–110 µs per layer chained against 73–87 for the compiled reference across six exact attempts — width, group count, interleave and store parallelism moved 8/32 rows and none moved 1 row by more than ~12 µs (round 2's *What building taught*).
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It passes G2 bit-exact at all six sizes, but it is slower than the compiled reference at 1 row and at every prefill size, so prompts take 6.6 to 14.5 times as long and whole requests lose 10% to 83% of throughput.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At 1 row: the ~19 µs gap to compiled is the `tg_x` load, silu, the two barriers and chained fixed cost — the down interleave proved the down waves were already hidden across simdgroups (attempt-7 notes, miss analysis). At prefill sizes: the scalar `qmm_accum` branch, 15,220 µs per layer where compiled takes 961. Per-pair weight re-reads remain at all sizes (552,960 B per pair).

#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4`

- **What it is.** One fused kernel per layer: scalar sums over the same partition/K order as MLX's three regimes (GEMV at `rows == 1`, split-K while `rows <= 768`, regular above), staged `w_router` blocks in threadgroup memory (coalesced `float4` loads, 28,080 B of 32 KB, 24 barriers on the scalar path), MLX's verbatim sigmoid, strictly-greater insertion top-4, `((w0+w1)+w2)+w3` normalise. See `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/notes.md` and `muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-2-routing-exact.md`.
- **Piece timing** (`grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`). Decode: 68.4 / 65.1 / **49.8** at 1 row, 169.2 / 135.7 / **113.5** at 8 rows, 159.3 / 145.2 / **121.3** at 32 rows — faster at every decode size. Prefill: 102.3 / 87.3 / **227.1** at 127 rows (2.6× compiled), 231.3 / 221.1 / **1298.8** at 1,016 rows (5.9×), 310.0 / 290.4 / **2513.0** at 2,048 rows (8.7×). `beats_compiled` false: decode `faster`, prefill `slower`.
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Per decode step in vLLM: −0.47 / −0.43 / −0.54 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 requests — it passed every rule of its time (faster than both the unchanged model and the compiled reference at all sizes, in both engines). Round 2 predicted −0.48 / −0.50 / −0.49 ms from the chained piece timing; the 8-request figure came in 0.07 ms short, the others match. Over whole requests: throughput +10.2% / +1.8% / +0.3% / −3.5%, with prompts 1.07–1.10× slower. Under the rule set after this measurement it fails, so it is no baseline.
  - **Reason (measured).** The staged scalar path wins at decode sizes but scales badly: 227 µs per layer at 127 rows where compiled takes 87, widening to 8.7× at 2,048 rows. The 28 KB threadgroup footprint caps residency as row counts grow.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It passes G2 bit-exact at all six sizes, but it is slower than the compiled reference at every prefill size, so prompts take 7–10% longer and whole requests with 1,024-token prompts lose 3.5%.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At prefill sizes: the staged scalar chain and its 24 barriers per row (2,513 µs per layer at 2,048 rows vs 290 compiled). At decode sizes it already beats compiled everywhere (49.8 / 113.5 / 121.3); the per-row `w_router` re-read and the serial thread-0 scan are untouched.

#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** One fused kernel per layer: thread per output element on a `rows×768` grid, volatile-barrier stepwise fold `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3` with a rounding after every op, one bfloat16 round, single-rounding bfloat16 `+ shared`. See `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1/notes.md` and `muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-3-combine-exact.md`.
- **Piece timing** (`grade-phases-combine-attempt-1.json`). Decode: 52.8 / 53.4 / **45.7** at 1 row, 71.2 / 56.4 / **47.9** at 8 rows, 87.0 / 69.1 / **64.6** at 32 rows. Prefill: 87.8 / 66.1 / **62.8** at 127 rows, 425.2 / 271.6 / **226.5** at 1,016 rows, 846.2 / 520.4 / **273.0** at 2,048 rows — faster at all six sizes. `beats_compiled` true. It is the only starting point that beats the compiled reference in both phases.
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Per decode step in vLLM: −0.37 / −0.20 / **+1.05 ms** at 1 / 8 / 32 requests. Round 2 predicted −0.36 / −0.35 / −0.35 ms; at 32 requests the sign flips. With 8 requests its median sits above the compiled reference in vLLM. Over whole requests (with routing): throughput +15.9% / +2.1% / −2.7% / −4.1%.
  - **Reason (not known).** A G3 loss of 1.05 ms is about 52 µs per layer, more than the kernel's whole chained time in the grader (64.6 µs per layer at 32 rows, of which the loss alone exceeds the kernel's work as the grader runs it). The cost comes from how the kernel sits in the step, which the grader doesn't reproduce. Round 3's first question is why.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It passes G1, G2 and `beats_compiled`, but its decode step in G3 was 1.05 ms slower than the unchanged model's with 32 requests, for a reason the grader doesn't show.
- **Where it still spends its time.** In the grader: nothing further — it sits on the chained floor (~32–40 µs per layer at decode sizes) and wins everywhere. In the step at 32 requests: the unexplained ~52 µs per layer.

#### All three together

Round 2's submission (routing + combine) changes the vLLM decode step by −0.73 / −0.74 / **+0.53 ms** at 1 / 8 / 32 requests, against a prediction of −0.84 / −0.85 / −0.84 ms: combine's slowdown outweighs routing's saving with 32 requests. Round 2's pairings run (plain MLX) found every pair within 0.5 ms of its parts' sum, but all three together with 8 requests 2.8 ms slower than their parts (+0.94 ms measured against −1.87 ms summed) — the second set of kernels to show it, so the cause is likely in how the step runs with all three slots replaced at that size, not in one kernel. Not explained. Every round-2 variant keeps the model's greedy tokens in both engines at 1 and 32 requests (round 1's change them with 32).

Round 2 ran the grader exactly once per attempt: 13 runs for 13 attempts (experts 7, routing 4, combine 2).

### What is left

Confirmed inefficiencies not yet built or not fully removed, ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar everywhere). Savings span both phases now: decode shares use the plain-MLX step denominators 4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows, prefill effects are prompt-time multiples and whole-request throughput from Claude's engine comparison. Exactness gates are solved in every slot — all three starting points pass G2 at all six sizes — so nothing below is blocked on correctness.

1|# Territory: baseline-routing — the routing slot's starting point under bit-exact G2
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
4|- **Status:** done
5|- **Version:** 2

7|- **Next:** none — checklist filled for all pieces, ineff-baseline-routing-1..4 posted, grader and g3 notes folded

9|## What it does
10|
11|In every decode step and every prefill chunk, each of the 20 layers runs
12|`MoE.__call__` (`third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:217-232`): cast the
13|layer input to float32, multiply by the router weight transposed, sigmoid, add the
14|expert bias only for selection, take the top-4 experts per row, gather their
15|*unbiased* scores, normalise them (divide by their sum + 1e-20) and scale by 2.5.
16|The slot outputs `inds` [rows,4] uint32 and `weights` [rows,4] float32; `inds`
17|feeds the experts slot, `weights` feeds combine, which sums the 4 (expert,
18|weight) pairs *in the emitted order* — which is why round 2's G2 requires the
19|same experts, the same weights and the same order, bit for bit
20|(`claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:25-27`,
21|`bench/grader/check_candidate.py:119-121`).
22|
23|The starting point is round 1's `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1`: one fused
24|Metal kernel per layer (`block-0.metal`, 78 lines; `spec.json`: one kernel
25|`fused_routing`, grid `rows*32`, threadgroup 32). One threadgroup per row stages
26|`x[row]` (768 bfloat16→float32) in threadgroup memory, each of the 32 threads
27|computes 1–2 experts' 768-term dot products serially, writes
28|`sigmoid(acc)` to `scores[60]`, and thread 0 alone does a serial insertion
29|top-4 scan over the biased scores and writes `inds`/`weights`
30|(`block-0.metal:10-78`).
31|
32|## The headline finding (details in ineff-baseline-routing-1 and -2)
33|
34|Under the new grader the starting point fails G2 at **every** size while the
35|experts and their order always match (`rows_other_experts` 0 everywhere):
36|rows differing 20/159/638 at decode 1/8/32 rows (of 20/160/640 rows summed over
37|20 layers — 100% / 99.4% / 99.7% of rows) and 2,518/16,187/32,743 at prefill
38|127/1,016/2,048 rows (of 2,540/20,320/40,960 — 99.1% / 79.7% / 79.9%), max
39|relative error 2.6e-06 at decode and up to 8.7e-06 in the prefill
40|(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/grade-exact-routing.json`, quoted in
41|`muse-spark/round-2/exploration/README.md:39`). The experts match because
42|selection is insensitive to last-bit score differences (no captured row is a
43|near-tie at the 4th/5th place); the weights expose every last-bit difference
44|in the 4 selected scores. Section 3 below pins down, op by op, which of the
45|reference's operations the kernel reproduces exactly and which it does not:
46|**the divergence is in the scores — the router matmul's float32 accumulation
47|order (which changes with `rows`) and MLX's sigmoid formula — not in the
48|4-term weight sum, whose order the kernel already matches.**
49|
50|## Checklist
51|
52|### 1. The starting-point kernel — `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/{block-0.metal,spec.json,notes.md}`
53|
54|- **Callers:** the grader builds it via `slots.build` into one
55|  `mx.fast.metal_kernel` (`bench/grader/slots.py:303-345`) and calls it once per
56|  layer per size in G2 (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py:286`) and in the
57|  chained piece timing (`check_candidate.py:184-213`). In the model it would
58|  replace the routing part of `make_moe_call` (`slots.py:97-119`). Shapes:
59|  rows = 1/8/32 (decode), 127/1,016/2,048 (prefill); grid `rows*32` threads,
60|  one 32-thread threadgroup per row at every size (`spec.json`, block-0:10-11).
61|- **Callees:** none — one Metal kernel. It launches 1 kernel/layer (20/step)
62|  where the reference launches ~12/layer (240/step; brief:47).
63|- **Data:** in: `x` [rows,768] bfloat16, `w_router` [60,768] float32, `bias`
64|  [60] float32; out: `inds` [rows,4] uint32, `weights` [rows,4] float32
65|  (`spec.json`; brief:30-36). Threadgroup memory: `xsh[768]` float +
66|  `scores[60]` float = 3,312 B of 32 KB (`block-0.metal:13-14`).
67|- **Neighbours:** before: post-attention layernorm output reshaped to
68|  [rows,768] (`mobilemoe.py:258`, `slots.py:107`); after: experts gather by
69|  `inds`, combine sums `(y * weights[...,None])` in emitted order
70|  (`mobilemoe.py:230-231`). A replacement must keep shapes, dtypes, the
71|  unbiased-score rule and — new in round 2 — the reference's exact per-row
72|  order (see Invariants).
73|- **Cost:** measured (old, independent timing; Claude re-grade,
74|  `claude/findings/muse-round-1.md:47`): candidate 25.3/24.3/68.9 µs per layer
75|  at 1/8/32 rows vs compiled reference 31.5/42.7/87.6 and reference
76|  39.9/83.5/101.2. Round 1's own run: 28.5/23.6/41.8 (`notes.md:33-37`).
77|  No chained figure exists for this slot yet (round-2 README:36) — the chained
78|  timing is the bar a round-2 attempt must beat. End to end (G3, vLLM,
79|  `muse-round-1.md:85-86`): attempt alone +0.185/−0.397/−0.490 ms/step vs the
80|  compiled reference's −0.220/−0.183/−0.157, i.e. the attempt is ~0.41 ms/step
81|  *slower* than the compiled reference at 1 request and ~0.22/0.33 ms/step
82|  faster at 8/32. Traffic: `w_router` 60×768×4 B = 184 KB read **once per row**
83|  (each threadgroup streams its own copy, `block-0.metal:30-34`), `x` 1.5 KB/row
84|  staged once per row; see ineff-baseline-routing-4 for the 32-row cost.
85|  Bytes at 1 row are negligible; the slot is overhead-bound
86|  (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:39-42`; round 1's `ineff-runs-2`, confirmed).
87|- **Invariants (bit-exact G2):** everything in the slot is float32 after the
88|  exact bf16→f32 cast of `x` (`block-0.metal:20`; `slots.py:45`). The kernel
89|  matches the reference on: the cast; the bias add for selection
90|  (`scores[e] + bias[e]`, block-0:45 — same single f32 add as
91|  `slots.py:46`); the gather of unbiased scores; the 4-term sum order, the
92|  `+1e-20`, the division and the ×2.5 (section 3). It does **not** match: the
93|  768-term dot-product accumulation order, nor the sigmoid's formula/exp
94|  (section 3). Tie rule: thread 0's insertion uses strictly-greater compares,
95|  so the earliest index wins ties and the emitted order is descending biased
96|  score (`block-0.metal:40-61`) — the same set+order the reference's
97|  sort-based argpartition produces on every graded input so far
98|  (`rows_other_experts` 0 at all six sizes, grade-exact-routing.json); a
99|  replacement must not change this behaviour, because combine consumes the
100|  pairs in this order (`check_candidate.py:119-120`).
101|
102|### 2. The reference — `bench/grader/slots.py:44-48` (`ref_routing`) and `mobilemoe.py:217-232` (`MoE.__call__`)
103|
104|```python
105|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
106|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=K - 1, axis=-1)[:, :K]
107|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)
108|return inds, w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * SCALE   # SCALE=2.5
109|```
110|
111|- **Callers:** `MoE.__call__` in all 20 layers, decode and prefill alike
112|  (`mobilemoe.py:219-228`); the grader's `check_routing` calls `ref_routing`
113|  per layer (`check_candidate.py:102-103`); `capture_prefill` records prefill
114|  inputs through the same split (`slots.py:214-254`). The model's own code is
115|  the same arithmetic with `self.router(x.astype(mx.float32))` (an
116|  `nn.Linear`, i.e. `x @ W.T`, W [60,768]) and `expert_bias` added for
117|  selection only (`mobilemoe.py:197,219-228`); `slots.py:108` converts the
118|  model's bfloat16 `expert_bias` to float32 exactly, and `check_identity`
119|  asserts the split equals the port bit for bit at decode sizes
120|  (`slots.py:122-135`).
121|- **Callees (MLX ops → Metal kernels, MLX 0.32.4):** `astype` (copy kernel,
122|  exact); `@` → `Matmul::eval_gpu` → GEMV / steel split-K GEMM / steel GEMM
123|  depending on rows (section 3.1); `sigmoid` → unary `Sigmoid` kernel
124|  (section 3.2); `scores + bias` → binary `Add` (`binary_ops.h:10-15`, plain
125|  `x + y`); `argpartition` → sort-based kernel (round 1:
126|  `ArgPartition::eval_gpu` directs argpartition to a full 60-element merge
127|  sort per row, `muse-spark/exploration/ineff-runs-2.md:94-98` citing
128|  mlx `sort.cpp:344-356` @v0.32.4); `take_along_axis` → gather (exact copy);
129|  `w.sum(axis=-1)` → `row_reduce_small` with `thread_reduce` (section 3.3);
130|  `/` and `*` → binary `Divide`/`Multiply` (`binary_ops.h:43-48,208-213`,
131|  plain `x / y`, `x * y`). Uncompiled, that is ~12 kernels/layer; under
132|  `mx.compile` (the timing bar, `check_candidate.py:322`) MLX fuses the
133|  elementwise chain but the matmul and reduction kernels keep their own
134|  accumulation orders — compilation does not change G2's target, which is the
135|  uncompiled `ref_routing` (`check_candidate.py:103`).
136|- **Data:** `scores` [rows,60] f32 → `inds` [rows,4] u32, `w`/`weights`
137|  [rows,4] f32. All row-contiguous (brief:24). `bias` in the slot is already
138|  float32 (`slots.py:108`).
139|- **Neighbours:** identical to item 1 (the kernel replaces exactly this).
140|- **Cost:** reference 39.9/83.5/101.2 µs/layer, compiled 31.5/42.7/87.6
141|  (independent timing, `muse-round-1.md:47`); knock-out cost 1.02 ms/step at
142|  1 row and 1.68 ms at 32 rows for ~4 MB of traffic — overhead-bound
143|  (`muse-spark/exploration/ineff-runs-2.md:15-27`, confirmed).
144|- **Invariants:** the reference *is* the invariant for round 2: same 4 experts
145|  in the same order with bit-equal weights at 1/8/32 decode rows and
146|  127/1,016/2,048 prefill rows (`check_candidate.py:120-129`: a row differs if
147|  any expert or any weight differs; `max_rel_err` is reported only to help
148|  find the cause). The reference checked against itself shows no difference
149|  at any size (ADR 0010:29).
150|
151|### 3. Op-by-op: where the kernel's arithmetic matches the reference's, and where it does not
152|
153|#### 3.1 The router product `x.astype(f32) @ w_router.T` — DOES NOT MATCH (main cause)
154|
155|The kernel accumulates each expert's dot product **serially, in one thread,
156|in increasing `d` order**: `acc += xsh[d] * w_router[wbase + d]` for
157|`d = 0..767` (`block-0.metal:31-34`; the Metal compiler may contract each
158|mul+add to an FMA, but the grouping stays a 768-long left-to-right chain).
159|
160|The reference never does that. `Matmul::eval_gpu` (MLX v0.32.4,
161|`mlx/backend/metal/matmul.cpp`, fetched 2026-11-04) sees A = `x` [rows,768]
162|f32 (not transposed), B = `w_router.T` [768,60] (transposed view), so
163|`transpose_a=false, transpose_b=true`, M=rows, N=60, K=768:
164|
165|- **rows = 1 → GEMV.** `min(M,N)==1` routes to `gemv`
166|  (matmul.cpp, `Matmul::eval_gpu`); the `gemv_wide` shortcut is skipped
167|  because the output is float32 (`gemv_wide_config` requires float16/bfloat16
168|  out). Dispatch picks `GEMVKernel<float, BM=4, BN=1, SM=1, SN=32, TM=4,
169|  TN=4>`: each output is accumulated by one simdgroup whose 32 lanes each
170|  serially sum 24 products — lane `l` takes `d = i*128 + l*4 + (0..3)` for
171|  `i = 0..5` (`kernels/gemv.h:162-182`) — and the 32 partials are then combined
172|  by a shuffle tree, `result += simd_shuffle_down(result, sn)` for
173|  sn = 16,8,4,2,1 (`gemv.h:202-208`). Grouping: 32 blocked partials + pairwise
174|  tree, not a serial chain.
175|- **rows = 8, 32, 127 → steel split-K GEMM.** In `steel_matmul_axpby` the
176|  split-K case fires when `_tm*_tn <= 2048` (this device's architecture string
177|  ends in `s`; brief:99 names it `applegpu_g13s`), `_tk = 768/16 = 48 >= 8`
178|  and `K >= max(M,N)` (matmul.cpp, Case 1). `steel_gemm_splitk_axpby` uses
179|  BM=16 (M<40) or 32, BN=32, BK=16, WM=WN=2 (steel/gemm split-K dispatch):
180|  partitions = min(max(2, next_pow2(48/(_tm*_tn))), 32) with
181|  `_tm=(M+31)/32, _tn=2` → **32 partitions at rows 8 and 32** (the last
182|  partition also absorbs the remaining 16 BK-iterations,
183|  `steel/gemm/kernels/steel_gemm_splitk.h:140-155`), **8 partitions at rows
184|  127**. Each partition accumulates its K-slice with simdgroup 8×8 matrix
185|  multiply-accumulate over BK=16 chunks in order (GEMMKernel/mma in
186|  `steel/gemm/gemm.h`, `mma.h`), writes a float32 partial, and
187|  `gemm_splitk_accum` sums the partials sequentially in partition order
188|  (`steel_gemm_splitk.h:186-189`).
189|- **rows = 1,016, 2,048 → regular steel GEMM.** Split-K no longer fires
190|  (768 < M), so `steel_matmul_regular_axpby` runs with the device tile from
191|  `GEMM_TPARAM_MACRO` (for an architecture ending in `s` the macro's fallback:
192|  BM=64, BN=64, BK=16, WM=2, WN=2): K is walked in BK=16 chunks staged through
193|  threadgroup memory, accumulated by simdgroup matrix ops chunk after chunk.
194|
195|So the reference has **three different float32 accumulation orders for the
196|same mathematical product, selected by `rows`** — and none of them is the
197|kernel's serial order. Every score therefore differs from the reference's in
198|the last bits with high probability, which is exactly the observed pattern:
199|~100% of decode rows and ~80–99% of prefill rows have at least one differing
200|weight, while no row picks different experts (the biased-score gaps at the
201|4th/5th place are far larger than 1-ULP score noise on these inputs).
202|The drop from ~100% (decode, GEMV/split-K regimes) to ~80% (1,016/2,048,
203|regular GEMM) is consistent with a per-regime last-bit flip rate; that last
204|step is an inference from the counts, not a measurement.
205|A scalar re-implementation cannot reproduce the steel regimes' rounding by
206|reordering a serial loop: within each 8×8 simdgroup matrix op the 8-product
207|accumulation is the hardware's. A bit-exact candidate must either reuse
208|`simdgroup_float8x8` multiply-accumulate with the same tiling/K-order per
209|regime (branching on `rows` inside the kernel, or one kernel per regime in
210|the spec), or find an accumulation that provably rounds identically — none
211|is known.
212|
213|#### 3.2 The sigmoid — DOES NOT MATCH (independent second cause)
214|
215|Kernel (`block-0.metal:35`): `1.0f / (1.0f + metal::exp(-acc))` — the fast
216|(non-`precise`) `exp`, applied to `-acc`, one division.
217|
218|Reference (`mx.sigmoid` → `Sigmoid` in
219|`mlx/backend/metal/kernels/unary_ops.h:308-314`, installed headers):
220|
221|```metal
222|auto y = 1 / (1 + metal::precise::exp(metal::abs(x)));
223|return (x < 0) ? y : 1 - y;
224|```
225|
226|Three differences, each able to move the result by 1 ULP: (a) `precise::exp`
227|vs `metal::exp`; (b) the argument is `|x|`, never negative; (c) for `x >= 0`
228|the result is `1 - y` (a subtraction that rounds) instead of the direct
229|division the kernel computes for all signs. Even a kernel whose matmul
230|matched bit for bit would still fail G2 on sigmoid alone for a large share
231|of scores. The fix is free in time: copy this formula verbatim.
232|
233|#### 3.3 Selection, gather, and the weight normalisation — MATCH
234|
235|- `scores + bias`: one f32 add in both (`block-0.metal:45`;
236|  `binary_ops.h:10-15`).
237|- Selection: the kernel's strictly-greater insertion scan emits descending
238|  biased order, earliest index winning ties (`block-0.metal:44-61`). The
239|  reference's argpartition is a full sort of `-(scores+bias)`
240|  (round-1 note, `ineff-runs-2.md:94-98`); on all six graded sizes the emitted
241|  sets *and* order agree (`rows_other_experts` 0, and the grader's worst-row
242|  examples show identical expert lists, grade-exact-routing.json). This is
243|  the part of Claude's round-1 reading ("the reference's order of
244|  operations … differ", round-2 README:39) that does **not** need fixing —
245|  but a builder must preserve the exact tie behaviour, since G2 now also
246|  compares order (`check_candidate.py:120`).
247|- The 4-term sum: the reference's `w.sum(axis=-1)` on a [rows,4] f32 array
248|  takes `row_reduce_small` (row_size 4 <= 64, MLX v0.32.4
249|  `mlx/backend/metal/reduce.cpp`, `row_reduce_general_dispatch` Case 1) in its
250|  per-thread branch (`non_row_reductions=1 < 32 && row_size <= 8`,
251|  `row_reduce_small` dispatch), i.e. `thread_reduce` with `N_READS=4`
252|  (`defines.h:12`): `total = (((0 + w0) + w1) + w2) + w3` in memory order —
253|  and `w`'s memory order is the `inds` order from argpartition, the same
254|  sequence the kernel sums as `s0 + s1 + s2 + s3` (`block-0.metal:64-68`;
255|  `kernels/reduction/reduce_row.h:164-181`). The kernel then adds `1e-20f`
256|  inside the same expression (`denom = s0+s1+s2+s3 + 1e-20f`), the reference
257|  as a separate add after the reduction (`slots.py:48`) — same association,
258|  and in float32 `sum + 1e-20` equals `sum` for any sum above ~1e-27, so the
259|  epsilon cannot be the cause either. Division and ×2.5 are the same single
260|  ops (`binary_ops.h:43-48,208-213`; `block-0.metal:74-77`).
261|  **Conclusion:** once the 4 selected scores are bit-equal and in the same
262|  order, the weights are bit-equal. Builders should spend their effort on
263|  3.1 and 3.2, not on the normalisation — the opposite emphasis to round 2
264|  README:39's example list, which names "the float32 sum order of
265|  `x @ w_router.T` and of `w.sum(...)`" as co-equal suspects.

13|## What happens
14|
15|The starting point (`muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:31-34`)
16|computes each of the 60 router scores as one thread's serial float32 chain,
17|`acc += xsh[d] * w_router[e*768 + d]` for d = 0..767 (compiler FMA contraction
18|does not change the left-to-right grouping). The reference,
19|`mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)` (`bench/grader/slots.py:45`),
20|never accumulates that way. In MLX 0.32.4's `Matmul::eval_gpu`
21|(`mlx/backend/metal/matmul.cpp`, tag v0.32.4) with M=rows, N=60, K=768,
22|A not transposed, B transposed, the accumulation order is chosen by `rows`:
23|
24|| rows | MLX kernel | float32 accumulation order |
25||---|---|---|
26|| 1 | GEMV `gemv_float32_bm4_bn1_sm1_sn32_tm4_tn4` (`min(M,N)==1` → `gemv`; `gemv_wide` skipped, f32 out) | 32 lanes × serial 24 products (lane l: d = i*128 + l*4 + 0..3, i=0..5, `kernels/gemv.h:162-182`), then shuffle tree sn=16,8,4,2,1 (`gemv.h:202-208`) |
27|| 8, 32, 127 | steel split-K GEMM (Case 1: `_tm*_tn <= 2048` on this `…s` device, `_tk=48 >= 8`, `K >= max(M,N)`) | 32 K-partitions (8/32 rows) or 8 (127 rows); each partition: simdgroup 8×8 MMA over BK=16 chunks (BM=16/32, BN=32); partials summed sequentially in partition order (`steel_gemm_splitk.h:186-189`); last partition absorbs the remainder iterations (`splitk.h:140-155`) |
28|| 1,016, 2,048 | regular steel GEMM (split-K off: 768 < M) | BM=64/BN=64/BK=16 tiles (`GEMM_TPARAM_MACRO` fallback for `…s`), K walked in BK=16 chunks, simdgroup MMA accumulation chunk after chunk |
29|
30|A serial scalar loop cannot reproduce the two MMA regimes' rounding by
31|reordering: the 8-product accumulation inside each `simdgroup_float8x8`
32|multiply-accumulate is the hardware's. Bit-exactness therefore needs either
33|the same simdgroup matrix ops with the same tiling and K-order per regime
34|(branch on `rows`, or separate spec kernels), or a proof that another order
35|rounds identically (none known). Full derivation:
36|`territory-baseline-routing.md` section 3.1.

13|## What happens
14|
15|The starting point computes `scores[e] = 1.0f / (1.0f + metal::exp(-acc))`
16|(`muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:35`): the fast
17|(non-`precise`) Metal `exp` of `-acc`, then one division, for all signs.
18|The reference's `mx.sigmoid` (`bench/grader/slots.py:45`) is MLX's unary
19|`Sigmoid` (`mlx/include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/unary_ops.h:308-314`,
20|installed MLX 0.32.4):
21|
22|```metal
23|auto y = 1 / (1 + metal::precise::exp(metal::abs(x)));
24|return (x < 0) ? y : 1 - y;
25|```
26|
27|Three rounding differences, each independently able to move a score by
28|1 ULP: (a) `metal::precise::exp` vs `metal::exp`; (b) the exponent argument
29|is `|x|`, never negative; (c) for `x >= 0` the result is the subtraction
30|`1 - y` rather than a direct division. With 60 scores per row and 4 selected,
31|even a bit-exact matmul behind this sigmoid would still leave most rows
32|differing — this cause is independent of `ineff-baseline-routing-1`, and
33|both must be fixed for G2. (That the 4-term weight sum is *not* a third
34|cause is shown in `territory-baseline-routing.md` section 3.3.)

41|(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/grade-exact-routing.json`). The split
