1|# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.
6|
7|## Hardware limits
8|
9|**Peak bandwidth**:
10|The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
11|_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed
12|
13|**Peak compute**:
14|The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
15|_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)
16|
17|**Achieved bandwidth**:
18|The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
19|_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)
20|
21|**Arithmetic intensity**:
22|Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
23|_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio
24|
25|**Ridge point**:
26|The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.
27|
28|**Roofline**:
29|The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.
30|
31|## Bottlenecks and fixes
32|
33|**Bandwidth-bound**:
34|A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.
35|
36|**Compute-bound**:
37|A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.
38|
39|**Overhead-bound**:
40|A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
41|_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)
42|
43|**Bottleneck**:
44|The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
45|_Avoid_: issue, slowness
46|
47|**Kernel**:
48|One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
49|_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)
50|
51|**Occupancy**:
52|The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
53|_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)
54|
55|**Knock-out**:
56|A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
57|_Avoid_: ablation
58|
59|**Baseline**:
60|The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.
61|
62|**Fix**:
63|One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
64|_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak
65|
66|## Inference
67|
68|**Prefill**:
69|Processing a request's whole prompt through the model before its first token is generated, in chunks of up to the engine's token budget per pass (2,048 tokens here).
70|_Avoid_: prompt phase (say prefill, or prompt processing)
71|
72|**Decode step**:
73|One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.
74|
75|**Decode rows**:
76|The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
77|_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency
78|
79|**Client concurrency**:
80|The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.
81|_Avoid_: batch size
82|
83|## Mixture of experts
84|
85|**Expert**:
86|One of the interchangeable feed-forward blocks in a layer; MobileMoE-S has 60 routed experts per layer.
87|
88|**Active experts**:
89|The experts the router picks for one token in one layer (4 for MobileMoE-S).
90|_Avoid_: selected experts, top-k experts
91|
92|**Distinct experts**:
93|The number of different experts used by all decode rows together in one layer during one decode step; it decides how much expert weight data the step must read.
94|_Avoid_: unique experts, expert coverage
95|
96|## Models
97|
98|**MobileMoE-S**:
99|Meta's smallest on-device mixture-of-experts model (about 1.3B parameters in total, about 272M used per token), studied here in its SFT (full-precision) and QAT (int4) variants.
100|
101|**Muse Spark**:
102|Meta's hosted model, and the Muse agent in round 1.
103|
104|**Muse Wonder**:
105|Meta's most capable model family, in preview; its standard variant runs on Meta's Model API. The Muse agent in round 2.
106|
107|**Muse Wonder Full**:
108|The higher-capability variant of Muse Wonder, available only in Muse Code with a subscription; not used in this project.
109|
110|**Muse agent**:
111|The Meta model that chooses which pieces of the decode step to replace and writes their kernels, on the branch `muse-agent`: Muse Spark in round 1 and from round 3, Muse Wonder in round 2. It is never the model under study.
112|_Avoid_: Muse (alone), Meta agent
113|
114|**Muse Code**:
115|Meta's own coding agent for the terminal; the only program in which the Muse agent does its work in this project.
116|_Avoid_: Muse CLI, Meta Code
117|
118|**Muse agent session**:
119|A Muse Code session in which the Muse agent writes every turn, the lead's and every helper's, kept apart from Claude's work by its own branch, folder and commit trailer.
120|_Avoid_: Muse Spark session (round 2's model was Muse Wonder), guardrail (for the session itself), Meta mode
121|
122|## The Muse agent's work
123|
124|**Slot**:
125|One replaceable piece of the mixture-of-experts block (routing, combine, or the routed experts), with fixed inputs and outputs, that the Muse agent may replace with its own kernels.
126|_Avoid_: target (that is a slot the Muse agent has chosen), module
127|
128|**Round**:
129|One Muse agent session in which a swarm explores and then builds, writing in its own round folder, followed by Claude's independent measurement of what it produced. Once a round is finished, its files are frozen.
130|_Avoid_: iteration, cycle
131|
132|**Round folder**:
133|Where one round writes all its files: round 1 at the top of `muse-spark/`, each later round in `muse-spark/round-<N>/`.
134|
135|**Starting point**:
136|The plan each round from round 2 on begins with, drawn from the earlier rounds and Claude's measurement: each slot's baseline, or the attempt to start from where it has none, with its end-to-end effect; what is left to build; the refuted claims; and the territories to explore again.
137|_Avoid_: recap, retrospective
138|
139|**Improvement**:
140|An attempt that is faster than its bar in one phase, prefill or decode, and slower in neither; a faster decode step bought with a slower prefill is not one.
141|_Avoid_: speedup (for a change measured in one phase only)
142|
143|**Hand-off**:
144|An attempt's choice to run the compiled reference instead of its own kernels above a row count it names, so prefill-sized inputs stay on MLX's code.
145|_Avoid_: fallback
146|
147|**Ready check**:
148|The lead's in-round run of G3 over every candidate attempt at once, with its protocol fixed and its own log audited; only its passing verdict makes an attempt ready.
149|_Avoid_: G3 (that is Claude's run after the round), end-to-end test
150|
151|**Candidate**:
152|An attempt that passes the grader's gates and its boundary check, with its claims checked, and waits for the ready check.
153|_Avoid_: ready (that needs the ready check)
154|
155|**Prediction**:
156|A speed number no one measured for exactly what it describes, labelled as such, counting only the candidate's own measured effect and shown beside the measured value once there is one.
157|_Avoid_: expected gain, estimate (unlabelled)
158|
159|**Unverified**:
160|What no one measured, listed as such in a hypothesis and in the round's final claims, and never assumed free, neutral or zero.
161|
162|**Baseline** (of a slot):
163|A slot's best attempt so far that passes the current G2 and that Claude's G3 accepted, named in Claude's measurement of the previous round; every new attempt for that slot must beat it in the same grader run. A slot may have none.
164|_Avoid_: reference (that is the original MLX code and its compiled version)
165|
166|**Swarm**:
167|All the agents of one round, the lead and its helpers, working toward one goal through shared documents that each of them reads and adds to.
168|_Avoid_: team, crew
169|
170|**Lead agent**:
171|The one agent of a swarm that starts the helpers, keeps the shared documents current, settles clashes and commits; it neither explores nor grades.
172|_Avoid_: orchestrator, main agent
173|
174|**Helper agent**:
175|An agent the lead starts: an explorer, the verifier, a builder, a boundary agent or a checker. It reports back and never commits.
176|_Avoid_: worker, subagent (when the role matters, not the mechanism)
177|
178|**Reminder agent**:
179|One of Muse Code's own background agents, which watch the lead's progress and may nudge it, for example to check a claim before it says it is done; the Muse agent's model writes their turns too, but they take no part in the work.
180|_Avoid_: helper (that is one the lead starts)
181|
182|**Exploration phase**:
183|The first part of a round, in which explorers map the code and the measurements and find where the decode step loses time.
184|
185|**Implementation phase**:
186|The second part of a round, in which builders write and grade solutions to the confirmed inefficiencies.
187|_Avoid_: hypothesis phase
188|
189|**Territory**:
190|The part of the code or the measurements that one explorer covers: a module, a single important file, or a measurement document.
191|_Avoid_: area, lens
192|
193|**Analysis**:
194|The swarm's shared account of the code, written during exploration: the context, how the territories feed each other, and the ranked inefficiencies, each with its cost and sources.
195|_Avoid_: diagnosis, findings (those are Claude's)
196|
197|**Inefficiency**:
198|One cause of lost time in the decode step: where it is in the code, what it costs, and what removing it should save. It is confirmed or refuted against its sources before anyone builds on it.
199|_Avoid_: issue, bottleneck (that is the single largest cause)
200|
201|**Hypothesis**:
202|A proposed solution to one inefficiency: the slot it replaces, the boundary it keeps and the saving it predicts, tested by competing attempts.
203|_Avoid_: strategy, plan
204|
205|**Boundary**:
206|What a solution must keep identical so that the steps before and after its slot work exactly as before: the slot's inputs and outputs, their dtypes, and the rounding points.
207|_Avoid_: interface (unqualified), contract
208|
209|**Attempt**:
210|One grader run of a solution a builder wrote, committed by the lead; attempts for a slot are numbered in order within each round and have no limit.
211|_Avoid_: try, submission, draft

## What it does

Same slot as round 2 built on: each of the 20 layers returns
`out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(bf16) + shared`
(`bench/grader/slots.py:51-52`). The code now in the slot is the round-2
starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1/` (one fused
kernel/layer, exact at all six sizes, `beats_compiled` true) — it is no
baseline because G3 times it +1.05 ms/step slower than the unchanged model
with 32 requests. Round 2's
`muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-baseline-combine.md` (frozen)
mapped the reference chain, the sum association, the G2 gap and the dispatch
floor; this entry writes only what is new: the starting point's kernel and
spec as code in the slot, its two twins (round-1 attempt-1 without volatiles,
round-2 attempt-2 staged with volatiles), the G3 install path, and the
cross-run attribution of the +1 ms to the volatile barriers.

## Checklist

### A. Starting point: `fused_combine` (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1/`)

- **Callers:** unchanged from round 2's mapping (gradi `slots.build` +

- **Callees:** one `mx.fast.metal_kernel` launch per layer, 20 per step.

{"content":"# Inefficiency: baseline-combine-1 — volatile rounding barriers cost ~1.4 ms/step in the step, ~0 in the grader

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-combine
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1

## Slot

`combine`.

## What happens

The code in the slot
(`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1/block-0.metal:33-39`)
enforces the reference's per-op rounding with seven `volatile float`
thread variables (`p0..p3`, `s01`, `s012`, `acc`). By `volatile`
semantics each is a real memory access — 7 stores + 7 loads per output
element, 14 accesses × 4 B = 56 B of thread-private stack traffic per
thread — that the compiler cannot keep in registers, forward, elide, or
reorder. Everything else about the kernel is identical to round-1
attempt-1: the spec is byte-identical (empty `diff`), the index/base
lines and the final `bfloat(acc) + shared` line are verbatim; only the
sum's middle lines changed (one contracted expression → seven volatile
steps; `territory-baseline-combine.md` checklists A–B).

In the grader this kernel wins at all six sizes (decode 45.7 / 47.9 /
64.6 vs compiled 53.4 / 56.4 / 69.1 µs/layer). In the step it loses
+1.051 ms at 32 requests where its volatiles-free twin saved −0.390 ms
(`claude/findings/muse-round-2.md` §3 vs `claude/findings/muse-round-1.md`
§3). The twin swing — the only code delta is the barriers — is the
barriers' in-step cost (table under Cost). The prefill twin in
`ineff-g3-1` (+1501.7 ms on the 32×128 all-three prompt where the
prefill piece implies a saving) is the same barriers at prefill thread
counts (up to 88 MB/layer of spill bytes at 2,048 rows).

Ruled out as the main cause (detail in the territory entry): the G3
install path (lazy for candidate and compiled alike, checklist D — no
per-layer eval or sync exists to blame); hidden contiguity copies (exact
−80-kernel op balance, and any copy would hit the twin equally,
checklist E); grid/occupancy/wave shape (spec identical across the
twin, so shape cannot discriminate); tokens and noise (bit-exact at all
6 + 25 sizes and end to end; G3 ranges disjoint in both engines).

## Cost

Per layer, at decode 1 / 8 / 32 rows and prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048
rows (peak 200 GB/s, `claude/GLOSSARY.md`):

- Kernels × fixed cost: 1 kernel/layer either way — the barriers add no
  launch; the chained floor (~32–40 µs/layer decode) is shared with the
  twin. Not the cost.
- Bytes ÷ peak: slot traffic 9,232 B/row plus spill traffic 56
  B/thread = rows×43,008 B/layer, i.e. 52,240 B / 418 KB / 1.67 MB at
  decode = **0.26 / 2.1 / 8.4 µs**, and 6.6 / 53 / 107 MB at prefill =
  **33 / 265 / 533 µs**. Spill bytes alone: 43 KB / 344 KB / 1.375 MB
  decode, 5.5 / 43.7 / 88 MB prefill.
- Measured (the twin swing, round-2 G3 minus round-1 G3, per decode
  step over 20 layers; vLLM medians, plain in brackets):
  1 row **+0.142 (+0.433)** ms, 8 rows **+0.508 (+0.641)** ms, 32 rows
  **+1.441 (+1.574)** ms — i.e. **+7.1 / +25.4 / +72.1 µs/layer**
  (+21.7 / +32.1 / +78.7 plain). Cross-run drift is bounded at ±0.1 ms
  by the control both runs timed (round-1 triple within 0.06–0.09 ms;
  territory checklist B), so the 8- and 32-row swings are signal; the
  1-row swing is within 1-row cross-run noise and claimed as ≈0.
  At 32 rows the paid +72.1 µs/layer is ~9× the spill bytes' 8.4 µs
  bandwidth time — the cost is stalls on thread-private traffic
  (dependent store→load pairs the compiler cannot schedule across,
  fetched in cache lines far wider than the 4 B values), not bytes.

Why the grader prices it near zero is only partly understood: its
20-layer link chain runs the kernel against a quiet cache with nothing
but the tiny `link` kernel between layers, while the step buries each
call between megabytes of neighbouring traffic; the store→load reuse
that the quiet chain absorbs on-chip stalls in the busy step. The exact
on-chip accounting (L1 absorption, line amplification on strided
frames, register pressure) needs GPU counters and is **unverified** —
but the attribution does not depend on it: same spec, same grid, same
inputs, only delta the barriers, 1.44 ms swing with a ±0.1 ms control.

## Kind

Overhead-bound (`claude/GLOSSARY.md`): at decode 32 the kernel pays
+72 µs/layer for 1.375 MB of thread-private traffic (6.9 µs at peak)
and ~0.03 µs of arithmetic — far below both limits, the time going to
stalled memory traffic that reads no weights and does no arithmetic.

## Spans

`baseline-combine` (the barrier lines), `g3` (`ineff-g3-1` owns the
measurement side; this entry owns the mechanism), `grader` (the chained
timing cannot see context-dependent stall costs — note in round-3
`territory-grader.md`).

## Predicted saving

Remove the volatiles while keeping the exact per-op rounding — e.g.
`__attribute__((noinline))` device-function barriers for the mul and
the adds, which the compiler cannot contract across and which pass
values in registers with no memory traffic (expressible in the spec
surface: helpers in `header_block`, calls in the body; `slots.build`
supports both, `slots.py:313-322`). Predicted effect, labelled
prediction:

- Decode step (vLLM basis): recover the twin swing, i.e. return to
  ≈ −0.51 / −0.71 / −0.39 ms/step: **≈0.5 ms/step at 8 requests and
  ≈1.4 ms/step at 32 requests**; ≈0 claimed at 1 row (within noise).
- Prefill: the same barriers at prefill thread counts drive the
  +1501.7 ms prompt twin (`ineff-g3-1`); removing them is predicted to
  recover it (order 1 s on 32×128 combine-including prompts) — no
  round-1 prefill twin exists to calibrate against, so this is the
  looser half of the prediction.
- Grader basis: the kernel already beats compiled everywhere; fewer
  stalls can only improve the chained time, so `beats_compiled` is
  predicted kept with a wider margin — the fix risks exactness (G2),
  never speed, and a saving in decode cannot cost prefill here since
  both phases run the identical lines.
- Net vs the compiled reference if the fix lands: ≈ −0.5 / −0.9 /
  −0.2 ms/step at 1 / 8 / 32 requests (twin's engine numbers), plus
  the prompt recovery above.

Discriminating checks: the ready check must time the fix combine-alone
at 32 requests (reproduces-or-refutes in-round); G3-timing round-1
attempt-1 in the same run would isolate the barriers in-run but the
fix's own G3 supersedes it.

1|# Round 2 of the Muse agent, measured
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|In round 2 (2026-11-04, 03:13 to 04:16 UTC), the Muse agent (Muse Wonder, `muse-wonder-1.0`, at `max` effort) ran skill version 5. It started from [Claude's measurement of round 1](muse-round-1.md), under the stricter grader of [ADR 0010](../adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md):

7|- the piece timing chains the 20 layers.

16|- **re-grading** the two submitted kernels and experts attempt-7;
17|- **checking all three at 25 row counts** that G2 doesn't test;
18|- **checking tokens end to end and timing the decode step (G3),** in plain MLX and vLLM.

The scripts are:
23|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py`, the grader;
24|- `bench/grader/check_sizes.py`, G2's checks at the extra row counts;
25|- `bench/grader/time_candidates.py`, the end-to-end check and G3.

29|## Summary
30|
31|- **Every kernel round 2 graded is correct.** The two submitted kernels and experts attempt-7 are bit-exact with MLX's reference:
32|  - at the grader's six sizes;
33|  - at 25 more row counts, from 2 to 1,500 rows, on either side of MLX's switches at 16 and 60 rows, and inside each of routing's row-count regimes;
34|  - end to end, where the model's greedy tokens are identical in plain MLX and in vLLM, at 1 and 32 requests, for every round-2 variant.
35|
36|  Round 1's kernels, timed in the same runs as a control, still change the tokens with 32 requests.
37|- **routing attempt-4 passed G3 as it stood, on decode steps.** It is faster than both the unchanged model and the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 requests, in both engines. In vLLM it saves 0.47, 0.43 and 0.54 ms per step (8.7%, 3.0% and 1.8%). It is the project's first Muse kernel that passed every rule of its time. Over whole requests its gain is smaller, since it processes prompts 7–10% slower: throughput rises 10.2% with 1 request and 1.8% with 8, is flat with 32 and falls 3.5% with 32 requests of 1,024-token prompts ([section 5](#5-whole-requests-prompts-and-throughput)). Under the rule set after this measurement, that an improvement must hold in both phases ([ADR 0011](../adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)), it fails, so it is no baseline for round 3 ([For round 3](#for-round-3-baselines-and-starting-points)).

39|- **The submission (routing + combine), in vLLM:** −0.73 ms (−13%) with 1 request, −0.74 ms (−5%) with 8, **+0.53 ms (+2%) with 32**, against a prediction of −0.84 ms at each. combine's slowdown outweighs routing's saving with 32 requests.
40|- **experts attempt-7, not submitted, makes the decode step faster and whole requests much slower.** Per decode step in vLLM: −5.35 ms (−17.5%) with 32 requests, −1.22 ms (−8.4%) with 8, and +0.29 ms (+5.4%) with 1, which is why round 2 dropped it. But it processes prompts 6.6 to 14.5 times slower than the unchanged engine, so whole requests lose 10% to 83% of their throughput ([section 5](#5-whole-requests-prompts-and-throughput)). G3 times only decode steps, and this went unseen until the comparison in section 5.
41|- **All three slots replaced at once lose time with 8 requests,** as in round 1, although every pair of kernels adds up as expected. With 8 requests in plain MLX, the three alone save 1.87 ms together, and all three installed cost 0.94 ms ([section 4](#4-where-the-kernels-interfere)).

The absolute times also differ from round 2's runs by up to 2 times at 1 row. Only the comparison within one run means anything, and at 1 row even that is close to the noise. G3 decides.

57|## 2. Row counts G2 doesn't test
58|
59|`check_sizes.py` applies the grader's bit-exact checks to every layer's slot inputs in the first N tokens of a one-request prefill (`sizes-check.json`). The 25 values of N are:
60|- 2, 3, 5, 15, 16, 17, 31, 33, 40, 59, 60, 61, 64, 65;
61|- 100, 128, 129, 200, 256, 257, 500, 768, 769, 1,024 and 1,500.

70|## 3. End to end: tokens and G3
71|
72|**Tokens.** 24 greedy tokens after 128-token prompts, at 1 and 32 requests (`muse-plain.jsonl`, `muse-vllm.jsonl`, records of kind `check`). Every round-2 variant, alone or combined, gives the unchanged model's tokens in both engines. Round 1's three kernels together change them with 32 requests in both, as before.
73|
74|**G3, vLLM**, the change in decode step period against the unchanged model, in ms (median of 3 repeats, with their range in `console-vllm.txt`):
75|
76|| Variant | 1 request | 8 | 32 |
77||---|---|---|---|
78|| unchanged | 5.442 | 14.524 | 30.470 |
79|| routing attempt-4 | **−0.474** (−8.7%) | **−0.434** (−3.0%) | **−0.537** (−1.8%) |
80|| routing, compiled reference | −0.272 | −0.225 | −0.133 |
81|| combine attempt-1 | −0.372 | −0.197 | **+1.051** (+3.4%) |
82|| combine, compiled reference | −0.340 | −0.251 | −0.183 |
83|| **submission: routing + combine** | **−0.726** (−13.3%) | **−0.735** (−5.1%) | **+0.527** (+1.7%) |
84|| both compiled references | −0.404 | −0.505 | −0.179 |
85|| experts attempt-7, not submitted | +0.292 (+5.4%) | **−1.217** (−8.4%) | **−5.345** (−17.5%) |
86|| experts, compiled reference | −0.066 | +0.032 | −0.220 |
87|| submission + experts attempt-7 | −0.406 | +0.280 | −4.510 (−14.8%) |
88|| all three compiled references | −0.571 | −0.534 | −0.197 |
89|| round 1's three kernels | +0.923 | +0.127 | −1.849 |
90|| round 2's prediction for the submission | −0.84 | −0.85 | −0.84 |
91|
92|**Plain MLX** (`console-plain.txt`), the change in ms against an unchanged step of 4.740, 13.623 and 28.485 ms:
93|- routing attempt-4: −0.486, −0.482, −0.404;
94|- combine attempt-1: −0.424, −0.112, **+1.168**;
95|- submission: −0.898, −0.772, **+0.486**;
96|- experts attempt-7: +0.529, −1.263, −4.880;
97|- submission + experts attempt-7: −0.310, **+1.001**, −4.159;
98|- round 1's three kernels: +1.054, +0.774, −1.895.
99|
100|**Against the brief's G3,** an attempt must be faster than both the unchanged model and the compiled reference, beyond the spread of the repeats. Here, that means all three of its repeats are below all three of the others'.
101|- **routing attempt-4** passes at 1, 8 and 32 requests, in both engines.
102|- **combine attempt-1** fails:
103|  - with 32 requests it is slower than the unchanged model in both engines;
104|  - with 8, its range overlaps the compiled reference's in plain MLX, and its median is above it in vLLM;
105|  - with 1 request, its vLLM range touches the compiled reference's.
106|- **experts attempt-7** fails with 1 request, being slower than the unchanged model, and passes with 8 and 32.
107|
108|**Why combine is slow in the model** is not known. Its chained piece timing at 32 rows is 42.2 µs per layer against the compiled reference's 47.3. A G3 loss of 1.05 ms is about 52 µs per layer, more than the kernel's whole time in the grader. So the cost doesn't come from the kernel's own work as the grader runs it. It comes from how it sits in the step, which the grader doesn't reproduce.
109|
110|## 4. Where the kernels interfere
111|
112|A separate plain MLX run timed round 2's three kernels in every combination, each kernel alone again, and routing's compiled reference (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2-pairs/console-plain.txt`). Every combination kept the tokens identical. Change in ms against an unchanged step of 4.731, 13.528 and 28.442 ms:
113|
114|| Variant | 1 request | 8 | 32 |
115||---|---|---|---|
116|| routing attempt-4 | −0.469 | −0.383 | −0.392 |
117|| combine attempt-1 | −0.418 | −0.265 | +1.051 |
118|| experts attempt-7 | +0.323 | −1.219 | −5.048 |
119|| routing + combine | −0.938 | −0.776 | +0.413 |
120|| routing + experts | −0.266 | −1.345 | **−5.664** (−19.9%) |
121|| combine + experts | +0.205 | −1.130 | −4.491 |
122|| all three | −0.302 | **+0.937** | −4.197 |
123|| the three alone, added up | −0.564 | −1.867 | −4.389 |
124|
125|- **Every pair comes within 0.5 ms of its parts' sum.**
126|- **All three together, with 8 requests, are 2.8 ms slower than their parts.** It is the only case that misses by much.
127|- **Round 1 did the same.** Its three kernels, with 8 requests, came out at +0.88 ms in plain MLX against −1.95 ms for the parts ([round 1](muse-round-1.md#3-g3-the-decode-step)). Two different sets of kernels show it, so the cause is likely in how the step runs with all three slots replaced at that size, not in one kernel. It is not explained.
128|- **The fastest decode step with exact output** is routing attempt-4 with experts attempt-7: −20% with 32 requests, −10% with 8 and −6% with 1 in plain MLX, and −18.8% with 32 requests in vLLM (section 5). Over whole requests it is the slowest version measured, because of experts attempt-7's prompt processing.
129|
130|## 5. Whole requests: prompts and throughput
131|
132|A last vLLM run (`results/runs/2026-11-04-engine-comparison/`, tables built by `bench/grader/engine_table.py`) timed eight versions of the engine at four workloads: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts. Besides the decode step it recorded the time until every prompt was processed and each run's whole time, as generated tokens per second. Every version but round 1's kept the tokens identical. Throughput change against the unchanged engine (prompt time as a multiple of the unchanged engine's in brackets):
133|
134|| Version | 1 × 128 | 8 × 128 | 32 × 128 | 32 × 1,024 |
135||---|---|---|---|---|
136|| compiled references, all three slots | +11.9% (1.04×) | +3.1% (0.99×) | +0.6% (0.98×) | +0.9% (0.98×) |
137|| round 2: routing attempt-4 | +10.2% (1.07×) | +1.8% (1.09×) | +0.3% (1.10×) | −3.5% (1.10×) |
138|| round 2 submission: routing + combine | +15.9% (1.11×) | +2.1% (1.09×) | −2.7% (1.08×) | −4.1% (1.09×) |
139|| round 2: routing + experts attempt-7 | −10.0% (6.63×) | −37.5% (14.50×) | −48.0% (12.50×) | −82.5% (13.09×) |
140|| round 2: all three with experts attempt-7 | −10.7% (6.75×) | −43.0% (14.33×) | −53.7% (14.37×) | −83.3% (13.66×) |
141|| round 1: all three (changes the output) | −13.3% (1.60×) | −9.6% (2.30×) | −8.1% (2.30×) | −33.6% (2.32×) |
142|
143|- **Compiling MLX's own code for the three slots,** with no new kernel, gains 0.6% to 3.1% with 8 and 32 requests, where its repeats and the unchanged engine's don't overlap. With 1 request its median gain is 11.9%, but one of its three repeats falls inside the unchanged engine's range (1,374 to 1,559 ms against 1,486 to 1,580), so that gain is not certain. No Muse version gains in every workload.
144|- **The unchanged engine is vLLM's own.** It ran with Claude's step hooks and vLLM's engine in the script's process. Alternating runs on the same afternoon found it within −0.2% to +1.9% of vLLM with neither, inside the spread between repeats in every workload (`bench/micro/clean_vllm.py`, [results/runs/2026-11-04-clean-vllm/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-clean-vllm/)).
145|- **Round 2's kernels are slower than MLX's when processing prompts,** in every slot measured: routing alone by 7–10%, routing with combine by 8–11%, and experts attempt-7 by 6.6 to 14.5 times. Every prompt chunk here has at least 128 rows, so it runs experts attempt-7's path for 60 rows and more, which copies `gather_qmm_rhs`'s rounding but not its speed.
146|- **The grader checks the kernels' output at prompt sizes, and G3 times only decode steps,** so neither saw this. Its decode-step figures in sections 1 to 4 stand; they describe one part of a request.
147|
148|## 6. How round 2 worked
149|
150|- **Time:** 63 minutes; the lead and 34 helpers; 983 model calls. 981 were `muse-wonder-1.0`, and 2 were Muse Code's reminder agents on `muse-spark-1.3` (`muse-spark/transcripts/01a1a48b-e027-7462-898f-0b01290c8c9a.summary.json`).
151|- **Tokens:** 125.6M input, of which 121.1M were cached, and 0.77M output. At Muse Wonder's prices that is about $58: $18 uncached input, $24 cached input and $15 output. It would be about $65 if the 0.36M reasoning tokens are billed on top of the output.
152|- **Attempts:** one grader run per attempt, 13 in total, as the skill asks. Every graded attempt is committed.
153|- **What it got right:** it read round 1's measurement, made exactness its first goal, and met it in every slot. Its explorers found that routing's reference changes its matrix-product strategy in row-count regimes, and its builder copied each regime exactly. Those regimes are what section 2 tests.
154|- **What it missed:** its prediction for combine (−0.35 ms) and for the submission at 32 requests. The chained piece timing still doesn't show combine's cost in the step.
155|
156|## For round 3: baselines and starting points
157|
158|**The rule,** from round 3 ([ADR 0011](../adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)): a slot's baseline is its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3. Both of those now judge two phases, decode and prefill: faster in one, slower in neither, and in G3 no whole request slower, against the unchanged model and the compiled reference. An attempt that passes G2 but not the rest is a starting point, not a bar: making it the bar would ask a fix to beat it where it already wins.
159|
160|The current grader re-graded round 2's three kernels on 2026-11-04 (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-*.json`). Times are multiples of the compiled reference's, per layer:
161|
162|| Slot | Baseline | Starting point | Decode, 1 / 8 / 32 rows | Prefill, 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows | Why it is no baseline |
163||---|---|---|---|---|---|
164|| `routing` | none | `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4` | 0.76 / 0.84 / 0.84, faster | 2.6 / 5.9 / 8.7, slower | Slower at every prefill size, so prompts take 7–10% longer and whole requests with 1,024-token prompts lose 3.5% (section 5). |
165|| `combine` | none | `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1` | 0.86 / 0.85 / 0.93, faster | 0.95 / 0.83 / 0.52, faster | Its decode step in G3 was 1.05 ms slower than the unchanged model's with 32 requests, for a reason the grader doesn't show (section 3). |
166|| `experts` | none | `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7` | 1.17 / 0.69 / 0.65, slower at 1 row | 15.8 / 27.7 / 20.1, slower | Slower at 1 row and at every prefill size, so prompts take 6.6 to 14.5 times as long (section 5). |
167|
168|Round 3 has no baseline in any slot, so its bar is the compiled reference everywhere.
169|
170|**What round 3 has to find out,** in Claude's reading of these results:
171|1. **experts with 1 row.** attempt-7 keeps its 8- and 32-row speed and loses at 1 row, as every fused design in round 2 did (92 to 110 µs per layer chained, against 73 to 87 for the compiled reference, in round 2's runs). Round 2's summary suggests copying the reference's unfused structure exactly for small row counts.
172|2. **Why combine attempt-1 costs 1 ms in the step with 32 requests** and not in the grader.
173|3. **Why all three slots replaced at once lose 2.8 ms with 8 requests,** when every pair adds up (section 4).
174|4. **Prefill speed.** From round 3 the grader times the prefill sizes and G3 times prompts and whole requests (ADR 0011). routing attempt-4 and experts attempt-7 are slower than the compiled reference at every prefill size; combine attempt-1 is faster. An attempt may keep inputs above a row count it names on the compiled reference (`max_rows`, in the brief). Claude checked that hand-off on a copy of experts attempt-7 with `max_rows` 59: bit-exact at all six sizes, and the `same` as the compiled reference at every prefill size (`results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`).

1|# Territory: g3 — Claude's round-1 measurement, end to end vs piece by piece
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-g3
4|- **Status:** done
5|- **Version:** 2
6|- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T03:18:59Z
7|- **Next:** verifier to check ineff-g3-1; pairwise G3 + chained routing/combine timings (gap 3) belong to the implementation phase
8|
9|## What it does
10|
11|This territory is not code in the decode step. It is the measurement that decides whether round 1's three final attempts (`experts/attempt-4`, `routing/attempt-1`, `combine/attempt-1`) actually made the model faster: Claude's re-grading, the chained-vs-independent timing experiment, and the end-to-end token + step-period (G3) runs in plain MLX and vLLM, all written up in [claude/findings/muse-round-1.md](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-1.md) with raw data in `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/`. Its question for round 2 is where the end-to-end change differs from the piece timing, and why.
12|
13|## Checklist
14|
15|### 1. Re-grading under round 1's rules (`grade-<slot>.json`)
16|
17|- **Callers:** Claude's measurement on `main` after merging round 1 at `a4995e4` ([muse-round-1.md:7](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-1.md)), re-running `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` as round 1 ran it.
18|- **Callees:** the grader's G1 (compiles/runs), G2 (old tolerances: routing weights within 10⁻⁴ relative, combine/experts within 2 bfloat16 ULP), and the old piece timing (20 layers' calls, no wait between them, one `mx.eval` at the end, median of 30).
19|- **Data:** µs per layer, reference / compiled reference / attempt. Experts attempt-4: 143.8 / 139.5 / **92.1** at 1 row, 222.5 / 221.4 / **165.4** at 8, 770.1 / 762.4 / **529.9** at 32 (`grade-experts.json` `timing_us_per_layer`; [muse-round-1.md:46](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-1.md)). Routing attempt-1: 39.9 / 31.5 / **25.3**, 83.5 / 42.7 / **24.3**, 101.2 / 87.6 / **68.9** (`grade-routing.json`). Combine attempt-1: 23.1 / 23.8 / **18.6**, 22.5 / 26.1 / **17.0**, 39.5 / 32.0 / **18.9** (`grade-combine.json`). All three: G1 pass, G2 pass, `beats_compiled: true`.
20|- **Neighbours:** round 1's own runs gave experts 50.0 / 157.8 / 515.4 µs, routing 28.5 / 23.6 / 41.8, combine 17.2 / 17.0 / 18.5 ([muse-round-1.md:50](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-1.md)). The experts 1-row figure is the outlier (92.1 here vs 50.0 then); round 1 already warned 1-row timings shift between runs.
21|- **Cost:** this piece launches no decode kernels; it prices each slot. Converted to a step (×20 layers): against the compiled reference the three attempts promise −0.948 / −1.120 / −4.650 ms (experts), −0.124 / −0.368 / −0.374 ms (routing), −0.104 / −0.182 / −0.262 ms (combine) at 1 / 8 / 32 rows, summing to −1.176 / −1.670 / −5.286 ms per step. Round 1's prediction from its own runs was −0.54 / −1.81 / −5.72 ms ([muse-round-1.md:91](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-1.md)).
22|- **Invariants:** within one grader run the candidate-vs-compiled comparison is the valid one; cross-run 1-row absolutes are not (see piece 3). G2 here is the *old* rule set — passing it says nothing about the current bit-exact G2 (piece 2).
23|
24|### 2. Re-grading under round 2's rules (`grade-exact-<slot>.json`, ADR 0010)
25|
26|- **Callers:** same measurement, with the grader of [ADR 0010](../../../claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md): bit-exact G2 at decode 1 / 8 / 32 rows and prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows, chained piece timing ([check_candidate.py:8-9](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py), `link` at [check_candidate.py:178-181](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py), `chained` at [check_candidate.py:184-201](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)).
27|- **Callees:** `check_routing` / `check_combine` / `check_experts` with `differ == 0` required ([check_candidate.py:172-175](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)); prefill inputs from `slots.capture_prefill` ([slots.py](../../../bench/grader/slots.py) `capture_prefill`, 128-token prompts, 2,048-token chunks → 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows).

Routing attempt-1: rows differ 20 / 159 / 638 of 20 / 160 / 640 at decode, 2,518 / 16,187 / 32,743 at prefill; `rows_other_experts` 0 everywhere; max relative error 2.6×10⁻⁶ decode, 8.7×10⁻⁶ prefill (`grade-exact-routing.json`). Combine attempt-1: decode differ 0 / 2 / 2 (max 2.0 / 1.0 ULP), prefill 6 / 50 / 130 (max 1 / 16 / 32 ULP) (`grade-exact-combine.json`). Summarised at [muse-round-1.md:144-150](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-1.md).
29|- **Neighbours:** none of the three passes the new G2, so round 2 has no baseline in any slot; the bar is the compiled reference (README *Starting point*). The experts failure starts at 60 rows, where MLX switches `gather_qvm` → `gather_qmm_rhs` (territory `quantized-kernels`); routing's and combine's failures are last-bit sum-order/contraction differences (territories `baseline-routing`, `baseline-combine`).
30|- **Cost:** correctness only; no timing is printed when G2 fails (`beats_compiled: false` in all three `grade-exact-*.json`).

33|### 3. Chained vs independent piece timing (`bench/micro/chain_timing.py`, `console-chain.txt`)
34|
35|- **Callers:** Claude's experiment of 2026-11-04, run as `.venv/bin/python bench/micro/chain_timing.py muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4` ([chain_timing.py:12](../../../bench/micro/chain_timing.py)); output is `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/console-chain.txt`.
36|- **Callees:** `slots.load_inputs` / `load_expert_weights` for the 20 captured layers; the reference (`slots.ref_experts`) and the attempt loaded by `check_candidate.load`. Two modes per row count ([chain_timing.py:43-60](../../../bench/micro/chain_timing.py)): *independent* — the 20 calls share no data, one `mx.eval(outs)` at the end, as the old grader timed; *chained* — each call's `x` is the previous call's `y[:, 0, :]`, a real data dependency, so a call cannot start before the previous one finishes. Median of 32 repeats, first 2 dropped ([chain_timing.py:59](../../../bench/micro/chain_timing.py)).
37|- **Data:** µs per layer, reference / attempt-4. Independent: 86.0 / **61.0** at 1 row, 219.1 / **165.1** at 8, 767.3 / **535.0** at 32. Chained: 80.3 / **132.9** at 1, 239.6 / **175.9** at 8, 797.6 / **587.6** at 32 (`console-chain.txt`, all six lines; [muse-round-1.md:118-119](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-1.md)).
38|- **Neighbours:** in the model the chain is real: layer *n*+1's routing takes layer *n*'s combine output (via the residual stream, `mobilemoe.py:217-232` through `slots.make_moe_call`). The new grader's `link` kernel reproduces this ordering for every slot (piece 2); ADR 0010 records that the chained times match a real data chain within 10%, and that `mx.depends` does not wait (46 µs/layer at 1 row, as fast as no dependency, vs 133–195 µs chained).
39|- **Cost:** at 1 row the attempt goes from 29% faster than the reference independent ((86.0−61.0)/86.0) to 66% slower chained ((132.9−80.3)/80.3). The chained gap is +52.6 µs/layer × 20 layers = **+1.052 ms/step**, against G3's measured +1.162 ms in vLLM and +1.228 ms in plain MLX (piece 5/6) — the chain explains the 1-request experts slowdown to within 0.11–0.18 ms. At 8 / 32 rows the chained gaps are −63.7 / −210.0 µs/layer = −1.274 / −4.200 ms/step, the same sign and rough size as G3's experts-alone −0.817 / −4.154 ms (vLLM).
40|- **Invariants:** only the experts slot and only attempt-4 were measured this way. No chained figure exists in this data for routing or combine; any claim about their in-step latency is inference from G3, not a piece timing. Attempt-4's grid is `rows*4` threadgroups of 256 threads (`muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4/spec.json`), i.e. 4 threadgroups at 1 row — Claude's occupancy estimate for the chained latency ([muse-round-1.md:123](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-1.md)) is an estimate from the code, not a counter measurement.
41|
42|### 4. The G3 harness (`bench/grader/time_candidates.py`)
43|
44|- **Callers:** Claude's runs producing `console-plain.txt`, `console-vllm.txt`, `muse-plain.jsonl`, `muse-vllm.jsonl` in `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/`; invoked as `time_candidates.py plain|vllm <out> experts=<attempt-4> routing=<attempt-1> combine=<attempt-1>` ([time_candidates.py:16-17](../../../bench/grader/time_candidates.py)).

Token checks: `plain_checks` (24 greedy tokens after 128-token prompts, 1 and 32 requests, [time_candidates.py:98-120](../../../bench/grader/time_candidates.py)) and `rf.vllm_checks` ([repeat_fixes.py:174-224](../../../bench/micro/repeat_fixes.py)). 46|- **Data:** one `check` record and 27 `run` records (9 variants × 3 row counts × 3 repeats, per engine) in each `muse-*.jsonl`. Kernel counts come from `count_ops` ([repeat_fixes.py:136-143](../../../bench/micro/repeat_fixes.py)): the exported graph of one decode step, view ops excluded — a count of graph ops, where each `mx.compile` region and each custom kernel counts once. It is not a launch trace.
47|- **Neighbours:** G3's rule (brief, *How each attempt is judged*): an attempt must beat both the unchanged model and its compiled reference, by more than the spread between repeats. `compiled-all` is the control that shows what `mx.compile` of the untouched references already saves with no new kernel.
48|- **Cost:** the harness itself is not in the step. Machine caveat for every absolute number below: another job of surucuonur's was running and 21.3–22.7 GB of swap were in use; Docker was quit; vLLM ran with `VLLM_METAL_KV_COMMIT_PROBE=0` ([muse-round-1.md:19](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-1.md)). Shuffled repeats make variant-vs-variant comparisons usable; absolutes carry that caveat.
49|- **Invariants:** prompts for the token check are random tokens (`mx.random.seed(rows)` + `randint(0, 100000, (rows, 128))` in plain, [time_candidates.py:107-108](../../../bench/grader/time_candidates.py); `random.Random(7)` + `randrange(1000, 100000)` in vLLM, [repeat_fixes.py:179-185](../../../bench/micro/repeat_fixes.py)) — near-tie next-token margins are expected, which is why last-bit differences flip tokens (piece 7). Timing runs use their own seeds (`rows*10000+prompt`, [repeat_fixes.py:299](../../../bench/micro/repeat_fixes.py)), so the timed sequences are not the checked sequences.
50|
51|### 5. G3 alone and together — plain MLX (`console-plain.txt`, `muse-plain.jsonl`)
52|

15|Attempt-4 is one fused kernel per layer with grid `rows*1024` threads in threadgroups of 256 — `rows*4` threadgroups, one per (row, expert-slot) pair (`muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4/spec.json`). In the model, where layers are chained by construction, it slows the 1-request decode step by ~1.2 ms. Claude's estimate from the code: 4 threadgroups at 1 row cannot fill the 16-core GPU, so one call's latency is long even when many calls together go fast ([muse-round-1.md:123](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-1.md)).   "exit_code": 0,
  "terminal_status": "completed",
  "output": "# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write faster MobileMoE-S kernels, for decoding and prompt processing

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*

You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.

## The task

Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.

A request goes through two phases: **prompt processing** (the prefill), which runs its whole prompt through the model, and **decoding**, one step per generated token. An improvement must hold in both: faster in one, and no slower in the other ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A kernel that speeds up the decode step but slows the prefill is not an improvement.

1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.

**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.

## The slots

Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.

The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.

### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights

| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
|---|---|---|---|
| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |

Reference:

```python
scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
```

The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.

### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert

| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
|---|---|---|---|
| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |

Reference:

```python
out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
```

Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.

### `routing+combine`

Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.

### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products

| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
|---|---|---|---|
| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |

Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.

Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:

```python
y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
```

As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.

Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.

## Tools and limits

- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.

## Rules of this session

These keep your work apart from everyone else's. Git hooks and an audit script enforce them, and a commit that breaks them is refused.

- **Write only inside `muse-spark/`.** Never change `bench/`, `claude/`, `results/`, `tools/`, `third_party/`, or any other file. A copy of the grader you edit is never used.

# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*

How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.

## Hardware limits

**Peak bandwidth**:
The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed

**Peak compute**:
The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)

**Achieved bandwidth**:
The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)

**Arithmetic intensity**:
Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio

**Ridge point**:
The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.

**Roofline**:
The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.

## Bottlenecks and fixes

**Bandwidth-bound**:
A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.

**Compute-bound**:
A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.

**Overhead-bound**:
A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)

**Bottleneck**:
The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
_Avoid_: issue, slowness

**Kernel**:
One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)

**Occupancy**:
The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)

**Knock-out**:
A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
_Avoid_: ablation

**Baseline**:
The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.

**Fix**:
One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak

## Inference

**Prefill**:
Processing a request's whole prompt through the model before its first token is generated, in chunks of up to the engine's token budget per pass (2,048 tokens here).
_Avoid_: prompt phase (say prefill, or prompt processing)

**Decode step**:
One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.

**Decode rows**:
The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency

**Client concurrency**:
The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.
_Avoid_: batch size

## Mixture of experts

**Expert**:
One of the interchangeable feed-forward blocks in a layer; MobileMoE-S has 60 routed experts per layer.

**Active experts**:
The experts the router picks for one token in one layer (4 for MobileMoE-S).
_Avoid_: selected experts, top-k experts

**Distinct experts**:
The number of different experts used by all decode rows together in one layer during one decode step; it decides how much expert weight data the step must read.
_Avoid_: unique experts, expert coverage

## Models

**MobileMoE-S**:
Meta's smallest on-device mixture-of-experts model (about 1.3B parameters in total, about 272M used per token), studied here in its SFT (full-precision) and QAT (int4) variants.

**Muse Spark**:
Meta's hosted model, and the Muse agent in round 1.

**Muse Wonder**:
Meta's most capable model family, in preview; its standard variant runs on Meta's Model API. The Muse agent in round 2.

**Muse Wonder Full**:
The higher-capability variant of Muse Wonder, available only in Muse Code with a subscription; not used in this project.

**Muse agent**:
The Meta model that chooses which pieces of the decode step to replace and writes their kernels, on the branch `muse-agent`: Muse Spark in round 1 and from round 3, Muse Wonder in round 2. It is never the model under study.
_Avoid_: Muse (alone), Meta agent

**Muse Code**:
Meta's own coding agent for the terminal; the only program in which the Muse agent does its work in this project.
_Avoid_: Muse CLI, Meta Code

**Muse agent session**:
A Muse Code session in which the Muse agent writes every turn, the lead's and every helper's, kept apart from Claude's work by its own branch, folder and commit trailer.
_Avoid_: Muse Spark session (round 2's model was Muse Wonder), guardrail (for the session itself), Meta mode

## The Muse agent's work

**Slot**:
One replaceable piece of the mixture-of-experts block (routing, combine, or the routed experts), with fixed inputs and outputs, that the Muse agent may replace with its own kernels.
_Avoid_: target (that is a slot the Muse agent has chosen), module

**Round**:
One Muse agent session in which a swarm explores and then builds, writing in its own round folder, followed by Claude's independent measurement of what it produced. Once a round is finished, its files are frozen.
_Avoid_: iteration, cycle

**Round folder**:
Where one round writes all its files: round 1 at the top of `muse-spark/`, each later round in `muse-spark/round-<N>/`.

**Starting point**:
The plan each round from round 2 on begins with, drawn from the earlier rounds and Claude's measurement: each slot's baseline, or the attempt to start from where it has none, with its end-to-end effect; what is left to build; the refuted claims; and the territories to explore again.
_Avoid_: recap, retrospective

**Improvement**:
An attempt that is faster than its bar in one phase, prefill or decode, and slower in neither; a faster decode step bought with a slower prefill is not one.
_Avoid_: speedup (for a change measured in one phase only)

**Hand-off**:
An attempt's choice to run the compiled reference instead of its own kernels above a row count it names, so prefill-sized inputs stay on MLX's code.
_Avoid_: fallback

**Ready check**:
The lead's in-round run of G3 over every candidate attempt at once, with its protocol fixed and its own log audited; only its passing verdict makes an attempt ready.
_Avoid_: G3 (that is Claude's run after the round), end-to-end test

**Candidate**:
An attempt that passes the grader's gates and its boundary check, with its claims checked, and waits for the ready check.
_Avoid_: ready (that needs the ready check)

**Prediction**:
A speed number no one measured for exactly what it describes, labelled as such, counting only the candidate's own measured effect and shown beside the measured value once there is one.
_Avoid_: expected gain, estimate (unlabelled)

**Unverified**:
What no one measured, listed as such in a hypothesis and in the round's final claims, and never assumed free, neutral or zero.

**Baseline** (of a slot):
A slot's best attempt so far that passes the current G2 and that Claude's G3 accepted, named in Claude's measurement of the previous round; every new attempt for that slot must beat it in the same grader run. A slot may have none.
_Avoid_: reference (that is the original MLX code and its compiled version)

**Swarm**:
All the agents of one round, the lead and its helpers, working toward one goal through shared documents that each of them reads and adds to.
_Avoid_: team, crew

**Lead agent**:
The one agent of a swarm that starts the helpers, keeps the shared documents current, settles clashes and commits; it neither explores nor grades.
_Avoid_: orchestrator, main agent

**Helper agent**:
An agent the lead starts: an explorer, the verifier, a builder, a boundary agent or a checker. It reports back and never commits.
_Avoid_: worker, subagent (when the role matters, not the mechanism)

**Reminder agent**:
One of Muse Code's own background agents, which watch the lead's progress and may nudge it, for example to check a claim before it says it is done; the Muse agent's model writes their turns too, but they take no part in the work.
_Avoid_: helper (that is one the lead starts)

**Exploration phase**:
The first part of a round, in which explorers map the code and the measurements and find where the decode step loses time.

**Implementation phase**:
The second part of a round, in which builders write and grade solutions to the confirmed inefficiencies.
_Avoid_: hypothesis phase

**Territory**:
The part of the code or the measurements that one explorer covers: a module, a single important file, or a measurement document.
_Avoid_: area, lens

**Analysis**:
The swarm's shared account of the code, written during exploration: the context, how the territories feed each other, and the ranked inefficiencies, each with its cost and sources.
_Avoid_: diagnosis, findings (those are Claude's)

**Inefficiency**:
One cause of lost time in the decode step: where it is in the code, what it costs, and what removing it should save. It is confirmed or refuted against its sources before anyone builds on it.
_Avoid_: issue, bottleneck (that is the single largest cause)

**Hypothesis**:
A proposed solution to one inefficiency: the slot it replaces, the boundary it keeps and the saving it predicts, tested by competing attempts.
_Avoid_: strategy, plan

**Boundary**:
What a solution must keep identical so that the steps before and after its slot work exactly as before: the slot's inputs and outputs, their dtypes, and the rounding points.
_Avoid_: interface (unqualified), contract

**Attempt**:
One grader run of a solution a builder wrote, committed by the lead; attempts for a slot are numbered in order within each round and have no limit.
_Avoid_: try, submission, draft

2|
3|First attempt in this direction (round 2, `hyp-3-combine-exact`, slot
4|`combine`, baseline `none`). Builds on the starting point
5|`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1` (`block-0.metal:12-25`,
6|`spec.json`: grid `rows*768`, threadgroup [256,1,1], no threadgroup
7|memory). The starting point is not a baseline: under round 2's bit-exact
8|G2 it fails at five of six sizes on FMA contraction alone (decode
9|0 / 2 / 2 differ, prefill 6 / 50 / 130; `ineff-baseline-combine-1`,
10|`territory-baseline-combine.md` checklist D), so it counts as the attempt
11|this one changes.
12|
13|## What changed
14|
15|Only the arithmetic. Indexing, grid, threadgroup, inputs/outputs and the
16|final line `bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase]` are verbatim from the starting
17|point. The single-expression sum
18|
19|```metal
20|float acc = float(y0)*w0 + float(y1)*w1 + float(y2)*w2 + float(y3)*w3;
21|```
22|
23|which the compiler FP-contracts into FMAs (each product kept unrounded
24|into its add), becomes seven fma-free stepwise ops with explicit
25|rounding barriers:
26|
27|```metal
28|volatile float p0 = float(y[ybase]) * weights[wbase];        // rounded to f32
29|volatile float p1 = float(y[ybase+768u]) * weights[wbase+1u];
30|volatile float p2 = float(y[ybase+1536u]) * weights[wbase+2u];
31|volatile float p3 = float(y[ybase+2304u]) * weights[wbase+3u];
32|volatile float s01 = p0 + p1;                                // rounded to f32
33|volatile float s012 = s01 + p2;                              // rounded to f32
34|volatile float acc = s012 + p3;                              // rounded to f32
35|out[sbase] = bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase];                    // verbatim
36|```
37|
38|Each `volatile` store materialises its f32 value, so no product can stay
39|unrounded into the next add and no add can be fused with a later mul;
40|the fold is exactly `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3` with a rounding after every add,
41|then one bfloat16 round and the single-rounding bfloat16 `+ shared`,
42|matching the reference's separate kernels (`binary_g` multiply,
43|`col_reduce_small` sum, `copy_v`, `binary_vv`; `slots.py:51-52`,
44|Boundary steps 1–5). No reassociation, no `fma`, no threadgroup memory.
45|
46|Note on spelling: the literal `precise float` qualifier does not compile
47|under MLX 0.32.4 (`metal::precise` is a function namespace in the MLX
48|header, e.g. `metal::precise::exp`; a leading `precise` is parsed as
49|that namespace and rejected). Volatile stepwise barriers are the
50|"explicit rounding barriers" the hypothesis design names as the
51|alternative to `metal::precise` operations, with the same semantics:
52|every mul rounds once to f32, every add rounds once to f32. Probes
53|outside the grader (random [512,4,768] inputs vs the eager MLX
54|reference, 3 × 393,216 elements) gave differ 3–4 for the starting
55|point's contracted expression and differ 0 for this kernel.
56|
57|## Inefficiency removed
58|
59|`ineff-baseline-combine-1` (confirmed, gate): FMA contraction breaks
60|bit-exactness and forfeits the slot's whole saving while G2 fails.
61|`ineff-baseline-combine-2` (confirmed, keep) is retained, not removed:
62|the kernel stays on the ~17 µs/layer dispatch floor (one launch/layer,
63|traffic + compute < 1.6 µs even at 32 rows).
64|
65|## Prediction (µs per layer, decode 1 / 8 / 32 rows)
66|
67|Floor + traffic + barrier cost, on the old independent piece basis (the
68|only same-run basis available; round 2 ranks by chained timing, which
69|has never run on this slot and must replace these numbers):
70|
71|- Dispatch floor (starting point, both round-1 organisations):
72|  ~17 µs/layer, flat in rows (`ineff-baseline-combine-2`).
73|- Traffic: 9,232 B/row ÷ 200 GB/s = 0.05 / 0.37 / 1.48 µs at 1 / 8 / 32
74|  rows; compute ≈ 7 f32 ops × 768 outputs ≤ 0.03 µs.
75|- Barrier cost: 7 volatile thread-local f32 spills per output element,
76|  still under the floor; `ineff-baseline-combine-1` predicts < 0.5
77|  µs/layer for losing FMA fusion. Allow 0.3 µs.
78|
79|Predicted candidate: 17 + 0.05/0.37/1.48 + 0.3 ≈ **17.4 / 17.7 / 18.8
80|µs/layer**. Compiled reference on the same basis: 23.8 / 26.1 / 32.0
81|µs/layer (Claude re-grade, `ineff-baseline-combine-1` *Cost*), so the
82|attempt is predicted to pass G2 with differ 0 at all six sizes and to
83|beat the compiled reference at all three decode sizes. Starting point
84|on the same basis: 18.6 / 17.0 / 18.9 µs/layer (untimed under round 2 —
85|G2-gated); the prediction is that this attempt matches it within the
86|0.5 µs barrier allowance.
87|
88|## Verdict
89|
90|G1 pass, G2 pass at all six sizes, `beats_compiled` true. Baseline is
91|`none`, so there is no `beats_baseline` / `wins_vs_baseline` bar.
92|
93|Grader output (single run, `check_candidate.py ... combine`):
94|
95|- Correctness (differ / max ULP, summed over 20 layers): decode 1 row
96|  0 / 0.0, 8 rows 0 / 0.0, 32 rows 0 / 0.0; prefill 127 rows 0 / 0.0,
97|  1,016 rows 0 / 0.0, 2,048 rows 0 / 0.0 — every element bit-equal to
98|  the eager reference. First difference: none. The starting point's
99|  0 / 2 / 2 and 6 / 50 / 130 differs are closed.
100|- Chained timing (µs per layer, reference / compiled / candidate):
101|  1 row 59.0 / 35.4 / **31.8**, 8 rows 45.0 / 38.2 / **33.6**, 32 rows
102|  52.1 / 43.4 / **39.5**. Candidate beats the compiled reference at all
103|  three decode sizes by 3.6 / 4.6 / 3.9 µs/layer (0.072 / 0.092 /
104|  0.078 ms/step over 20 layers).
105|
106|### Why the timing missed the prediction (>20%)
107|
108|Predicted 17.4 / 17.7 / 18.8 µs/layer; measured (chained) 31.8 / 33.6 /
109|39.5 — +83% / +90% / +110%. The miss is the timing basis, not the

111|the 20 layer calls overlap on the GPU and hide per-call latency; round

{"content":"# Territory: g3 — Claude's round-2 measurement, end to end vs piece by piece

- **Owner:** explorer-g3
- **Status:** exploring
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T17:40:00Z
- **Next:** post ineff-g3-1 (combine 32-row in-step cost), ineff-g3-2 (three-at-8), ineff-g3-3 (prompt/whole-request)

## What it does

This territory is not code in the decode step. It is the measurement that decides whether round 2's attempts actually made the model faster: Claude's re-grading of the two submitted kernels (routing attempt-4, combine attempt-1) and experts attempt-7, the 25 extra row-count checks, the end-to-end token + decode-step (G3) runs, the pairings run, and the whole-request engine comparison, all written up in [claude/findings/muse-round-2.md](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-2.md). Raw data in `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2-pairs/` and `results/runs/2026-11-04-engine-comparison/`. Starting point: round 2's [territory-g3.md](../../round-2/exploration/territory-g3.md) and [ineff-g3-1.md](../../round-2/exploration/ineff-g3-1.md) / [ineff-g3-2.md](../../round-2/exploration/ineff-g3-2.md) (frozen; cited, not repeated). Its question for round 3 is where the end-to-end change differs from the piece timing, and why.

## Checklist

### 1. Re-grading under round 2's rules (`grade-<slot>.json`)

- **Callers:** Claude's measurement on `main` after merging round 2 at `4033cae` ([muse-round-2.md:15](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-2.md)), re-running `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` as round 2 ran it (decode-only chained timing).
- **Callees:** G1 (compiles/runs), G2 (bit-exact at all six sizes), chained piece timing (20 layers, median).
- **Data:** µs per layer, reference / compiled / candidate. Routing attempt-4: 82.0 / 63.4 / **47.7** at 1 row, 196.6 / 128.6 / **117.0** at 8, 160.9 / 129.4 / **126.2** at 32. Combine attempt-1: 62.9 / 55.8 / **44.3**, 65.7 / 60.1 / **46.3**, 62.3 / 47.3 / **42.2**. Experts attempt-7: 151.4 / 143.5 / **140.7**, 235.3 / 233.6 / **168.9**, 801.6 / 800.6 / **512.4**. All three G2 pass, `beats_compiled: true` here — including experts at 1 row (140.7 vs 143.5), where round 2's own run had it slower (93.8 vs 74.8).
- **Neighbours:** absolute times differ from round 2's runs by up to 2× at 1 row; only the within-run comparison means anything ([muse-round-2.md:55](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-2.md)).
- **Cost:** piece pricing only. Against the compiled reference × 20 layers: routing −0.314 / −0.232 / −0.064, combine −0.230 / −0.276 / −0.102, experts −0.056 / −1.294 / −5.764 ms/step at 1 / 8 / 32 rows.
- **Invariants:** decode-only basis; says nothing about prefill (piece 2 does that).

### 2. Re-grading with the two-phase grader (`grade-phases-<slot>-*.json`)

- **Callers:** same measurement, current grader (ADR 0011): `beats_compiled` needs faster-in-one-phase, slower-in-neither, at decode 1 / 8 / 32 and prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows.
- **Data:** µs per layer, reference / compiled / candidate. Routing: decode 68.4 / 65.1 / **49.8**, 169.2 / 135.7 / **113.5**, 159.3 / 145.2 / **121.3** (faster); prefill 102.3 / 87.3 / **227.1** (2.6×), 231.3 / 221.1 / **1298.8** (5.9×), 310.0 / 290.4 / **2513.0** (8.7×). ## Where the end-to-end change differs from the piece timing, and why

Three gaps, all new measurements (round 2's gaps 1–3 were round-1 kernels; gap 3's separating measurement — pairwise G3 — is piece 5 here):

1. **Combine at 32 requests: piece says −0.45 ms/step, step says +1.05/+1.17 ms — not explained.** Piece-implied (piece 2, vs unchanged): (64.6−87.0)×20 = −0.448 ms/step. G3 combine-alone: +1.051 (vLLM) / +1.168 (plain). Swing: +1.499 / +1.616 ms/step = **+75.0 / +80.8 µs per layer** — the loss alone (≈52–59 µs/layer vs unchanged) exceeds the kernel's whole chained time in the grader (64.6 µs/layer). 2. **All three together at 8 requests: parts sum −1.87 ms, measured +0.94 ms — measured, narrowed to three-way, not explained.** Three-way interaction +2.804 ms (pairs, plain) / +2.858 (main, plain) / +2.128 (main, vLLM) / +2.435 (engine, vLLM, from combos) — four runs, both engines, +2.1 to +2.9 ms. Rules out (as before): kernel count (additive, piece 5), token divergence (exact), noise (no overlap), pairs (additive — new).
3. **Prompt time and whole requests: decode-only piece predictions overstate every whole-request gain — measured, and the prefill piece timing predicts the prompt side.** Round 2's decode-only prediction (−0.84/step) implied whole-request wins; measured throughput: submitted +15.9% / +2.1% / −2.7% / −4.1%, routing-only −3.5% at 32×1024, experts variants −10% to −83%. ## Relations

- **Fed by:** the three starting-point attempts (territories `baseline-experts`, `baseline-routing`, `baseline-combine` — their piece timings are pieces 1/2 here), and the grader (territory `grader` — pieces 2/4/6 define the two-phase judgment and the ready check that must reproduce pieces 4–6 inside round 3).

- **For `baseline-combine`:** gap 1 is your in-step cost at 32 rows, measured end to end: +75.0 µs/layer swing from the piece figure in vLLM (+80.8 plain), penalty vs compiled growing +6.1 / +11.2 / +66.2 µs/layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows, plus a +1501.7 ms prompt excess at 32×128 when added to routing+experts (piece 6). {"content":"# Inefficiency: combine attempt-1 costs ~1.1 ms per decode step at 32 requests where the piece timing says faster

- **Owner:** explorer-g3
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T17:40:00Z
- **Next:** verifier to check; mechanism belongs to baseline-combine

## Slot

`combine`. Measurement side owned by territory `g3`; kernel-side mechanism owned by territory `baseline-combine` (starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1`).

## What happens

`time_candidates.py` installs combine attempt-1 alone (`muse-combine`) in every layer's `MoE.__call__` and times the decode step (median of 3 shuffled repeats, 128-token prompts, 256 tokens; [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) piece 4). At 32 requests the step is **slower than the unchanged model by +1.051 ms (vLLM) / +1.168 ms (plain MLX)** — +52.6 / +58.4 µs per layer — while the chained piece timing has the same kernel **faster** than the reference (64.6 vs 87.0 µs/layer) and than the compiled reference (64.6 vs 69.1) in `grade-phases-combine-attempt-1.json`. Full derivation in [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) gap 1. A prefill twin: adding combine-a1 to routing+experts-a7 slows the 32×128 prompt by **+1501.7 ms** (11533.4 vs 10031.7, no range overlap) where the prefill piece says combine saves 11.5 ms/layer/chunk at 2048 rows.

## Cost

Piece-vs-step swing = (G3 change vs unchanged) − (candidate − reference piece × 20 layers), ms per decode step. Piece from `grade-phases-combine-attempt-1.json` (reference / candidate: 52.8 / 45.7 at 1 row, 71.2 / 47.9 at 8, 87.0 / 64.6 at 32); G3 from `console-vllm.txt` / `console-plain.txt` (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/`).

| Engine | 1 request | 8 requests | 32 requests |
|---|---|---|---|
| vLLM: piece-implied | −0.142 | −0.466 | −0.448 |
| vLLM: G3 measured | −0.372 | −0.197 | **+1.051** |
| vLLM: **swing** | −0.230 | +0.269 | **+1.499** |
| plain: piece-implied | −0.142 | −0.466 | −0.448 |
| plain: G3 measured | −0.424 | −0.112 | **+1.168** |
| plain: **swing** | −0.282 | +0.354 | **+1.616** |

Per layer (÷20): vLLM −11.5 / +13.5 / **+75.0 µs**, plain −14.1 / +17.7 / **+80.8 µs**. Against the compiled reference (G3 muse-combine minus G3 compiled-combine, vs piece candidate−compiled × 20): in-step penalty +6.1 / +11.2 / **+66.2 µs/layer** at 1 / 8 / 32 rows in vLLM (+0.122 / +0.224 / +1.324 ms/step) — the penalty grows with rows and explodes at 32.

Reproduction: pairs run (plain, `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2-pairs/`) combine-a1 at 32: +1.051 ms — identical to the main vLLM figure; engine comparison submitted-minus-routing at 32×128: +0.537 − (−0.374) ≈ +0.91 ms. Four runs, both engines. Prefill twin per chunk per layer: +1501.7 ms / (2 chunks × 20 layers) = +37.5 µs/layer/chunk at 2048 rows vs piece −573.2 (273.0 − 846.2).

In bytes: the slot's traffic is 9,232 B/row (`notes.md`), 295 KB/layer at 32 rows ≈ 1.5 µs at peak bandwidth; the paid +52.6 µs/layer is ~35× the traffic floor.

## Kind

Overhead-bound (in the terms of `claude/GLOSSARY.md`): the step is far from peak bandwidth and peak compute, and the lost time scales with neither weight bytes (traffic floor 1.5 µs vs 52.6 paid) nor kernel count (one kernel replaces five, additively — piece 5). Ruled out: the kernel's own chained work (measured faster), token divergence (bit-exact at all 6 + 25 sizes and end to end), repeat noise (no range overlap anywhere it is claimed: vLLM muse-combine [31.433–31.547] vs base [30.346–30.513]).

## Spans

`g3` (measurement), `baseline-combine` (the kernel: grid `rows*768` threads in 256-thread threadgroups, volatile-stepwise fold, no threadgroup memory), `grader` (the chained piece timing is the instrument that cannot see this cost).

## Predicted saving

If the in-step penalty were removed while keeping the kernel's chained work, the step gains back the swing: up to **1.50 ms/step at 32 requests in vLLM** (1.62 plain), i.e. muse-combine would measure ≈ −0.45 ms (the piece-implied value) instead of +1.05 ms; **0.27 ms/step at 8 requests** (0.35 plain); nothing claimed at 1 request, where the swing is negative (over-delivers) and within 1-row noise. At prefill sizes, removing the twin recovers **up to 1.5 s of 32×128 prompt time** on the all-three variant (measured 11533.4 ms, would be ≈10032 ms). Per prefill chunk (chained basis): nothing further — the kernel already beats compiled at 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows (62.8 / 226.5 / 273.0 vs 66.1 / 271.6 / 520.4 µs/layer), so no per-chunk saving is predicted on the grader basis; the prize is the in-step composition only. This is an upper bound on the prize, not a prediction that a specific kernel change recovers it: the mechanism is unknown, and any fix must hold the bit-exact G2 at all six sizes.
