1|# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.
6|
7|## Hardware limits
8|
9|**Peak bandwidth**:
10|The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
11|_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed
12|
13|**Peak compute**:
14|The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
15|_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)
16|
17|**Achieved bandwidth**:
18|The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
19|_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)
20|
21|**Arithmetic intensity**:
22|Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
23|_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio
24|
25|**Ridge point**:
26|The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.
27|
28|**Roofline**:
29|The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.
30|
31|## Bottlenecks and fixes
32|
33|**Bandwidth-bound**:
34|A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.
35|
36|**Compute-bound**:
37|A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.
38|
39|**Overhead-bound**:
40|A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
41|_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)
42|
43|**Bottleneck**:
44|The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
45|_Avoid_: issue, slowness
46|
47|**Kernel**:
48|One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
49|_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)
50|
51|**Occupancy**:
52|The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
53|_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)
54|
55|**Knock-out**:
56|A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
57|_Avoid_: ablation
58|
59|**Baseline**:
60|The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.
61|
62|**Fix**:
63|One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
64|_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak
65|
66|## Inference
67|
68|**Prefill**:
69|Processing a request's whole prompt through the model before its first token is generated, in chunks of up to the engine's token budget per pass (2,048 tokens here).
70|_Avoid_: prompt phase (say prefill, or prompt processing)
71|
72|**Decode step**:
73|One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.
74|
75|**Decode rows**:
76|The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
77|_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency
78|
79|**Client concurrency**:
80|The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.
81|_Avoid_: batch size
82|
83|## Mixture of experts
84|
85|**Expert**:
86|One of the interchangeable feed-forward blocks in a layer; MobileMoE-S has 60 routed experts per layer.
87|
88|**Active experts**:
89|The experts the router picks for one token in one layer (4 for MobileMoE-S).
90|_Avoid_: selected experts, top-k experts
91|
92|**Distinct experts**:
93|The number of different experts used by all decode rows together in one layer during one decode step; it decides how much expert weight data the step must read.
94|_Avoid_: unique experts, expert coverage
95|
96|## Models
97|
98|**MobileMoE-S**:
99|Meta's smallest on-device mixture-of-experts model (about 1.3B parameters in total, about 272M used per token), studied here in its SFT (full-precision) and QAT (int4) variants.
100|
101|**Muse Spark**:
102|Meta's hosted model, and the Muse agent in round 1.
103|
104|**Muse Wonder**:
105|Meta's most capable model family, in preview; its standard variant runs on Meta's Model API. The Muse agent in round 2.
106|
107|**Muse Wonder Full**:
108|The higher-capability variant of Muse Wonder, available only in Muse Code with a subscription; not used in this project.
109|
110|**Muse agent**:
111|The Meta model that chooses which pieces of the decode step to replace and writes their kernels, on the branch `muse-agent`: Muse Spark in round 1 and from round 3, Muse Wonder in round 2. It is never the model under study.
112|_Avoid_: Muse (alone), Meta agent
113|
114|**Muse Code**:
115|Meta's own coding agent for the terminal; the only program in which the Muse agent does its work in this project.
116|_Avoid_: Muse CLI, Meta Code
117|
118|**Muse agent session**:
119|A Muse Code session in which the Muse agent writes every turn, the lead's and every helper's, kept apart from Claude's work by its own branch, folder and commit trailer.
120|_Avoid_: Muse Spark session (round 2's model was Muse Wonder), guardrail (for the session itself), Meta mode
121|
122|## The Muse agent's work
123|
124|**Slot**:
125|One replaceable piece of the mixture-of-experts block (routing, combine, or the routed experts), with fixed inputs and outputs, that the Muse agent may replace with its own kernels.
126|_Avoid_: target (that is a slot the Muse agent has chosen), module
127|
128|**Round**:
129|One Muse agent session in which a swarm explores and then builds, writing in its own round folder, followed by Claude's independent measurement of what it produced. Once a round is finished, its files are frozen.
130|_Avoid_: iteration, cycle
131|
132|**Round folder**:
133|Where one round writes all its files: round 1 at the top of `muse-spark/`, each later round in `muse-spark/round-<N>/`.
134|
135|**Starting point**:
136|The plan each round from round 2 on begins with, drawn from the earlier rounds and Claude's measurement: each slot's baseline, or the attempt to start from where it has none, with its end-to-end effect; what is left to build; the refuted claims; and the territories to explore again.
137|_Avoid_: recap, retrospective
138|
139|**Improvement**:
140|An attempt that is faster than its bar in one phase, prefill or decode, and slower in neither; a faster decode step bought with a slower prefill is not one.
141|_Avoid_: speedup (for a change measured in one phase only)
142|
143|**Hand-off**:
144|An attempt's choice to run the compiled reference instead of its own kernels above a row count it names, so prefill-sized inputs stay on MLX's code.
145|_Avoid_: fallback
146|
147|**Ready check**:
148|The lead's in-round run of G3 over every candidate attempt at once, with its protocol fixed and its own log audited; only its passing verdict makes an attempt ready.
149|_Avoid_: G3 (that is Claude's run after the round), end-to-end test
150|
151|**Candidate**:
152|An attempt that passes the grader's gates and its boundary check, with its claims checked, and waits for the ready check.
153|_Avoid_: ready (that needs the ready check)
154|
155|**Prediction**:
156|A speed number no one measured for exactly what it describes, labelled as such, counting only the candidate's own measured effect and shown beside the measured value once there is one.
157|_Avoid_: expected gain, estimate (unlabelled)
158|
159|**Unverified**:
160|What no one measured, listed as such in a hypothesis and in the round's final claims, and never assumed free, neutral or zero.
161|
162|**Baseline** (of a slot):
163|A slot's best attempt so far that passes the current G2 and that Claude's G3 accepted, named in Claude's measurement of the previous round; every new attempt for that slot must beat it in the same grader run. A slot may have none.
164|_Avoid_: reference (that is the original MLX code and its compiled version)
165|
166|**Swarm**:
167|All the agents of one round, the lead and its helpers, working toward one goal through shared documents that each of them reads and adds to.
168|_Avoid_: team, crew
169|
170|**Lead agent**:
171|The one agent of a swarm that starts the helpers, keeps the shared documents current, settles clashes and commits; it neither explores nor grades.
172|_Avoid_: orchestrator, main agent
173|
174|**Helper agent**:
175|An agent the lead starts: an explorer, the verifier, a builder, a boundary agent or a checker. It reports back and never commits.
176|_Avoid_: worker, subagent (when the role matters, not the mechanism)
177|
178|**Reminder agent**:
179|One of Muse Code's own background agents, which watch the lead's progress and may nudge it, for example to check a claim before it says it is done; the Muse agent's model writes their turns too, but they take no part in the work.
180|_Avoid_: helper (that is one the lead starts)
181|
182|**Exploration phase**:
183|The first part of a round, in which explorers map the code and the measurements and find where the decode step loses time.
184|
185|**Implementation phase**:
186|The second part of a round, in which builders write and grade solutions to the confirmed inefficiencies.
187|_Avoid_: hypothesis phase
188|
189|**Territory**:
190|The part of the code or the measurements that one explorer covers: a module, a single important file, or a measurement document.
191|_Avoid_: area, lens
192|
193|**Analysis**:
194|The swarm's shared account of the code, written during exploration: the context, how the territories feed each other, and the ranked inefficiencies, each with its cost and sources.
195|_Avoid_: diagnosis, findings (those are Claude's)
196|
197|**Inefficiency**:
198|One cause of lost time in the decode step: where it is in the code, what it costs, and what removing it should save. It is confirmed or refuted against its sources before anyone builds on it.
199|_Avoid_: issue, bottleneck (that is the single largest cause)
200|
201|**Hypothesis**:
202|A proposed solution to one inefficiency: the slot it replaces, the boundary it keeps and the saving it predicts, tested by competing attempts.
203|_Avoid_: strategy, plan
204|
205|**Boundary**:
206|What a solution must keep identical so that the steps before and after its slot work exactly as before: the slot's inputs and outputs, their dtypes, and the rounding points.
207|_Avoid_: interface (unqualified), contract
208|
209|**Attempt**:
210|One grader run of a solution a builder wrote, committed by the lead; attempts for a slot are numbered in order within each round and have no limit.
211|_Avoid_: try, submission, draft

7|all six, 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8 µs/layer chained vs compiled
8|75.9 / 234.6 / 798.2 — loses only at 1 row by 16.2 µs) with the
9|down-interleave `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-6` tried
10|(one simdgroup, two down blocks, merged K loop), made to compile
11|within the pipeline threadgroup limit. Attempt-6 failed G1:
12|`Thread group size (512) is greater than the maximum allowed
13|threads per threadgroup (448)` — its compiled pipeline's
14|`maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` fell to 448 for the identical
15|512-thread launch.
16|
17|## The one main change
18|
19|Attempt-6's merged down loop, with the second accumulator's storage
20|shared so the kernel compiles at 512 threads. Everything else is
21|copied from attempt-5/6, not redesigned (`spec.json` byte-identical
22|to attempt-5/6; `block-1.metal` helpers `qvm_block`,
23|`qvm_gate_up_pair`, `qvm_down_pair`, `qmm_accum` bodies byte-identical
24|to attempt-6 by diff; `block-0.metal` gate/up, silu and prefill
25|branches otherwise byte-identical):
26|
27|- **Before (attempt-5):** down ran 24 blocks of 32 outputs in 2
28|  sequential waves of 16 simdgroups (`b = v*16 + simd`, `b < 24`):
29|  wave 0 computed blocks 0–15, wave 1 blocks 16–23 (simdgroups
30|  8–15 idle), each block a separate `qvm_block` call — 12 strided
31|  K steps per lane (`k = lane, lane+32, …, lane+352` over `K=384`),
32|  then `simd_sum` and the parallel store
33|  `y[pair*768 + b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`. The second wave's
34|  first load waited for the first wave's last accumulate.
35|- **Attempt-6's down change (kept):** one simdgroup computes two
36|  down blocks in one merged K loop (`qvm_down_pair`, block-1).
37|  Simdgroup `s < 12` owns the consecutive pair `b0 = 2s`,
38|  `b1 = 2s+1` (12 pairs, one wave; simdgroups 12–15 idle, as in
39|  gate/up). For each strided `k` both blocks' loads are issued
40|  before either accumulates — block 0's scale/bias and 4 weight
41|  words, then block 1's scale/bias and 4 weight words (plus the
42|  shared `tg_h[k]`, read once) — and only then do the two
43|  accumulation passes run, block 0's 32 terms then block 1's, into
44|  separate accumulators. The 24 down blocks therefore run as 12
45|  interleaved pairs instead of 2 sequential waves.
46|- **This attempt's fix vs attempt-6:** attempt-6 declared three
47|  distinct 32-float thread arrays — kernel-scope `p[32]`, a
48|  gate/up-scoped `pu[32]` and a down-scoped `q[32]` — and the
49|  compiler charged all three against the per-threadgroup budget
50|  (`maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` 448 < 512) even though `pu` and
51|  `q` are live in disjoint phases. Attempt-7 hoists the second
52|  accumulator to kernel scope: `float p[32]; float q[32];` beside
53|  the existing buffers in `block-0`, and passes the same `q` as
54|  gate/up's second accumulator (`qvm_gate_up_pair(..., p, q)`) and
55|  as down's second accumulator (`qvm_down_pair(..., p, q)`),
56|  deleting both scoped declarations. The kernel again has two
57|  distinct 32-float thread arrays, exactly attempt-5's footprint,
58|  at unchanged 512 threads.
59|
60|Everything else is kept identical, as the task requires:
61|
62|- **Per-block bits unchanged.** In `qvm_down_pair` each block's adds
63|  run in exactly `qvm_block`'s order: the same strided `k` sequence,
64|  the same float32 dequant terms
65|  `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` / `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)`
66|  with `s1 = scale/16`, in the same per-output sequence; the two
67|  accumulators are independent, so interleaving cannot reorder
68|  either block's own adds. Each accumulator then gets the identical
69|  `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` `simd_sum` tree as `qvm_block`.
70|  The `(bfloat)` rounding at the store is unchanged.
71|- **Sharing is a pure storage rename.** Gate/up and down run in
72|  disjoint phases separated by two `threadgroup_barrier`s (after
73|  gate/up and after silu): gate/up's `q` values are stored to
74|  `tg_up` before the first barrier, silu consumes only
75|  `tg_gate`/`tg_up`/`tg_h`, and `qvm_down_pair` re-zeroes both
76|  `p[0..31]` and `q[0..31]` on entry (as `qvm_gate_up_pair` does),
77|  so no value can leak across the barrier through the shared array.
78|  Peak live floats per phase is unchanged (64 in gate/up, 64 in
79|  down); only the distinct-array count charged by the compiler
80|  drops from three to two.
81|- **Parallel lane stores kept.** After the two `simd_sum`s every
82|  lane holds both blocks' full reduced 32-vectors, so lane `j`
83|  stores element `j` of each block — one store per lane per block:
84|  `y[pair*768 + b0*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`,
85|  `y[pair*768 + b1*32 + lane] = (bfloat)q[lane]`.
86|- **Gate/up interleave, silu, prefill scalar branch, grids and
87|  rounding points identical.** Gate/up still calls
88|  `qvm_gate_up_pair` with attempt-5's parallel `tg_gate`/`tg_up`
89|  stores; the full-bfloat16 silu-mul is byte-identical; the
90|  `rows >= 60` prefill branch still uses the scalar `qmm_accum`
91|  (bfloat16-rounded dequant, contiguous `BK=32` order) for gate,
92|  up and down, with the same `x_shape[0] >= 60` dispatch
93|  threshold; `spec.json` (one kernel, `rows*2048` threads =
94|  `rows*4` groups of 512) is byte-identical. No kernel split, no
95|  new device-memory intermediate, same four bfloat16 rounding
96|  points and positional `y[r,j]`.
97|
98|## Which inefficiency it removes, and how
99|
100|- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-5's
101|  miss analysis left the still-sequential down chain as the
102|  largest named remainder at 1 row — 12 strided steps × 2 waves
103|  behind the silu barrier, plus the `tg_x` load, silu, barriers
104|  and chained fixed cost. Attempts 1–3 showed threadgroup count
105|  past 4 is not the lever and attempt-4/5 showed overlapping the
106|  per-block serial K chain is. The down product was the last
107|  product still running its blocks in fully sequential waves with
108|  only one block's loads in flight per simdgroup; merging two
109|  blocks per simdgroup puts both blocks' loads (8 weight words +
110|  2 scales/biases per step) in flight in every step, so each
111|  block's load latency has the other block's loads/compute to
112|  hide behind, without touching any block's `simd_sum` order.
113|  The shared-`q` fix is what lets this merged loop launch at all:
114|  attempt-6 proved the three-array form exceeds the pipeline
115|  threadgroup budget at 512 threads.
116|- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
117|  attempt-5's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
118|  verbatim — the interleave does not touch prefill arithmetic.
119|- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
120|  kept, as in attempts 1–6 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
121|  the interleave changes load scheduling, not bytes.
122|
123|## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)
124|
125|512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 (`spec.json` identical to attempt-5/6).
126|Threadgroup memory unchanged: `tg_x[768] + tg_gate[384] +
127|tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]` bfloat16 = **3,840 B** of 32,768 B,
128|rows-independent. Distinct thread arrays are two 32-float
129|accumulators (`p`, shared `q`) — attempt-5's count, one fewer than
130|attempt-6's three. Grid scales as `rows*4` groups, so the kernel
131|is valid at every `rows ≥ 1`, on both sides of 60. Decode coverage:
132|12 simdgroups × 2 blocks × 32 lanes = 768 outputs per pair, each
133|written exactly once, as before.
134|
135|## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)
136|
137|Attempt-5 (other run): 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8 µs/layer vs compiled
138|75.9 / 234.6 / 798.2 and reference 95.7 / 232.4 / 802.3. Attempt-6
139|predicted 85 / 156 / 540 but never launched, so that prediction is
140|untested, not missed. Baseline `none`, so no
141|`wins_vs_baseline` / `beats_baseline`. Weight bytes per layer
142|(552,960 B/pair): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs;
143|bandwidth floors at 200 GB/s: 11.1 / 88.5 / 353.9 µs.
144|Attempt-5 effective: 24.0 / 109.2 / 132.3 GB/s.
145|
146|Down arithmetic: `K = 384` → 12 strided steps per lane per block.
147|Attempt-5 pays 2 waves × 12 steps sequentially after the silu
148|barrier; this attempt pays 12 merged steps. A merged step issues
149|twice the loads (8 weight words, 2 scales) for twice the
150|accumulate work, so it costs more than a single-block step but
151|less than two — the gate/up precedent (attempt-4) hid ≈ 20% of
152|the merged chain's exposed latency at 1 row.
153|
154|- **1 row: 85.** Latency-bound (floor 11.1 µs). The down phase
155|  sits alone behind the silu barrier; at attempt-5's 92.1 µs the
156|  product chains (gate/up merged 24 steps + down 2×12 steps)
157|  dominate, so the down waves are roughly a third of the layer
158|  (≈ 30 µs). Collapsing 24 sequential steps into 12 merged ones
159|  at ≈ 1.3× the per-step cost (8 loads share the `tg_h[k]` read
160|  and the loop control) cuts the down phase to ≈ 23 µs, saving
161|  ≈ 7 µs → 92.1 − 7 ≈ **85 µs**. Still above compiled 75.9 — the
162|  `tg_x` load, silu, barriers and chained launch/link cost
163|  remain untouched — but it should roughly halve the 16.2 µs gap.
164|  The shared `q` itself is arithmetic-neutral; its only timing
165|  effect is restoring a legal 512-thread pipeline.
166|- **8 rows: 156.** 32 groups per call partly hide one group's
167|  down tail behind other groups' K loops (attempt-5 already at
168|  109.2 GB/s), so only part of the 1-row saving survives:
169|  162.0 − 6 ≈ **156 µs**, keeping the win over compiled 234.6.
170|- **32 rows: 540.** Streaming-bound (attempt-5: 132.3 GB/s).
171|  Group parallelism already hides load latency, so the merged
172|  loop buys nothing; the peak live accumulator count is the same
173|  64 floats gate/up already held in attempt-5, so no new spill
174|  tax is expected beyond attempt-6's identical merged step:
175|  534.8 + 5 ≈ **540 µs**, keeping the win over compiled 798.2.
176|
177|G1 prediction: pass — the launch is attempt-5's (512 threads,
178|3,840 B threadgroup memory) and the only change from attempt-5's
179|register footprint is that down now also holds a second live
180|accumulator, which gate/up already held in the same kernel that
181|launched at 512; the distinct-array count is attempt-5's two,
182|not attempt-6's three.
183|G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — each
184|down block's dequant terms, add order and `simd_sum` are
185|attempt-5's by construction (separate logical accumulators,
186|shared storage re-zeroed per call), gate/up and prefill are
187|byte-identical to attempt-5's, and the parallel store writes the
188|same `(bfloat)p[j]` values, just one merged loop earlier.
189|
190|## Verdict
191|
192|G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0
193|everywhere** (decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048 — no first
194|difference, `experts` reports the first differing element only on
195|failure and there is none) — the shared-storage rename preserves
196|attempt-5/6 bits by construction and the grader confirms it: the
197|merged down loop's per-block order and the parallel stores are
198|bit-exact, and the `rows >= 60` scalar `qmm_accum` branch is
199|untouched. The 512-thread launch now compiles: sharing one
200|kernel-scope `q[32]` between gate/up's second accumulator and
201|down's second block restores the pipeline's threadgroup budget
202|that attempt-6's three distinct arrays exceeded (512 > 448).
203|Chained timing µs/layer (this run; candidate vs reference vs
204|compiled): **1 row 93.8 / 78.9 / 74.8 (loses to compiled by
205|19.0, loses to reference by 14.9)**; 8 rows 160.1 / 235.8 /
206|236.5 (wins); 32 rows 510.1 / 797.0 / 792.7 (wins).
207|`beats_compiled` false — only the 1-row size misses, as in
208|attempt-5. Baseline `none` — no `wins_vs_baseline` /
209|`beats_baseline`.
210|
211|Against attempt-5 (different run; compiled shifted 75.9 → 74.8
212|at 1 row and 798.2 → 792.7 at 32 rows between runs, so treat
213|cross-run deltas as indicative): 93.8 vs 92.1 at 1 row
214|(**+1.8%**), 160.1 vs 162.0 at 8 rows (**−1.2%**), 510.1 vs
215|534.8 at 32 rows (**−4.6%**). Effective bandwidth on pair
216|bytes: 23.6 / 110.5 / 138.8 GB/s (attempt-5: 24.0 / 109.2 /
217|132.3). The down interleave therefore helps where group
218|parallelism already hides load latency (32 rows, +4.9% GB/s,
219|new best 32-row time in this hypothesis) and is neutral at
220|8 rows, but it does not move the latency-bound 1-row size.
221|
222|## Miss analysis (prediction 85 / 156 / 540, measured 93.8 / 160.1 / 510.1)
223|
224|Misses are +10.4% / +2.6% / −5.5% — all inside the 20% bar, so
225|no formal miss, but the size pattern was inverted versus the
226|prediction (saving predicted largest at 1 row, actually largest
227|at 32 rows) and that needs explaining:
228|
229|1. **The compilation fix worked exactly as predicted, the
230|   latency saving did not.** G1 passes at 512 threads with the
231|   same 3,840 B of threadgroup memory, confirming attempt-6's
232|   failure was the third distinct accumulator array, not
233|   threadgroup memory or the merged loop itself: two distinct
234|   arrays (`p`, shared `q`) fit, three do not. That part of the
235|   prediction (pure rename, identical bits) is confirmed by
236|   G2's differ 0 at all six sizes.
237|2. **At 1 row the down waves were not a third of the layer's
238|   latency in the way the arithmetic assumed.** The prediction
239|   priced the down phase at ≈ 30 µs and the merged step at
240|   1.3× a single-block step. Measured 93.8 ≈ attempt-5's 92.1
241|   says the merged step costs closer to 2× at this size: with
242|   only 4 threadgroups (one per pair) on 16 cores, the down
243|   phase's latency was already hidden *across* simdgroups —
244|   attempt-5's wave 0 runs 16 blocks concurrently per group,
245|   attempt-7 runs 12 simdgroups each serially merging two
246|   blocks, so concurrent in-flight loads per group fall
247|   (48 vs 64 simdgroup-block chains per call at 1 row) while
248|   each chain's step doubles its loads. The gate/up precedent
249|   hid ≈ 20% because gate and up *share* the `tg_x[k]` read and
250|   both blocks' loads were previously fully sequential phases;
251|   down's two blocks share only `tg_h[k]` and already overlapped
252|   across the 16-simdgroup wave. The remaining ≈ 19 µs gap to
253|   compiled (93.8 vs 74.8) is therefore still the `tg_x` load,
254|   silu, the two barriers and the chained launch/link cost —
255|   none of which this change touches.
256|3. **At 32 rows the merged loop pays for a different reason.**
257|   One wave instead of two removes a wave-quantization tail
258|   (wave 1 ran 8 of 16 simdgroups) on every pair and halves the
259|   down loop's barrier-free step count, which at 128 groups
260|   shows up as throughput: 138.8 vs 132.3 GB/s. The predicted
261|   +5 µs register tax did not appear (measured −24.7 µs vs
262|   attempt-5 cross-run) — consistent with the shared `q`: peak
263|   live accumulators never exceed gate/up's 64 floats, so there
264|   is no new spill, and claim 2's cross-simdgroup overlap loss
265|   is hidden by group parallelism at this size.
266|
267|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: a merged pair helps only
268|where the two blocks were previously *phases* (gate then up,
269|fully sequential, shared activation read); where the blocks
270|already ran as concurrent simdgroups in one wave (down's 24
271|blocks), merging trades cross-simdgroup parallelism for
272|in-step parallelism and is latency-neutral at 4 groups — the
273|1-row remainder is fixed cost and the serial gate/up chain,
274|not the down wave count. Register headroom at 512 threads is
275|exactly two 32-float accumulators; a third distinct array,
276|however short-lived, fails G1.
277|
278|## Next change
279|
280|Leave the down interleave in (it is the best 32-row time and
281|G2-exact) and attack the actual 1-row remainder named above:
282|the `tg_x` load + silu + barrier chain and the chained fixed
283|cost. Concretely, overlap the down product's first K steps with
284|the silu tail (down blocks whose `tg_h` slice is already
285|written) or narrow the silu barrier to a simdgroup-local one —
286|but any such change must keep the full-bfloat16 silu bits and
287|every accumulation order, and must not add a third accumulator
288|array (this attempt's G1 lesson).

180|## How each attempt is judged
181|
182|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.
183|
184|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
185|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
186|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
187|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
188|
189|   At every size:
190|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
191|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
192|
193|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
194|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
195|3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
196|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
197|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
198|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
199|
200|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
201|
202|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).
203|
204|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
205|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
206|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
207|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same` or `slower`); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.
208|
209|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
210|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
211|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
212|- **Per phase:** decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) are each `faster` when every size is, `slower` when any size is, and `not slower` otherwise.
213|- **`beats_compiled`** is true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
214|
215|It is a guide; the ready check in the round, and Claude's G3 after it, decide.
216|
217|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, or after 5 attempts. {"content":"# Territory: quantized-kernels (round 3 — prefill SPEED)

- **Owner:** explorer-quantized-kernels
- **Status:** done
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T18:05:00Z
- **Next:** none — rhs speed anatomy mapped (§S1–§S7), 2 inefficiencies posted, note left on `territory-baseline-experts`

## What it does

This territory is MLX 0.32.4's `mx.gather_qmm` Metal kernels behind the
`experts` slot (`quantized.h`, `quantized_utils.h`). Round 1 mapped the
decode kernel (`affine_gather_qvm`) and round 2 mapped the prefill
kernel's ROUNDING (`affine_gather_qmm_rhs`: bfloat-rounded dequant +
8-wide frag accumulation, and why a size branch at rows ≥ 60 is
required) —
[`muse-spark/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md`](../../exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md)
and
[`muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md`](../round-2/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md)
(both frozen; cited, not rewritten). Round 3 needs its SPEED: the
compiled prefill runs at 960.8 / 4306.0 / 11998.9 µs per layer at
127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows
(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`),
15–28× faster than the starting point's scalar prefill branch, and any
fast exact prefill branch — or `max_rows` hand-off that skips one —
must match or avoid what is mapped here. This entry writes only what is
new: tiling, occupancy, dequant/x/MMA dataflow, rate analysis, and the
match-or-avoid list. Rounding facts are round 2's (§D/§E/§F there).

## The checklist

### S1. Tiling and grid — what `gather_qmm_rhs` launches (speed view)

- **Callers:** same dispatch as round 2 §A (frozen): `M==1 && B>=16 &&
  right_sorted_ && B/E>=4`, i.e. rows ≥ 60. Legacy tiles `bm=16, bn=32,
  bk=32`, `wm=1, wn=2` (round 2 §B; NAX never runs on this GPU).
- **Callees:** `affine_gather_qmm_rhs<bfloat16,32,4,BM=16,BN=32,BK=32,
  WM=1,WN=2,transpose=false>` (`quantized.h:2570-2593`) with
  `group_dims=(32,2,1)=64` threads and `grid_dims=((N+31)/32,
  min(B,ceil(B/16)+E-1),1)` (round 2 §B; host formula at
  `quantized.cpp:1817-1819`). Per call:

  | prefill rows | B | grid_y | gate/up groups (12×gy) | down groups (24×gy) | per layer (3 prods) |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 127 | 508 | 91 | 1,092 | 2,184 | 4,368 dispatched (2,880 useful + 1,488 empty) |
  | 1,016 | 4,064 | 313 | 3,756 | 7,512 | 15,024 dispatched (14,400 + 624) |
  | 2,048 | 8,192 | 571 | 6,852 | 13,704 | 27,408 dispatched (25,920 + 1,488) |

  Useful counts use balanced-expert `T=60/300/540` row tiles (round 2
  §C); empty counts are round-2 `ineff-quantized-kernels-1`'s table ×
  48 N-tiles per layer. Each group runs `K_it=K/32` loop iterations
  (24 gate/up, 12 down) over §S2–§S4's dataflow, then one
  `store_result(_safe)`.
- **Data:** threadgroup `Xs[16×40]+Ws[32×40]` bfloat16 = 1,280+2,560 =
  3,840 B per group (round 2 §C; `BK_padded=BN_padded=40`,
  `quantized.h:2596-2597`). 64 threads × 3.84 KB is a small, cheap
  group — the opposite of the decode `qvm` grid's occupancy problem.
- **Neighbours:** 3 offsets kernels + sort/unsort + `swiglu` share the
  chained slot time (§S5); the mains dominate by byte floors (§S5).
- **Cost:** no per-kernel prefill timing exists (grader times the
  chained slot only); §S5 prices the mains from the chained totals.
- **Invariants:** regrouping rows is free (round 2 §C invariant):
  padded rows never mix into valid rows (`store_result_safe`,
  `:2694`), so a replacement may use any BM, variable tiles, or no
  tiles, as long as each row's own accumulation matches round 2
  §D+§E. Grid over-provisioning (≤59 y-tiles) is pure waste (§S6).

### S2. Dequant dataflow — `QuantizedBlockLoader`, per-K-tile (new)

- **Callers:** the rhs kernel instantiates the loader with
  `BROWS=BK=32, BCOLS=BN=32, tgp_size=64` (`quantized.h:2613-2621`).
- **Callees:** `load_unsafe` (`quantized.h:736-747`) → `dequantize`
  bits=4 (`:617-623`): per packed byte, `w[2i]=(bfloat)(s·(b&0x0f)+b)`,
  `w[2i+1]=(bfloat)((s/16)·(b&0xf0)+b)`, with `s,b` the float-upcast
  scale/bias. The `s/16` high-nibble form equals `s·(b>>4)+b` as a
  float (power-of-two scaling is exact), so both forms round
  identically — attempt-7's `qmm_accum` relies on this
  (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/block-1.metal:203-205`).
- **Data:** `n_reads=(16·32)/64=8`: each of the 64 threads loads 1
  scale + 1 bias (threads pair up on 32 distinct `bi` rows, so
  scales are fetched 2× — negligible), reads 8 consecutive packed
  bytes, and writes 16 dequantized bfloat into `Ws`
  (`:686-734`). Per K-iteration per group: a full 32×32 tile,
  1,024 elements from 512 B packed + 128 B scales/biases.
  `next()` advances scales by `group_stride=BROWS·src_ld/group_size`
  per K tile (`:772-790`) — exactly one scale group per (K tile,
  N tile), matching the `[E,K,N/32]` layout.
- **Neighbours:** weights stream per (row tile, N tile, K tile)
  visit; NOTHING is reused across visits — each extra row tile of
  an expert re-reads and re-dequantizes its full 184,320 B
  (147,456 weights + 36,864 scales/biases; round 2 §C). Dequant
  element-ops per product per layer = `T·K·N` = 17.7M / 88.5M /
  159.2M (round 2 §D). At ~10 ALU ops each (and/shift, mul, add,
  round, tg store) that is ≈0.18/0.89/1.59 GOP per product,
  ≈0.5/2.7/4.8 GOP per layer — under 10% of the measured time even
  at scalar rates, so dequant ALU is a real but minor share; the
  design win is AMORTIZATION (one dequant serves ≤16 rows) plus
  coalescing, not ALU savings.
- **Cost:** weight bytes per layer = `3·T·184,320` = 33.2 / 165.9 /
  298.6 MB → floors at 200 GB/s (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:10`) of 166 /
  829 / 1,493 µs (§S5). Coalescing: `BlockLoader`-style row runs —
  thread pairs `(2i,2i+1)` share K-row `bi` and read bytes 0–7 and
  8–15 of it (consecutive, one 16 B line), pairs stride by
  `N/2=192/384 B` per K-row (`:727-734`) — the standard tiled-GEMM
  pattern, full lines, no `qvm`-style 192 B-stride scalar loads
  (contrast round-1 §A / round-2 §F).
- **Invariants:** the bfloat16 rounding into `Ws` is rounding point
  1 (round 2 §D) — a fast branch must reproduce these exact rounded
  weights (same `s·q+b` float value, same cast), whatever its
  grouping.

### S3. Activation (x) dataflow — re-read per N-tile (new)

- **Callers:** `BlockLoader<bfloat16,BM=16,BK=32,dst_ld=40,
  reduction_dim=1,tgp_size=64>` (`quantized.h:2611-2612`).
- **Callees:** `load_unsafe` (`steel/gemm/loader.h:74-80`) copies
  verbatim bfloat16→bfloat16 (exact, no rounding); partial row
  tiles (`tgp_bm<16`) take `load_safe` (`loader.h:83-128`), which
  zero-pads via a per-element `tmp_idx/tmp_val` bound-check dance —
  strictly slower loads on every partial tile.
- **Data:** `n_reads=512/64=8, TCOLS=4, TROWS=16`: threads `(4i..4i+3)`
  own x-row `bi=i`, each reading 8 consecutive bfloat (one 16 B
  vector) — a full coalesced 16×32 tile per K-iteration, 1 KB per
  group per iteration. But EVERY (row tile, N tile) group loads its
  own copy of the same x rows: issued x bytes per product =
  `T·(N/32)·K_it·1KB` = T·12·24 KB (gate/up) = 17.3 / 86.4 /
  155.5 MB per product per layer — the x row-tile (24 KB) is
  re-read 12× (gate/up) or 24× (down), once per N-tile. Total
  issued x per layer ≈ 52 / 259 / 467 MB — EXCEEDS issued weight
  bytes (33/166/299 MB). Counterpart: the 12–24 sharing groups run
  concurrently on 24 KB of shared addresses, so all but the first
  read per row tile should hit in cache; distinct x per layer is
  only `B·(768+768+384)·2B` = 2.0 / 15.6 / 31.4 MB. DRAM x-traffic
  is therefore between 2/16/31 MB (all hits) and 52/259/467 MB
  (all miss) — unmeasured, and a replacement that loads each x
  row-tile once per N-slab (or once per row, qvm-style into
  registers) banks the difference for free.
- **Neighbours:** at 127 rows EVERY useful tile is partial
  (`cnt_e≈8.5<16`, all 60 tiles): 100% of useful work takes
  `gemm_loop_unaligned` + `load_safe` + `store_result_safe`. At
  1,016 ≈20% of tiles are partial (5th of 5 per expert), at 2,048
  ≈11% (9th of 9). The 127-row size thus pays the safe-path tax
  everywhere — a regrouped branch with full tiles (e.g. smaller or
  variable BM) avoids it.
- **Cost:** folded into §S5's mains range; the safe-path tax has no
  separate measured figure (no per-tile timing exists).
- **Invariants:** x values are exact through the loader (no rounding
  point) — regrouping never changes them.

### S4. MMA structure — what each K-iteration does (new)

- **Callers:** `gemm_loop_aligned` (full tiles) /
  `gemm_loop_unaligned` (partial) (`quantized_utils.h:6-75`): per
  iteration, barrier → load x + dequant w → barrier → `mma()`.
  TWO threadgroup barriers per 32-K step, 48 per gate/up group, 24
  per down group — the kernel's latency skeleton.
- **Callees:** `BlockMMA<...,BM=16,BN=32,BK=32,WM=1,WN=2>`
  (`steel/gemm/mma.h:439-537`), `AccumType=float` default
  (`mma.h:451`). Per simdgroup: `TM=16/8=2`, `TN=32/16=2` frags;
  `mma()` steps `kk` over BK in 4 8-wide steps, each
  `tile_matmad` issuing 2·2·1=4 `simdgroup_matrix` 8×8×8
  multiply-accumulates (`mma.h:406-427,513-537`) with 3
  `simdgroup_barrier`s per step. Per group per K-iteration:
  2 simdgroups × 4 steps × 4 MMAs = 32 MMAs = 32,768 flops;
  per gate group total: 24 × 32,768 = 786K flops.
- **Data:** operands reload from threadgroup (`Ws` bfloat→float
  widen on load, `mma.h:57-67`); accumulators stay in float frag
  registers across the whole K loop; one float→bfloat16 store per
  output (`store_result`, `mma.h:540-592`) — rounding point 2's
  container (round 2 §E). Useful MMA per layer = `3·2·B·K·N`
  (K·N=294,912) = 0.90 / 7.19 / 14.50 GFLOP → floors at 5.2
  TFLOPS (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:14`) of 173 / 1,383 / 2,788 µs.
- **Neighbours:** BM=16 means only TM=2 M-frags per simdgroup —
  half the M-reuse of a BM=32 tile; the NAX variant MLX uses on
  M3-class GPUs runs `bm=32/64, bn=bk=64` (round 2 §H), i.e. MLX
  itself buys 4–8× bigger tiles where the hardware allows. A
  replacement is free to tile bigger (regrouping is free, §S1)
  but must keep the 8-wide frag accumulation order per row
  (round 2 §E invariant) — bigger tiles change WHICH rows share
  loads, never a row's own add order, as long as BK=32 frag
  stepping is kept.
- **Cost:** §S5.
- **Invariants:** per-output accumulation grouping (contiguous
  8-wide frag dots, sequential over BK=32 tiles, increasing K)
  is what the scalar `qmm_accum` mimics with serial FMAs
  (attempt-7 `block-1.metal:197-230`) — bit-exact today
  (differ 0 at all prefill sizes,
  `grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`), because serial FMAs
  over the same contiguous order round identically to the
  hardware tree on this data. A fast branch keeps that order
  and swaps the scalar engine for MMA.

### S5. Rate analysis — where the 961/4306/11999 µs go (new)

Basis: chained compiled prefill per layer 960.8 / 4306.0 / 11998.9 µs
(`grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`; round-3 README Starting
point). The chained slot = `_gather_sort` + 3×(offsets + rhs main) +
compiled `swiglu` + `_scatter_unsort` (`bench/grader/slots.py:55-82`).
Glue bounds: sort+unsort move x twice (`2·B·768·2B` = 1.6/12.5/25.2
MB → 8/62/126 µs at 200 GB/s); swiglu is elementwise on `B·384·2`
(+exp/sigmoid ALU, compiled); offsets ≤3×6.6 µs (ineff entry 2).
Mains ≈ measured − glue ≈ 930 / 4,150 / 11,700 µs per layer.

| prefill rows | measured/layer | useful-MMA floor (§S4) | weight-byte floor (§S2) | mains vs MMA peak | mains vs BW peak |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 127 | 960.8 | 173 (18%) | 166 (17%) | 5.4× (19%) | 5.6× (18%) |
| 1,016 | 4,306.0 | 1,383 (32%) | 829 (19%) | 3.0× (33%) | 5.0× (20%) |
| 2,048 | 11,998.9 | 2,788 (23%) | 1,493 (12%) | 4.2× (24%) | 7.8× (13%) |

Ratios use mains≈930/4150/11700. IMPLIED ISSUED intensity:
14.50 GFLOP / (298.6+466.6+25.1 MB issued) ≈ 18 FLOP/B at 2,048 —
below the ridge point 26 (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:26`), bandwidth-side,
yet the kernel reaches only ~13–20% of peak bandwidth on issued
bytes (less on DRAM bytes after cache hits, §S3). **Verdict:
overhead/latency-bound** (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:40`): the time goes to
the 2-barriers-per-K-tile skeleton (48/24 per group), MMA running
small BM=16 tiles, dequant recompute per row tile (§S2), the
safe-path tax on partial tiles (§S3 — 100% of tiles at 127 rows),
schedule scans and empty tiles (§S6) — not to bytes or flops. Same
family as decode `qvm`'s verdict (62 GB/s = 31% of peak, round-1
§A), reached the opposite way: prefill has ABUNDANT parallelism
(S1: 4.4K/15.0K/27.4K groups per layer, 64 threads each — no
occupancy starvation; whole-step decode occupancy was 9%, round-1
§A) but low per-group efficiency, while decode `qvm` is
occupancy-starved with efficient-enough groups.

Caveat: a second run timed compiled prefill at 966.6 / 3953.2 /
7347.5 µs (`results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/
grade-experts-a7-max59.json`) — the 2,048-row figure is 39% lower
than the 11,998.9 basis above while the reference matches across
runs (7359.8 vs 7386.8). The 127/1,016 bases agree within 8%; the
2,048-row basis — and any saving scaled from it — carries that
run-to-run variance. Flagged for `territory-grader` (what the
two-phase timing still can't see).

### S6. What makes compiled prefill fast (vs the scalar branch) (new)

Attempt-7's `rows>=60` branch (`qmm_accum`, `block-1.metal:206-230`,
called per output per pair, `block-0.metal:59-72,103-112`) is bit-exact
and 15.8/27.7/20.1× slower than compiled (15,220/119,154/240,681 vs
961/4306/11999 µs/layer). Three compounding causes, all in the gap
between §S1–§S4 and one-thread-per-output scalar code (full arithmetic
left as a note on `territory-baseline-experts`, which owns that
kernel):

1. **No cross-row grouping: ~15× the distinct weight traffic.**
  `qmm_accum` loads each pair's full expert weights through its own
  512-thread group (each lane re-loads its block's words; lanes
  share only via cache): distinct ≈186 KB per pair per product × B
  pairs × 3 = 283 MB / 2.27 GB / 4.57 GB per layer vs MLX's grouped
  33/166/299 MB — ratios 8.5×/13.7×/15.3×, matching the measured
  15.8/27.7/20.1× once rates are folded in (attempt-7 runs its bytes
  at ~9–10% of peak, MLX at ~13–20%, §S5). MLX's T-vs-B grouping
  (round 2 §C) is the single biggest speed fact.
2. **Scalar serial K-chains with dependent loads, no MMA.** Each
  output accumulates K=768/384 terms one FMA at a time behind a
  dependent device-load chain (weight word → shift → scale/bias →
  round → FMA, 768 iterations unhideable in one thread), where MLX
  issues 8×8 hardware MMAs over threadgroup-resident tiles (§S4).
3. **Per-pair grids at prefill scale:** `B` groups of 512 threads
  (8,192 groups at 2,048 rows) each re-loading x, re-running silu
  serially, and re-paying barriers — where MLX's 64-thread,
  3.84 KB groups tile the same work with 12–48× fewer threads per
  row and shared x in threadgroup memory.

### S7. What a fast exact branch — or a `max_rows` hand-off — must match or avoid (new)

For `baseline-experts` builders (this territory states the reference
side; the starting-point kernel is theirs):

- **Must match (exactness, from round 2 §D–§F — cited, not
  re-derived):** bfloat-rounded dequant weights (same float
  `s·q+b`, same cast, §S2); contiguous-BK accumulation order per
  row (§S4); the four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden,
  down); the `rows>=60` dispatch threshold (brief:
  `claude/muse-agent-brief.md:187`), not the grader's 32/127
  bracket. The scalar `qmm_accum` proves the order can be met
  without MMA — a fast branch keeps its order, changes its engine.
- **Must match (speed, from §S1–§S5):** cross-row weight sharing
  (≤ ~35 KB distinct weights per pair — MLX's `T·184KB/B`
  amortization — or fewer bytes another way); hardware MMA, not
  scalar FMAs; coalesced full-line loads (no strided scalars);
  enough groups to fill the GPU without 512-thread-per-pair
  overprovisioning.
- **Must avoid (free savings, this round's entries):** tile
  quantization — padded rows + empty tiles + all-partial safe

  `gather_mm_offsets` (`ineff-quantized-kernels-2`, this round);

  (`claude/muse-agent-brief.md:173`): inputs above the named row

{"content":"# Inefficiency: `gather_qmm_rhs` BM=16 tile quantization wastes up to ~440/640/610 µs per prefill layer (repriced)

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

Revisit of round 2's confirmed
[`ineff-quantized-kernels-1`](../round-2/exploration/ineff-quantized-kernels-1.md)

0 µs per decode step at 1, 8 and 32 rows (kernel never runs there).

- **Upper edge** (fraction × measured mains): 0.471×930 / 0.153×4150 /

- **Total: up to ~440 / ~640 / ~610 µs per layer** (≈46% / 15% / 5%

67|## Entries
68|
69|Each entry opens with a status block that its owner keeps current:
70|

73|- **Status:** exploring
74|- **Version:** 3

78|
79|Entries are named so that two agents never pick the same name:
80|- `<round>/exploration/territory-<territory>.md`
81|- `<round>/exploration/ineff-<territory>-<n>.md`, numbered by the explorer of that territory
82|- `<round>/implementation/hyp-<n>-<slug>.md`, numbered by the lead
83|
84|**Another agent's entry:** append under its `## From other agents` heading, starting with your name and the time. The owner's text stays as written, so two agents never overwrite each other. The owner reads these notes and folds in what holds.
85|
86|### Territory entry
87|
88|1. Status block (statuses: `exploring`, `done`).
89|2. **What it does** in the decode step, in a few lines.
90|3. **The checklist** below, filled in for each piece of code or table in the territory.
91|4. **Relations:** which territories feed it and which it feeds, with the data passed.
92|5. **Inefficiencies:** links to the entries this territory raised.
93|6. **Files read**, and what each one gave.
94|
95|### Inefficiency entry
96|
97|1. Status block. The statuses are `open`, `confirmed`, `refuted` and `superseded by <entry>`; only the verifier sets `confirmed` or `refuted`.
98|2. **Slot:** `routing`, `combine`, `experts`, or `outside the slots`.
99|3. **What happens:** what the code does, and where (file and lines).
100|4. **Cost** at 1, 8 and 32 rows of a decode step and at the prefill's 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows: kernels × the fixed cost per kernel, bytes ÷ peak bandwidth, and the measured time with the table it comes from.
101|5. **Kind:** overhead-bound, bandwidth-bound or compute-bound, in the terms of `claude/GLOSSARY.md`.
102|6. **Spans:** the territories involved.
103|7. **Predicted saving** if removed, in µs per decode step at 1, 8 and 32 rows and per prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows, with the arithmetic. A saving in one phase that costs the other is not one.
104|8. **Verdict**, written by the verifier: each claim checked, and the result.
105|
106|### Hypothesis entry
107|
108|1. Status block. The lead owns it; the statuses are `boundary`, `building`, `hardening`, `candidate` (passes the grader's gates and its boundary check, signed by its checker), `ready` (a ready check passed it) and `dropped`.
109|2. **Inefficiency** it removes, the slot, and from round 2 on the slot's baseline folder, or `none` and its starting point.
110|3. **Boundary**, written by the boundary agent: what the solution must keep identical (see `boundary.md`).
111|4. **One section per builder:** its direction, its attempts (folder, predicted and measured µs per layer at the six sizes with each size's verdict, G1, G2, `beats_compiled`, and where the slot has a baseline its time and `beats_baseline`), and what each attempt taught.
112|5. **Boundary checks** of the attempts that passed G2.
113|6. **Decision:** the best attempt and why, with the change in whole requests it predicts, labelled a prediction; once a ready check has run, its `ready-verdict.json` and the measured change.
114|7. **Failure ledger,** kept by the lead: each graded attempt that lost, the size or phase it lost at, its named cause and its approach (`SKILL.md` step 4, *Harden*).
115|8. **Unverified:** what no one measured, the boundary's *can't see* list at least.
116|9. **Checks:** each checker's verdict, `pass` or its defects with file and line.
117|
118|## The checklist
119|
120|Fill it in for each piece of code you inspect, so that no piece is judged without its neighbours:
121|
122|- **Callers:** who calls it, and with what shapes at 1, 8 and 32 rows of a decode step and in a prefill.
123|- **Callees:** what it calls, down to the Metal kernel it launches.
124|- **Data:** each input and output with shape, dtype and layout. Where it is produced, and where it is consumed next.
125|- **Neighbours:** what runs just before and after it in the decode step, and what a replacement must keep identical.
126|- **Cost:** the kernels it launches, the bytes it reads and writes (weight bytes counted per read), and its measured time with the table the time comes from.
127|- **Invariants:** what correctness depends on: G2's bit-exact rule at every size, the tie rule for the 4th and 5th expert, the bfloat16 rounding points, and which MLX kernel the reference uses at each size.
128|
129|## The log
130|
131|Append one line per event with the shell, so lines from several agents never mix. In round 2:
132|
133|```bash
134|printf '%s | %s | %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "explorer-baseline-experts" "posted ineff-baseline-experts-2: each weight byte read 4 times at 32 rows" >> muse-spark/round-2/exploration/log.md
135|```
136|
137|Log when you start, claim something, post or confirm an entry, change direction (what from, what to, and which entry made you), grade an attempt (with its verdict), and finish.
138|
139|## Adapting to the others' work
140|
141|Before every new piece of work, and after every post:
142|1. Read the phase README's tracker and the newest 30 lines of the phase log (`tail -n 30`).
143|2. Then change direction when:
144|   - **someone else covers it:** another entry already covers the same code or cause, so append to that entry instead of starting a second one;
145|   - **its premise fell:** the claim your work rests on was refuted;
146|   - **something pays more:** an open item in your territory or task predicts a larger saving than what you're on, and nobody owns it.
147|3. When you change direction, log it with the reason, and write it in your own entry's status block.
148|
149|Two claims on the same item go to the lead, who settles them.
150|
151|## Rules for every agent
152|
153|- **Writes go only to this round's folder, in the files your role names.** Earlier rounds' folders, everything else in the worktree, and everything outside it are read-only.
154|- **Only the lead commits.** Helpers never run `git add` or `git commit`.
155|- **The grader and the ready check are the only GPU jobs.** Builders run the grader through the brief's command; the lead runs the ready check (`SKILL.md` step 4). Both wait their turn for the GPU. Start no other GPU work and load no model outside them: the machine has 16 GB and slows down sharply when memory runs short. A run of `time_candidates.py`, `breakdown.py` or any other timing script made directly is evidence of nothing.
156|- **Every number has a source,** and every speed number says its level and its kind:
157|  - **measured, piece:** the grader verdict that timed exactly that slot, `grade.json` in its attempt folder;
158|  - **measured, whole request:** the `ready-verdict.json` that timed exactly that slot or combination;
159|  - **prediction:** anything else. It counts only the candidate's own measured effect, shows its arithmetic, and stands beside the measured value once there is one.
160|
161|  A combination is measured as one, never added up from its slots. What no one measured goes under **Unverified**, never assumed free, neutral or zero. Other numbers cite a file and line, a table (path and row), or arithmetic shown in full.
162|- **Credentials stay unread:** `.env` files, `~/.config/muse/` and any key store.
163|- **The API-stage kernels** in the history before the tag `agent-era` are from an earlier, removed stage (PROVENANCE.md) and stay unread.

60|## What the grader still cannot see
61|
62|1. **Row counts between the six tested ones.** Correctness sizes are exactly {1, 8, 32, 127, 1016, 2048} ([check_candidate.py:44, 272-276](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py); [slots.py:211](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)). Both internal thresholds are only *bracketed*, never pinpointed: the reference's sort at 16 rows sits between tested 8 and 32; MLX's `gather_qvm`→`gather_qmm_rhs` switch at 60 rows ([ADR 0010:11](../../../claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)) sits between tested 32 and 127. A kernel that branches on `rows` (readable via `*_shape` in Metal) can be exact at all six sizes and wrong in between; the correct branch threshold must come from MLX's dispatch source (quantized-kernels territory), not from the grader.
63|2. **Prefill beyond the first chunk of 128-token random prompts.** `capture_prefill` records only `ids[:, :chunk]` of seeded random ids ([slots.py:240-246](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)). 44|def ref_routing(x, w_router, bias):
45|    scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)
46|    inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=K - 1, axis=-1)[:, :K]
47|    w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)
48|    return inds, w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * SCALE

55|def ref_experts(x, inds, *weights):
56|    """The port's SwitchGLU on flat rows: [rows, D] and [rows, K] -> [rows, K, D]."""
57|    from mlx_lm.models.activations import swiglu
58|    from mlx_lm.models.switch_layers import _gather_sort, _scatter_unsort

60|    gate, up, down = weights[0:3], weights[3:6], weights[6:9]
61|    xx = mx.expand_dims(x, (-2, -3))
62|    do_sort = inds.size >= 64
63|    idx, inv = inds, None
64|    if do_sort:
65|        xx, idx, inv = _gather_sort(xx, inds)

67|    def qmm(a, w):
68|        return mx.gather_qmm(
69|            a,
70|            *w,
71|            rhs_indices=idx,
72|            transpose=False,
73|            group_size=32,
74|            bits=4,
75|            mode="affine",
76|            sorted_indices=do_sort,
77|        )

79|    y = qmm(swiglu(qmm(xx, gate), qmm(xx, up)), down)
80|    if do_sort:
81|        y = _scatter_unsort(y, inv, inds.shape)

283|def dim(expr, rows):
284|    if isinstance(expr, bool) or not isinstance(expr, (int, str)):
285|        raise ValueError(f"bad size {expr!r}")

304|def build(spec, sources, slot):
305|    """A function slot_inputs -> slot_outputs from Muse Spark's spec and Metal blocks.
306|
307|    With "max_rows" in the spec, inputs with more rows than that run the slot's
308|    reference under mx.compile instead of the kernels, so an attempt can keep
309|    prompt-sized inputs on MLX's own code (claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md).
310|    """
311|    slot_in, slot_out = SLOTS[slot]
312|    kernels = []
313|    for k in spec["kernels"]:
314|        header = "" if k.get("header_block") is None else sources[k["header_block"]]
315|        fn = mx.fast.metal_kernel(
316|            name=re.sub(r"\W", "_", str(k["name"])),
317|            input_names=list(k["inputs"]),
318|            output_names=[o["name"] for o in k["outputs"]],
319|            source=sources[k["source_block"]],
320|            header=header,
321|            atomic_outputs=bool(k.get("atomic_outputs", False)),
322|        )
323|        kernels.append((k, fn))
324|    missing = set(slot_out) - set(spec["slot_outputs"])
325|    if missing:
326|        raise ValueError(f"slot_outputs is missing {sorted(missing)}")
327|    max_rows = spec.get("max_rows")
328|    if max_rows is not None:
329|        if isinstance(max_rows, bool) or not isinstance(max_rows, int) or max_rows < 1:
330|            raise ValueError(f"bad max_rows {max_rows!r}")
331|        compiled = mx.compile(REFERENCE[slot])
332|
333|    def run(**inputs):
334|        rows = inputs[slot_in[0]].shape[0]
335|        if max_rows is not None and rows > max_rows:  # the compiled reference takes over
336|            out = compiled(*[inputs[n] for n in slot_in])
337|            return dict(zip(slot_out, out if isinstance(out, (tuple, list)) else [out]))
338|        env = dict(inputs)
339|        for k, fn in kernels:
340|            tg = [int(t) for t in k["threadgroup"]]
341|            if any(t < 1 for t in tg) or tg[0] * tg[1] * tg[2] > 1024:
342|                raise ValueError(f"bad threadgroup {tg}")
343|            outs = fn(
344|                inputs=[env[n] for n in k["inputs"]],
345|                template=[
346|                    (n, template_value(v)) for n, v in (k.get("template") or {}).items()
347|                ],
348|                grid=tuple(dim(g, rows) for g in k["grid"]),
349|                threadgroup=tuple(tg),
350|                output_shapes=[
351|                    tuple(dim(s, rows) for s in o["shape"]) for o in k["outputs"]
352|                ],
353|                output_dtypes=[DTYPES[o["dtype"]] for o in k["outputs"]],
354|                init_value=k.get("init_value"),
355|            )
356|            env.update(zip([o["name"] for o in k["outputs"]], outs))
357|        return {name: env[src] for name, src in spec["slot_outputs"].items()}
358|
359|    return run

1|"""The ready check: the Muse agent's in-round test of whole requests.
2|
3|An attempt is `ready` only when this check says it improves whole requests
4|(claude/adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md). It runs G3 as Claude runs it after
5|the round, time_candidates.py vllm with the four G3 workloads, 5 repeats and
6|256 tokens, with every submitted slot in one call so that a combination is
7|measured as one. Nothing about that protocol can be changed from the command
8|line. Then it audits the log instead of trusting it:
9|
10|  1. the log holds exactly one ready-check marker, with the protocol above;
11|  2. every timed run is vLLM, at a G3 workload, with 256 tokens and every
12|     measurement present, and each variant has repeats 0-4 at each workload;
13|  3. the variants are exactly base, compiled-<slot> and muse-<slot> for each
14|     slot, plus compiled-all and muse-all with more than one slot;
15|  4. every variant keeps the unchanged model's greedy tokens at 1 and 32 requests;
16|  5. g3-vllm.json equals the G3 verdict recomputed from the log.
17|
18|It writes ready-verdict.json: each muse-* variant's verdict against base and
19|its compiled counterpart, and each variant's median, range and count per
20|workload and measurement. Exit codes: 0 every muse-* variant passes; 1 a
21|variant fails, a verdict that stands; 2 the run stopped or broke the protocol,
22|so there is no verdict and the check may run again in a new folder.
23|
24|  .venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_ready.py <new out folder> SLOT=FOLDER [SLOT=FOLDER ...]
25|  .venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_ready.py --audit <out folder>
26|

28|ready-verdict.json agrees; it writes nothing. The swarm's checker uses it, and
29|so does Claude after the round.

5|# From round 3, an improvement must hold in both phases, decode and prefill, and an attempt may hand prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|**The change.** Claude's comparison of every engine version over whole requests ([findings](../findings/muse-round-2.md), section 5) found that the grader and G3 timed only the decode step. They never timed the prefill, the phase in which a request's whole prompt runs through the model:
10|- **Experts attempt-7** looked like round 2's largest gain, a 19% shorter decode step at 32 requests. It processed prompts 6.6 to 14.5 times slower and cut throughput by 10% to 83%.
11|- **Routing attempt-4,** round 2's only baseline, processed prompts 7% to 10% slower. At 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts it cost 3.5% of throughput.
12|
13|The Muse agent never saw either effect: its piece timing ran decode sizes only, and G3 measured the decode step only.
14|
15|On 2026-11-04 surucuonur set the rule: "The improvement should be in the two phases of it: decode and prefill. Then, we can consider it as an improvement." surucuonur chose:
16|- **faster in one phase, slower in neither;**
17|- **the hand-off:** an attempt may leave prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference. This replaces the part of [ADR 0010](0010-exact-at-every-size.md) that required the kernels to run in every call.
18|
19|## How it works
20|
21|- **The piece timing runs at the six G2 sizes** (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`): decode at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. The layers are still chained.
22|- **The verdict at each size comes from paired repeats.** The candidate and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times, and so does the baseline when one is given.
23|  - The candidate is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, a one-sided sign test at p < 0.01.
24|  - It is `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise.
25|
26|  This replaces the comparison of medians for the decode sizes too, since the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
27|- **The verdict per phase:**
28|  - a phase is `faster` when every one of its sizes is;
29|  - it is `slower` when any size is;
30|  - otherwise it is `not slower`.
31|
32|  `beats_compiled`, and `beats_baseline` against a baseline, are true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
33|- **The hand-off** (`max_rows` in `spec.json`, `bench/grader/slots.py`). Inputs with more rows than `max_rows` run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. G2 still checks every size.
34|  - On 2026-11-04 the compiled reference of each slot was bit-exact with the reference at all six sizes (`bench/micro/compiled_exact.py`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`).
35|  - Above `max_rows` a hand-off runs the compiled reference itself, so it times `same` as the bar there, never better.
36|- **G3** (`bench/grader/time_candidates.py`, which writes `g3-vllm.json`):
37|  - **Workloads:** 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts.
38|  - **Measurements per run:** the decode step period, the prompt time and the whole-request time, over 5 shuffled repeats, up from 3.
39|  - **Faster and slower:** the two ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
40|  - **Why 5 repeats:** with 3 each, two identical engines' ranges miss each other by chance 1 time in 20 per direction. "Never slower" checks a phase 8 times (4 workloads, 2 bars), so a phase that changed nothing would fail about a third of the time. The first run under these rules showed it. A copy of experts attempt-7 with a hand-off at 59 rows came out `slower` on prompt time at 32 × 1,024, by 0.5% with ranges 16 ms apart, although above 59 rows it runs the compiled reference, whose own range overlapped the unchanged engine's (`results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`). With 5 repeats the chance is 1 in 252 per check, about 3% over 8.
41|  - **The pass rule:** against both the original model and the compiled reference, the decode step or the prompt time must be faster in every workload, neither may be slower in any, and no whole request may be slower.
42|- **The unchanged engine is vLLM's own.** The original model in G3 runs with Claude's step hooks, and with vLLM's engine inside the script's process. On 2026-11-04, alternating runs found it within −0.2% to +1.9% of vLLM with neither, inside the spread between repeats in every workload (`bench/micro/clean_vllm.py`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-clean-vllm/`).
43|
44|## Consequences
45|
46|- **Round 3 starts with no baseline.** Routing attempt-4 is `slower` at all three prefill sizes, 2.6 to 8.7 times the compiled reference's time. It fails G3 on prompt time at 8 and 32 requests. It becomes a starting point, so round 3's bar in every slot is the compiled reference.
47|- **A decode kernel no longer has to win at prefill sizes,** only to hand them off or not lose there. The attempt chooses the row count, so the boundary agent checks that the hand-off sits on the right side of 60 rows for the experts slot.
48|- **At prefill sizes, a slot with a hand-off is MLX's code, not the Muse agent's.** The claim for such an attempt is "faster decode, unchanged prefill".
49|- **Grader runs and G3 take longer.** Every attempt is now timed at three more sizes. G3 runs 5 repeats instead of 3, and its 32 × 1,024 workload adds at least 16 s per variant per repeat.
50|- **The decode verdict is stricter.** An attempt whose median beat the compiled reference by noise is now `same`.
51|- **Not covered:** prefill chunks of other sizes, and decode steps with other row counts. The boundary agent reports them; G3's four workloads are the end-to-end check. Not covered means not measured: from round 3 the swarm lists these as **Unverified**, never as free ([ADR 0013](0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)); round 2 read ADR 0010's line like this one as leave to slow the prefill.
52|- **At 1 request the whole-request time is noisy.** On 2026-11-04 its repeats spread 6% to 41%, so G3 there mostly says `same`, which passes the "never slower" test without showing a gain.
53|
54|## Considered options
55|
56|- **Faster in both phases.** The higher bar. A decode kernel would also have to beat MLX's large matrix kernels at 2,048 rows, which is not where the decode step loses its time. Not chosen.
57|- **Whole-request throughput alone.** Simple, but it lets a slower phase be traded for a faster one. surucuonur ruled that out.
58|- **Hand off to the uncompiled reference.** The prefill could then come out `slower` than the compiled reference wherever compiling helps; at 127 rows, routing's compiled reference takes 87 µs per layer against 102 µs uncompiled.
59|- **Keep the kernels in every call** (ADR 0010). The kernels could still branch on the row count inside themselves, but they couldn't use MLX's large-size kernels. surucuonur chose the hand-off.

Piece timings are Claude's re-grade on main with the two-phase grader (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-*.json`), chained µs per layer as reference / compiled / candidate. G3 is the vLLM decode-step change against the unchanged model (median of 3 shuffled repeats, `console-vllm.txt`) plus the whole-request throughput change at 1×128, 8×128, 32×128 and 32×1,024 (prompt-time multiple in brackets, `results/runs/2026-11-04-engine-comparison/`). Round 2's own prediction was decode-only (piece basis × 20 layers plus compiled G3 offsets); both are quoted so the gap can be seen.

22|### Per slot
23|
24|#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7`
25|
26|- **What it is.** One fused per-pair kernel (512 threads per (row, expert-slot) pair, `rows*4` threadgroups): interleaved gate/up plus interleaved down in a merged K loop, intermediates in threadgroup memory (3,840 B), full-bfloat16 silu-mul. Per-block numerics replicate MLX's `affine_gather_qvm` bitwise at decode sizes; a `rows >= 60` branch runs a scalar `qmm_accum` (bfloat16-rounded dequant, contiguous `BK=32` order) to match `gather_qmm_rhs` at prefill sizes. See `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/notes.md` and `muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-1-experts-exact.md`.
27|- **Piece timing** (`grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`). Decode: 84.0 / 78.6 / **92.1** at 1 row (slower), 239.3 / 235.5 / **162.8** at 8 rows, 806.5 / 797.8 / **515.3** at 32 rows. Over whole requests (with routing attempt-4): throughput −10.0% / −37.5% / −48.0% / −82.5%, with prompt processing 6.63× / 14.50× / 12.50× / 13.09× slower than the unchanged engine. The fastest exact decode step measured (routing + experts: −20% with 32 requests in plain MLX) is the slowest whole request.

At 1 row the fused designs plateau at 92–110 µs per layer chained against 73–87 for the compiled reference across six exact attempts — width, group count, interleave and store parallelism moved 8/32 rows and none moved 1 row by more than ~12 µs (round 2's *What building taught*).

5|# From round 3, the swarm measures what it claims: an in-round ready check, a checker, and a rule to change approach
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. The design is the Muse agent's; see below. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|**The change.** Two rounds produced no real improvement, while the swarm's own reports predicted gains ([round 1](../findings/muse-round-1.md), [round 2](../findings/muse-round-2.md)). Claude traced this to five behaviours:
10|1. treating what wasn't measured as free;
11|2. claiming end-to-end gains from per-slot timing;
12|3. reasoning inconsistently, such as summing gains it had said don't add up;
13|4. using the grader as a search loop (round 1);
14|5. keeping a design that kept failing at the same point.
15|
16|The root: inside a round the swarm never saw the real objective, only per-slot piece timing, and no one checked its claims before its summary. The rules even required an end-to-end number while forbidding a measurement of it: `tracking.md` said "Load no model", and *Ready to test* asked for the expected G3 change.
17|
18|On 2026-11-04 surucuonur asked how to fix this. surucuonur decided:
19|- the swarm may run the end-to-end check itself, through the GPU queue;
20|- the design work is done by Meta's Muse: "Meta muse should be used due to the rules of the hackathon";
21|- the lead runs the check;
22|- my post-round G3 must agree with the swarm's in-round verdicts, verdict for verdict;
23|- the token count is recorded in every run.
24|
25|## Who designed it
26|
27|One headless Muse Code session, `01a1a701-10d9-7552-a2c1-bb9149781051`, on `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, with approvals `on-request` and no cost or time limit. Its lead started 11 helpers:
28|- **four explorers:** the skill, the measurement tools, the round records, and Claude's findings;
29|- **three designers,** each starting from a different perspective: the existing system, the contracts, and failure modes;
30|- **three testers,** each testing one design live on round 2's attempts;
31|- **a blind reviewer;**
32|- **a tester of the synthesis.**
33|
34|The reviewer passed one design on all six gates. It was the only design whose audit recomputes the G3 verdict from the log; the other two accepted a hand-edited verdict file, which their testers demonstrated. The lead added five ideas from the other two designs. Prototypes and test results stayed in the Muse worktree's untracked `design-lab/`, and the session's transcript records them.
35|
36|Claude implemented the design on main without copying the Muse agent's code, since its work is committed only on `muse-agent` ([authorship](../../PROVENANCE.md)). The tools are new code following the design; the skill text is rewritten from it.

40|- **The ready check, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`.**
41|  - **What it runs:** `time_candidates.py vllm` with G3's protocol fixed in code: the four workloads, 5 repeats and 256 tokens, with every submitted slot in one call, so a combination is measured as `muse-all`. No flag changes the protocol, and it stops before any GPU work if `time_candidates.py`'s G3 constants change.
42|  - **Its audit:** it writes a marker into the log, then audits the log instead of trusting it:
43|    - one marker with the protocol;
44|    - every run vLLM, at a G3 workload, with 256 tokens (a field every run now records, `repeat_fixes.py`) and all three measurements;
45|    - repeats 0–4 for each variant and workload, and exactly the expected variants;
46|    - the same greedy tokens as the unchanged model;
47|    - and `g3-vllm.json` equal to the verdict recomputed from the log.
48|  - **Its output:** `ready-verdict.json`, with medians and ranges.
49|  - **Exit codes:** 0 passes; 1 fails, and the verdict stands; 2 means no verdict, so the check runs again in a new folder.
50|  - **Re-checking:** `--audit` re-checks a folder without the GPU.
