From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.

1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.

   At every size:
   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.

   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.

   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.

   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).

**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;

**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.

{"content":"# Attempt 2 — builder-1-b, direction (b): FP-contract-off pragma barrier

First attempt in this direction (round 3, `hyp-1-combine-devolatilize`,
slot `combine`, baseline `none`). Builds on the starting point
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1`, which passes G1+G2 and
`beats_compiled` but fails G3 (+1.051 ms/step in vLLM at 32 requests).

## What changed

Only the barrier mechanism. Grid (`rows*768`), threadgroup [256,1,1],
index/base lines, inputs/outputs and the final
`bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase]` line are verbatim from the starting
point. The seven `volatile float` locals (`p0..p3`, `s01`, `s012`,
`acc`) become seven plain `float` locals with the identical 7-op
sequence, and a new header block (`block-1.metal`, wired via
`"header_block": 1` — the only `spec.json` delta) disables FP
contraction for the kernel:

```metal
#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF
#pragma clang fp contract(off)
```

MLX emits `header` before the main function, so the pragmas precede the
kernel definition, which is where FP-option pragmas take effect. No
`volatile` anywhere in code, no `__attribute__((noinline))` helpers,
no extra functions, calls, or memory traffic of any kind.

Why this is contraction-proof: with contract(off) the backend may not
fuse any fmul+fadd into an fma — this is the compiler's own
contraction switch, so there is no transform left that can keep a
product unrounded into its consumer add. Each of the 7 statements is
then one rounded f32 op on register values: the same 7 materialisation
points, same fold order `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3`, same two bfloat16 roundings
as the starting point. Reassociation needs no pragma: it is off without
fast-math flags, and the grader sets none. The proof is G2 itself: any
surviving contraction shows the starting point's old signature (decode
0/2/2, prefill 6/50/130 differ).

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-combine-1` (confirmed): the seven volatiles' 7 stores +
7 loads per output (56 B/thread of thread-private traffic, 43,008
B/row/layer) stall the decode step (+7.1/+25.4/+72.1 µs/layer vLLM)
and the 32×128 prompt (+1,501.7 ms twin). The pragmas keep every value
in registers — ~10 live floats, no spill pressure — so the barrier
costs zero bytes and zero instructions. Same fix covers both phases:
both run these identical lines.

## Prediction (µs per layer, chained paired basis)

Starting point (re-grade `grade-phases-combine-attempt-1.json`, via
`ineff-g3-1`): decode reference/candidate 52.8/45.7 @1, 71.2/47.9 @8,
87.0/64.6 @32; compiled 53.4/56.4/69.1. Prefill candidate
62.8/226.5/273.0 vs compiled 66.1/271.6/520.4.

Arithmetic:

- Slot traffic unchanged: 9,232 B/row ÷ 200 GB/s = 0.05 / 0.37 / 1.48
  µs decode, 5.9 / 46.9 / 94.5 µs prefill. Floor dominates decode.
- Spill floor removed: 43,008 B/row ÷ 200 GB/s = 0.22 / 1.7 / 6.9 µs
  decode, 27 / 218 / 440 µs prefill — an upper bound the quiet grader
  chain mostly does not price (the inefficiency entry), so decode is
  predicted at the starting point ±5% paired noise, prefill
  same-or-slightly-better.
- Predicted candidate: **45 / 47 / 63** decode, **61 / 220 / 265**
  prefill. Margins to compiled (≈8/9/6 decode, ≈5/50/255 prefill)
  reproduce the starting point's 28–30/30 wins: `faster` at all six
  sizes, both phases `faster`, `beats_compiled` true.
- G1 pass, G2 differ 0 / max ULP 0.0 at all six sizes.

The piece prize is keeping `beats_compiled`; the real prize (vLLM
≈0.5 ms/step at 8 requests, ≈1.4 ms/step at 32; order-1-s prompt
recovery) is invisible to the piece timing by construction and needs
the ready check.

None. The kernel runs identical lines at all sizes, combine has no
MLX kernel switch underneath, and the boundary's grader note says no
hand-off is needed for this hypothesis's direction.

## What this attempt leaves unmeasured

For the hypothesis entry's **Unverified** list: the in-step stall
recovery (only the ready check / G3 at 32 requests shows it);
exactness at row counts other than the six graded ones (boundary tool
`check_sizes.py` can probe 25 sizes incl. 59/60/61); the 33–126 band;
sizes above 2,048; prefill beyond the first seeded-random chunk;
whether the pragma pair is honoured by any toolchain other than the
graded one (irrelevant to the verdict, which runs on this one).

3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Part of the [muse-round skill](SKILL.md). [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are `builder-<n>-<letter>`. You write one solution for one hypothesis and grade it. That is one attempt. The lead's prompt names the hypothesis entry and your direction. Other builders take other directions on the same hypothesis, so keep to yours. [tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the documents and the rules.
6|
7|First read:
8|- the hypothesis entry, its **Boundary** above all;
9|- the inefficiency and territory entries it links;
10|- in the brief, `claude/muse-agent-brief.md`: your slot, *Tools and limits*, *Your files* (the attempt layout and launch spec) and *How each attempt is judged*;
11|- the `notes.md` of the slot's earlier attempts: this round's in `<round>/kernels/<slot-folder>/`, and earlier rounds', the baseline's or starting point's above all.
12|
13|**One grader run is one attempt.** After a run, any change, even a one-line fix, is a new attempt with its own number, built by copying the files you keep. Scratch kernels and timing experiments that aren't attempts go in `probes/` inside your attempt folder and are never graded. You return after one attempt; the brief's *When a slot stops* rule no longer applies, and the lead decides what comes next.
14|
15|## Steps
16|
17|1. **Claim an attempt number.**
18|   - N is one more than the highest `attempt-<N>` in this round's slot folder, or 1. Run `mkdir -p <round>/kernels/<slot-folder>` once, then `mkdir <round>/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>`.
19|   - If it fails, another builder took N: try N+1.
20|   - Log the claim.
21|2. **Write the attempt** in the brief's layout, plus a `notes.md` that says:
22|   - what changed since the attempt it builds on (the baseline counts), or that it is the first in your direction; from round 2 on, a starting point that fails G2 counts too;
23|   - which inefficiency it removes, and how;
24|   - the predicted µs per layer at the six sizes, decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows), with the arithmetic; from round 2 on, against the baseline's where the slot has one;
25|   - with `max_rows`, the row count and why: the sizes above it run the compiled reference;
26|   - what the attempt leaves unmeasured, for the hypothesis entry's **Unverified** list.
27|   
28|   Make one main change, the simplest kernel that removes the cause, and stay inside the boundary.
29|3. **Grade it** with the brief's grader command, once, keeping its verdict in the attempt folder: add `--out <attempt folder>/grade.json`. When the hypothesis entry names a baseline, add `--baseline <baseline folder>`; for `routing+combine`, `--baseline routing=<folder> --baseline combine=<folder>`. It times your attempt, the compiled reference and any baseline in paired repeats at the six sizes. At each size your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs and `slower` when it loses 22. `beats_compiled` and `beats_baseline` are true when one phase is `faster` at every size and neither phase is `slower` at any. The grader may print "waiting for the GPU" while another run has it; keep waiting. A run itself takes under 3 minutes once it starts, for an attempt about as fast as the reference; one much slower at the prefill sizes takes longer (round 2's experts attempt-7: 5 minutes). The grader prints only when it finishes; stop a run only after 15 minutes, and record it.
30|4. **Record the verdict** in `notes.md` and in your section of the hypothesis entry, citing `grade.json`: G1; G2 at each size, decode and prefill, with the first difference; your timings at each size next to the original's, the compiled reference's and any baseline's, with the verdicts, `phases_vs_compiled`, `beats_compiled` and, with a baseline, `beats_baseline`. Log it.
31|5. **Learn.** If the attempt failed, or its time missed your prediction by more than 20%, find out why. Write the answer in `notes.md`, and add it to the inefficiency entry as a note.
32|
33|**Done** when the attempt is graded, recorded and any miss is explained. Return the attempt folder, its verdict, and the one change you would make next.
34|
35|## What you write
36|
37|Your attempt folder, your section of the hypothesis entry, notes in other entries, and log lines.

118|## The checklist
119|
120|Fill it in for each piece of code you inspect, so that no piece is judged without its neighbours:
121|
122|- **Callers:** who calls it, and with what shapes at 1, 8 and 32 rows of a decode step and in a prefill.
123|- **Callees:** what it calls, down to the Metal kernel it launches.
124|- **Data:** each input and output with shape, dtype and layout. Where it is produced, and where it is consumed next.
125|- **Neighbours:** what runs just before and after it in the decode step, and what a replacement must keep identical.
126|- **Cost:** the kernels it launches, the bytes it reads and writes (weight bytes counted per read), and its measured time with the table the time comes from.
127|- **Invariants:** what correctness depends on: G2's bit-exact rule at every size, the tie rule for the 4th and 5th expert, the bfloat16 rounding points, and which MLX kernel the reference uses at each size.

151|## Rules for every agent
152|
153|- **Writes go only to this round's folder, in the files your role names.** Earlier rounds' folders, everything else in the worktree, and everything outside it are read-only.
154|- **Only the lead commits.** Helpers never run `git add` or `git commit`.
155|- **The grader and the ready check are the only GPU jobs.** Builders run the grader through the brief's command; the lead runs the ready check (`SKILL.md` step 4). Both wait their turn for the GPU. Start no other GPU work and load no model outside them: the machine has 16 GB and slows down sharply when memory runs short. A run of `time_candidates.py`, `breakdown.py` or any other timing script made directly is evidence of nothing.
156|- **Every number has a source,** and every speed number says its level and its kind:
157|  - **measured, piece:** the grader verdict that timed exactly that slot, `grade.json` in its attempt folder;
158|  - **measured, whole request:** the `ready-verdict.json` that timed exactly that slot or combination;
159|  - **prediction:** anything else. It counts only the candidate's own measured effect, shows its arithmetic, and stands beside the measured value once there is one.
160|
161|  A combination is measured as one, never added up from its slots. What no one measured goes under **Unverified**, never assumed free, neutral or zero. Other numbers cite a file and line, a table (path and row), or arithmetic shown in full.
162|- **Credentials stay unread:** `.env` files, `~/.config/muse/` and any key store.
163|- **The API-stage kernels** in the history before the tag `agent-era` are from an earlier, removed stage (PROVENANCE.md) and stay unread.

Slot: `experts`. Baseline: `none` (starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7`, which passes G1+G2 but is `slower` at 1 row and at every prefill size).
12|
13|Predicted effect if the prefill path matches compiled speed at equal bits: save 14,259/114,848/228,682 µs/layer = 285 ms / 2.30 s / 4.57 s per chunk, recovering the throughput loss to whatever the decode phase then gives (decode wins at 8/32 rows must be kept: ahead 72.7/282.5 µs/layer). Fix shapes: (a) vectorized per-pair scalar (one thread per word's 8 outputs, 8 accumulators, each output keeping contiguous `BK=32` order); (b) grouped/tiled replica of `qmm_rhs` issue (takes the tile-waste and offsets prizes, ranked prefill items 7–8, for free); (c) `max_rows` hand-off (Claude checked 59 bit-exact; decode stays on the fused path). The 1-row decode gap ([ineff-baseline-experts-2.md](../exploration/ineff-baseline-experts-2.md)) is a disjoint cause and a later hypothesis (hyp-4) built on this one's winner; a prefill fix that slows decode, or vice versa, is not an improvement (ADR 0011).

**The targets JSON** at the end of `strategy.md`:

```json
===
# attempt-7 (round 2): hardening — interleaved down, shared second accumulator (builder-1-g)

Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
`none`). Builds on the best attempt
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-5` (fused single kernel,
512 threads/pair, interleaved gate/up + parallel block stores, G2 pass
all six, 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8 µs/layer chained vs compiled
75.9 / 234.6 / 798.2 — loses only at 1 row by 16.2 µs) with the
down-interleave `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-6` tried
(one simdgroup, two down blocks, merged K loop), made to compile
within the pipeline threadgroup limit. Attempt-6 failed G1:
`Thread group size (512) is greater than the maximum allowed
threads per threadgroup (448)` — its compiled pipeline's
`maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` fell to 448 for the identical
512-thread launch.

## The one main change

Attempt-6's merged down loop, with the second accumulator's storage
shared so the kernel compiles at 512 threads. Everything else is
copied from attempt-5/6, not redesigned (`spec.json` byte-identical
to attempt-5/6; `block-1.metal` helpers `qvm_block`,
`qvm_gate_up_pair`, `qvm_down_pair`, `qmm_accum` bodies byte-identical
to attempt-6 by diff; `block-0.metal` gate/up, silu and prefill
branches otherwise byte-identical):

- **Before (attempt-5):** down ran 24 blocks of 32 outputs in 2
  sequential waves of 16 simdgroups (`b = v*16 + simd`, `b < 24`):
  wave 0 computed blocks 0–15, wave 1 blocks 16–23 (simdgroups
  8–15 idle), each block a separate `qvm_block` call — 12 strided
  K steps per lane (`k = lane, lane+32, …, lane+352` over `K=384`),
  then `simd_sum` and the parallel store
  `y[pair*768 + b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`. The second wave's
  first load waited for the first wave's last accumulate.
- **Attempt-6's down change (kept):** one simdgroup computes two
  down blocks in one merged K loop (`qvm_down_pair`, block-1).
  Simdgroup `s < 12` owns the consecutive pair `b0 = 2s`,
  `b1 = 2s+1` (12 pairs, one wave; simdgroups 12–15 idle, as in
  gate/up). For each strided `k` both blocks' loads are issued
  before either accumulates — block 0's scale/bias and 4 weight
  words, then block 1's scale/bias and 4 weight words (plus the
  shared `tg_h[k]`, read once) — and only then do the two
  accumulation passes run, block 0's 32 terms then block 1's, into
  separate accumulators. The 24 down blocks therefore run as 12
  interleaved pairs instead of 2 sequential waves.
- **This attempt's fix vs attempt-6:** attempt-6 declared three
  distinct 32-float thread arrays — kernel-scope `p[32]`, a
  gate/up-scoped `pu[32]` and a down-scoped `q[32]` — and the
  compiler charged all three against the per-threadgroup budget
  (`maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` 448 < 512) even though `pu` and
  `q` are live in disjoint phases. Attempt-7 hoists the second
  accumulator to kernel scope: `float p[32]; float q[32];` beside
  the existing buffers in `block-0`, and passes the same `q` as
  gate/up's second accumulator (`qvm_gate_up_pair(..., p, q)`) and
  as down's second accumulator (`qvm_down_pair(..., p, q)`),
  deleting both scoped declarations. The kernel again has two
  distinct 32-float thread arrays, exactly attempt-5's footprint,
  at unchanged 512 threads.

Everything else is kept identical, as the task requires:

- **Per-block bits unchanged.** In `qvm_down_pair` each block's adds
  run in exactly `qvm_block`'s order: the same strided `k` sequence,
  the same float32 dequant terms
  `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` / `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)`
  with `s1 = scale/16`, in the same per-output sequence; the two
  accumulators are independent, so interleaving cannot reorder
  either block's own adds. Each accumulator then gets the identical
  `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` `simd_sum` tree as `qvm_block`.
  The `(bfloat)` rounding at the store is unchanged.
- **Sharing is a pure storage rename.** Gate/up and down run in
  disjoint phases separated by two `threadgroup_barrier`s (after
  gate/up and after silu): gate/up's `q` values are stored to
  `tg_up` before the first barrier, silu consumes only
  `tg_gate`/`tg_up`/`tg_h`, and `qvm_down_pair` re-zeroes both
  `p[0..31]` and `q[0..31]` on entry (as `qvm_gate_up_pair` does),
  so no value can leak across the barrier through the shared array.
  Peak live floats per phase is unchanged (64 in gate/up, 64 in
  down); only the distinct-array count charged by the compiler
  drops from three to two.
- **Parallel lane stores kept.** After the two `simd_sum`s every
  lane holds both blocks' full reduced 32-vectors, so lane `j`
  stores element `j` of each block — one store per lane per block:
  `y[pair*768 + b0*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`,
  `y[pair*768 + b1*32 + lane] = (bfloat)q[lane]`.
- **Gate/up interleave, silu, prefill scalar branch, grids and
  rounding points identical.** Gate/up still calls
  `qvm_gate_up_pair` with attempt-5's parallel `tg_gate`/`tg_up`
  stores; the full-bfloat16 silu-mul is byte-identical; the
  `rows >= 60` prefill branch still uses the scalar `qmm_accum`
  (bfloat16-rounded dequant, contiguous `BK=32` order) for gate,
  up and down, with the same `x_shape[0] >= 60` dispatch
  threshold; `spec.json` (one kernel, `rows*2048` threads =
  `rows*4` groups of 512) is byte-identical. No kernel split, no
  new device-memory intermediate, same four bfloat16 rounding
  points and positional `y[r,j]`.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-5's
  miss analysis left the still-sequential down chain as the
  largest named remainder at 1 row — 12 strided steps × 2 waves
  behind the silu barrier, plus the `tg_x` load, silu, barriers
  and chained fixed cost. Attempts 1–3 showed threadgroup count
  past 4 is not the lever and attempt-4/5 showed overlapping the
  per-block serial K chain is. The down product was the last
  product still running its blocks in fully sequential waves with
  only one block's loads in flight per simdgroup; merging two
  blocks per simdgroup puts both blocks' loads (8 weight words +
  2 scales/biases per step) in flight in every step, so each
  block's load latency has the other block's loads/compute to
  hide behind, without touching any block's `simd_sum` order.
  The shared-`q` fix is what lets this merged loop launch at all:
  attempt-6 proved the three-array form exceeds the pipeline
  threadgroup budget at 512 threads.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
  attempt-5's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
  verbatim — the interleave does not touch prefill arithmetic.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
  kept, as in attempts 1–6 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
  the interleave changes load scheduling, not bytes.

## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)

512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 (`spec.json` identical to attempt-5/6).
Threadgroup memory unchanged: `tg_x[768] + tg_gate[384] +
tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]` bfloat16 = **3,840 B** of 32,768 B,
rows-independent. Distinct thread arrays are two 32-float
accumulators (`p`, shared `q`) — attempt-5's count, one fewer than
attempt-6's three. Grid scales as `rows*4` groups, so the kernel
is valid at every `rows ≥ 1`, on both sides of 60. Decode coverage:
12 simdgroups × 2 blocks × 32 lanes = 768 outputs per pair, each
written exactly once, as before.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)

Attempt-5 (other run): 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8 µs/layer vs compiled
75.9 / 234.6 / 798.2 and reference 95.7 / 232.4 / 802.3. Attempt-6
predicted 85 / 156 / 540 but never launched, so that prediction is
untested, not missed. Baseline `none`, so no
`wins_vs_baseline` / `beats_baseline`. Weight bytes per layer
(552,960 B/pair): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs;
bandwidth floors at 200 GB/s: 11.1 / 88.5 / 353.9 µs.
Attempt-5 effective: 24.0 / 109.2 / 132.3 GB/s.

Down arithmetic: `K = 384` → 12 strided steps per lane per block.
Attempt-5 pays 2 waves × 12 steps sequentially after the silu
barrier; this attempt pays 12 merged steps. A merged step issues
twice the loads (8 weight words, 2 scales) for twice the
accumulate work, so it costs more than a single-block step but
less than two — the gate/up precedent (attempt-4) hid ≈ 20% of
the merged chain's exposed latency at 1 row.

- **1 row: 85.** Latency-bound (floor 11.1 µs). The down phase
  sits alone behind the silu barrier; at attempt-5's 92.1 µs the
  product chains (gate/up merged 24 steps + down 2×12 steps)
  dominate, so the down waves are roughly a third of the layer
  (≈ 30 µs). Collapsing 24 sequential steps into 12 merged ones
  at ≈ 1.3× the per-step cost (8 loads share the `tg_h[k]` read
  and the loop control) cuts the down phase to ≈ 23 µs, saving
  ≈ 7 µs → 92.1 − 7 ≈ **85 µs**. Still above compiled 75.9 — the
  `tg_x` load, silu, barriers and chained launch/link cost
  remain untouched — but it should roughly halve the 16.2 µs gap.
  The shared `q` itself is arithmetic-neutral; its only timing
  effect is restoring a legal 512-thread pipeline.
- **8 rows: 156.** 32 groups per call partly hide one group's
  down tail behind other groups' K loops (attempt-5 already at
  109.2 GB/s), so only part of the 1-row saving survives:
  162.0 − 6 ≈ **156 µs**, keeping the win over compiled 234.6.
- **32 rows: 540.** Streaming-bound (attempt-5: 132.3 GB/s).
  Group parallelism already hides load latency, so the merged
  loop buys nothing; the peak live accumulator count is the same
  64 floats gate/up already held in attempt-5, so no new spill
  tax is expected beyond attempt-6's identical merged step:
  534.8 + 5 ≈ **540 µs**, keeping the win over compiled 798.2.

G1 prediction: pass — the launch is attempt-5's (512 threads,
3,840 B threadgroup memory) and the only change from attempt-5's
register footprint is that down now also holds a second live
accumulator, which gate/up already held in the same kernel that
launched at 512; the distinct-array count is attempt-5's two,
not attempt-6's three.
G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — each
down block's dequant terms, add order and `simd_sum` are
attempt-5's by construction (separate logical accumulators,
shared storage re-zeroed per call), gate/up and prefill are
byte-identical to attempt-5's, and the parallel store writes the
same `(bfloat)p[j]` values, just one merged loop earlier.

## Verdict

G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0
everywhere** (decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048 — no first
difference, `experts` reports the first differing element only on
failure and there is none) — the shared-storage rename preserves
attempt-5/6 bits by construction and the grader confirms it: the
merged down loop's per-block order and the parallel stores are
bit-exact, and the `rows >= 60` scalar `qmm_accum` branch is
untouched. The 512-thread launch now compiles: sharing one
kernel-scope `q[32]` between gate/up's second accumulator and
down's second block restores the pipeline's threadgroup budget
that attempt-6's three distinct arrays exceeded (512 > 448).
Chained timing µs/layer (this run; candidate vs reference vs
compiled): **1 row 93.8 / 78.9 / 74.8 (loses to compiled by
19.0, loses to reference by 14.9)**; 8 rows 160.1 / 235.8 /
236.5 (wins); 32 rows 510.1 / 797.0 / 792.7 (wins).
`beats_compiled` false — only the 1-row size misses, as in
attempt-5. Baseline `none` — no `wins_vs_baseline` /
`beats_baseline`.

Against attempt-5 (different run; compiled shifted 75.9 → 74.8
at 1 row and 798.2 → 792.7 at 32 rows between runs, so treat
cross-run deltas as indicative): 93.8 vs 92.1 at 1 row
(**+1.8%**), 160.1 vs 162.0 at 8 rows (**−1.2%**), 510.1 vs
534.8 at 32 rows (**−4.6%**). Effective bandwidth on pair
bytes: 23.6 / 110.5 / 138.8 GB/s (attempt-5: 24.0 / 109.2 /
132.3). The down interleave therefore helps where group
parallelism already hides load latency (32 rows, +4.9% GB/s,
new best 32-row time in this hypothesis) and is neutral at
8 rows, but it does not move the latency-bound 1-row size.

## Miss analysis (prediction 85 / 156 / 540, measured 93.8 / 160.1 / 510.1)

Misses are +10.4% / +2.6% / −5.5% — all inside the 20% bar, so
no formal miss, but the size pattern was inverted versus the
prediction (saving predicted largest at 1 row, actually largest
at 32 rows) and that needs explaining:

1. **The compilation fix worked exactly as predicted, the
   latency saving did not.** G1 passes at 512 threads with the
   same 3,840 B of threadgroup memory, confirming attempt-6's
   failure was the third distinct accumulator array, not
   threadgroup memory or the merged loop itself: two distinct
   arrays (`p`, shared `q`) fit, three do not. That part of the
   prediction (pure rename, identical bits) is confirmed by
   G2's differ 0 at all six sizes.
2. **At 1 row the down waves were not a third of the layer's
   latency in the way the arithmetic assumed.** The prediction
   priced the down phase at ≈ 30 µs and the merged step at
   1.3× a single-block step. Measured 93.8 ≈ attempt-5's 92.1
   says the merged step costs closer to 2× at this size: with
   only 4 threadgroups (one per pair) on 16 cores, the down
   phase's latency was already hidden *across* simdgroups —
   attempt-5's wave 0 runs 16 blocks concurrently per group,
   attempt-7 runs 12 simdgroups each serially merging two
   blocks, so concurrent in-flight loads per group fall
   (48 vs 64 simdgroup-block chains per call at 1 row) while
   each chain's step doubles its loads. The gate/up precedent
   hid ≈ 20% because gate and up *share* the `tg_x[k]` read and
   both blocks' loads were previously fully sequential phases;
   down's two blocks share only `tg_h[k]` and already overlapped
   across the 16-simdgroup wave. The remaining ≈ 19 µs gap to
   compiled (93.8 vs 74.8) is therefore still the `tg_x` load,
   silu, the two barriers and the chained launch/link cost —
   none of which this change touches.
3. **At 32 rows the merged loop pays for a different reason.**
   One wave instead of two removes a wave-quantization tail
   (wave 1 ran 8 of 16 simdgroups) on every pair and halves the
   down loop's barrier-free step count, which at 128 groups
   shows up as throughput: 138.8 vs 132.3 GB/s. The predicted
   +5 µs register tax did not appear (measured −24.7 µs vs
   attempt-5 cross-run) — consistent with the shared `q`: peak
   live accumulators never exceed gate/up's 64 floats, so there
   is no new spill, and claim 2's cross-simdgroup overlap loss
   is hidden by group parallelism at this size.

Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: a merged pair helps only
where the two blocks were previously *phases* (gate then up,
fully sequential, shared activation read); where the blocks
already ran as concurrent simdgroups in one wave (down's 24
blocks), merging trades cross-simdgroup parallelism for
in-step parallelism and is latency-neutral at 4 groups — the
1-row remainder is fixed cost and the serial gate/up chain,
not the down wave count. Register headroom at 512 threads is
exactly two 32-float accumulators; a third distinct array,
however short-lived, fails G1.

## Next change

Leave the down interleave in (it is the best 32-row time and
G2-exact) and attack the actual 1-row remainder named above:
the `tg_x` load + silu + barrier chain and the chained fixed
cost. Concretely, overlap the down product's first K steps with
the silu tail (down blocks whose `tg_h` slice is already
written) or narrow the silu barrier to a simdgroup-local one —
but any such change must keep the full-bfloat16 silu bits and
every accumulation order, and must not add a third accumulator
array (this attempt's G1 lesson).

# Inefficiency: scalar prefill branch runs 15–28× slower than compiled — serial chain, scalar redundant loads, no cross-row reuse

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-experts
- **Status:** confirmed
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T17:46:33Z
- **Next:** done — confirmed by verifier (see Verdict)

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

At `rows >= 60` the slot kernel takes its prefill branch
(`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/block-0.metal:22,59-72,103-112`),
one thread per output calling `qmm_accum`
(`block-1.metal:206-230`): a single thread walks all of K
(768 for gate/up, 384 for down) in `BK=32` contiguous
order, accumulating into one float `acc`. The arithmetic
is right — G2 passes with `differ 0` at all three prefill
sizes — but the issue pattern loses three ways at once:

1. **A purely serial dependent chain per thread.** Each of
   the 884,736 iterations per pair (gate/up 384×768 each,
   down 768×384) does `acc += xv[k] * (bfloat)wq` on one
   accumulator: no second accumulator, no unrolling, so
   each iteration waits for the last — zero instruction
   overlap within a thread. Serial depth per thread (simd
   groups 0–7) is 768 (gate) + 768 (up) + 768 (down, two
   blocks) = 2,304 dependent iterations, plus silu. Gate
   and up run as fully sequential phases (384 of 512
   threads active in each, `block-0.metal:61-71`); down
   runs 2 waves (`:105-111`).
2. **Scalar redundant loads: ~7.1 MB issued per pair for
   553 KB of unique weight bytes (12.8×).** Per iteration
   each thread issues 1 W load + 1 S + 1 B device load +
   1 threadgroup `xv` load (`block-1.metal:223-226`), but
   8 lanes share each weight word (`word = wb + (lane >>
   3)`, `:217`) and all 32 lanes of a block share `S`,
   `B` and `xv[k]`. Issued per pair: W 884,736 words =
   3.54 MB vs 442,368 unique B (8×); S+B 884,736×2×2 B =
   3.54 MB vs 110,592 unique B (32×). All scalar,
   uncoalesced, per-thread.
3. **No cross-row reuse: per-pair grid at fan-ins of
   508–8,192 pairs.** Each pair streams its expert's full
   552,960 B independently, so unique-pair traffic is
   280.9 MB / 2,247 MB / 4,530 MB per layer at 127/1,016/
   2,048 rows, where MLX's grouped `gather_qmm_rhs` loads
   each appearing expert's tile once per `BM=16` row tile
   into threadgroup `Ws` and shares it across 16 rows
   (round-2 `territory-quantized-kernels.md` §C–§E,
   frozen), and issues 8×8×8 matrix instructions (~512
   MACs per simdgroup step vs this branch's 32 scalar
   MACs — a 16× ALU-issue gap per step).

direction (a): the `max_rows` hand-off. Starting point

## The one main change

`block-0.metal` and `block-1.metal` are byte copies of the starting
point's (verify: `diff` against
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/`). `spec.json` is the
starting point's plus one key: `"max_rows": 59`.

Rows 1–59 run the candidate kernels; rows above 59 run the slot's
reference under `mx.compile` through the attempt's own dispatch
(`bench/grader/slots.py:327-337`). The fused decode path, the
`x_shape[0] >= 60` dispatch threshold (`block-0.metal:22`), the scalar
`qmm_accum` prefill branch, grids, and all four bfloat16 rounding
points are untouched — the scalar branch is now dead code at every
graded size (it can only trigger at rows ≥ 60, which all hand off),
kept as fallback so the kernels stay valid if `max_rows` is ever
raised.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

`ineff-baseline-experts-1` (confirmed): the `rows >= 60` scalar
`qmm_accum` branch runs 15.8/27.7/20.1× slower than compiled
(15,220/119,154/240,681 vs 961/4,306/11,999 µs/layer) — ~29.5
µs/pair serial issue at 18.8 GB/s. This attempt removes the whole
branch from the graded path: every prefill size (127/1,016/2,048
rows) runs the compiled reference, so prefill times `same` as
compiled by construction. Decode is untouched, so the 8/32-row wins
(ahead 72.7/282.5 µs/layer per the hypothesis entry) are kept.

## max_rows: 59, and why

The boundary's hand-off window is 32 ≤ `max_rows` ≤ 59:
decode steps run 1–32 rows and must stay on the fused path
(`max_rows >= 32`), while MLX switches its own experts kernel at 60
rows (`gather_qvm` below, `gather_qmm_rhs` at/above), so `qvm`-only
kernels must never see rows ≥ 60 (`max_rows <= 59`). This attempt's
kernels replicate both arithmetics (the scalar branch is G2-exact),
but decode rows 33–59 take the `qvm` decode path in both the kernels
(`block-0.metal:22`) and the reference, so keeping them on the
candidate is exact and keeps the fast path where it wins. 59 is the
top of the window: every decode-size input (≤ 32, plus 33–59) stays
on the candidate, every prefill-size input hands off. Round 2's
checked hand-off copy also used 59
(`results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`), and the compiled
reference was bit-exact with the reference at all six sizes there.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 / 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows (chained)

Baseline `none`: predictions are against the starting point's
measured times and the compiled bar from its run.

- **Decode 1/8/32: 93.8 / 160.1 / 510.1.** Identical kernels,
  identical grids, identical dispatch at rows ≤ 32 — the chained
  time should reproduce attempt-7's 93.8 / 160.1 / 510.1 vs

  modulo run-to-run noise (compiled shifted 75.9 → 74.8 at 1 row
  between attempt-5/7 runs). Verdicts: `slower` at 1 row, `faster`
  at 8 and 32.
- **Prefill 127/1,016/2,048: 961 / 4,306 / 11,999 (= compiled).**
  The hand-off runs literally the compiled reference, so each
  prefill size times `same` as the compiled bar measured in the
  same run; the numbers are attempt-7's run (hypothesis entry,
  *Inefficiency*). Saving vs the starting point: 14,259 / 114,848
  / 228,682 µs/layer = 285 ms / 2.30 s / 4.57 s per chunk
  (hypothesis entry arithmetic).
- **G1: pass** — the launch is attempt-7's (512 threads, 3,840 B
  threadgroup memory); `max_rows` adds no kernel.
- **G2: pass, differ 0 at all six sizes** — rows ≤ 59 run
  attempt-7's G2-exact kernels; rows above run the compiled
  reference, bit-exact with the reference at all six sizes on
  2026-11-04 (`results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`).
- **`beats_compiled`: false** — prefill `same` at all three sizes
  by construction, decode `faster` at 8/32 but `slower` at 1 row;

  `slower` anywhere. The claim is "faster decode, unchanged
  prefill" (ADR 0011): this attempt banks the prefill prize
  (removes `slower` at all three prefill sizes) and leaves the
  1-row decode gap to hyp-4.

## What this attempt leaves unmeasured

- Kernel speed at 33–59 rows (runs the candidate's `qvm` decode
  path in real serving; the grader times only 1/8/32 there).
- Sizes above 2,048 rows; prefill beyond the first chunk of seeded
  128-token prompts; other lengths/distributions; mixed batches.
- The boundary's full *can't see* list (unwritten threadgroup
  reads, thread-timing dependence, 32 KB limit by hand — 3,840 B,
  unchanged — NaN-vs-NaN equality, 1-request G3 noise).

13|decode kernel (`affine_gather_qvm`) and round 2 mapped the prefill
14|kernel's ROUNDING (`affine_gather_qmm_rhs`: bfloat-rounded dequant +
15|8-wide frag accumulation, and why a size branch at rows ≥ 60 is
16|required) —
17|[`muse-spark/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md`](../../exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md)
18|and
19|[`muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md`](../round-2/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md)
20|(both frozen; cited, not rewritten). Round 3 needs its SPEED: the
21|compiled prefill runs at 960.8 / 4306.0 / 11998.9 µs per layer at
22|127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows
23|(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`),
24|15–28× faster than the starting point's scalar prefill branch, and any
25|fast exact prefill branch — or `max_rows` hand-off that skips one —

32|### S1. Tiling and grid — what `gather_qmm_rhs` launches (speed view)
33|
34|- **Callers:** same dispatch as round 2 §A (frozen): `M==1 && B>=16 &&
35|  right_sorted_ && B/E>=4`, i.e. rows ≥ 60. Legacy tiles `bm=16, bn=32,
36|  bk=32`, `wm=1, wn=2` (round 2 §B; NAX never runs on this GPU).
37|- **Callees:** `affine_gather_qmm_rhs<bfloat16,32,4,BM=16,BN=32,BK=32,
38|  WM=1,WN=2,transpose=false>` (`quantized.h:2570-2593`) with
39|  `group_dims=(32,2,1)=64` threads and `grid_dims=((N+31)/32,
40|  min(B,ceil(B/16)+E-1),1)` (round 2 §B; host formula at
41|  `quantized.cpp:1817-1819`). Per call:
42|
43|  | prefill rows | B | grid_y | gate/up groups (12×gy) | down groups (24×gy) | per layer (3 prods) |
44|  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
45|  | 127 | 508 | 91 | 1,092 | 2,184 | 4,368 dispatched (2,880 useful + 1,488 empty) |
46|  | 1,016 | 4,064 | 313 | 3,756 | 7,512 | 15,024 dispatched (14,400 + 624) |
47|  | 2,048 | 8,192 | 571 | 6,852 | 13,704 | 27,408 dispatched (25,920 + 1,488) |

49|  Useful counts use balanced-expert `T=60/300/540` row tiles (round 2
50|  §C); empty counts are round-2 `ineff-quantized-kernels-1`'s table ×
51|  48 N-tiles per layer. Each group runs `K_it=K/32` loop iterations
52|  (24 gate/up, 12 down) over §S2–§S4's dataflow, then one
53|  `store_result(_safe)`.
54|- **Data:** threadgroup `Xs[16×40]+Ws[32×40]` bfloat16 = 1,280+2,560 =
55|  3,840 B per group (round 2 §C; `BK_padded=BN_padded=40`,
56|  `quantized.h:2596-2597`). 64 threads × 3.84 KB is a small, cheap
57|  group — the opposite of the decode `qvm` grid's occupancy problem.

59|  chained slot time (§S5); the mains dominate by byte floors (§S5).

61|  chained slot only); §S5 prices the mains from the chained totals.
62|- **Invariants:** regrouping rows is free (round 2 §C invariant):
63|  padded rows never mix into valid rows (`store_result_safe`,
64|  `:2694`), so a replacement may use any BM, variable tiles, or no
65|  tiles, as long as each row's own accumulation matches round 2

68|### S2. Dequant dataflow — `QuantizedBlockLoader`, per-K-tile (new)
69|
70|- **Callers:** the rhs kernel instantiates the loader with
71|  `BROWS=BK=32, BCOLS=BN=32, tgp_size=64` (`quantized.h:2613-2621`).
72|- **Callees:** `load_unsafe` (`quantized.h:736-747`) → `dequantize`
73|  bits=4 (`:617-623`): per packed byte, `w[2i]=(bfloat)(s·(b&0x0f)+b)`,
74|  `w[2i+1]=(bfloat)((s/16)·(b&0xf0)+b)`, with `s,b` the float-upcast
75|  scale/bias. The `s/16` high-nibble form equals `s·(b>>4)+b` as a
76|  float (power-of-two scaling is exact), so both forms round
77|  identically — attempt-7's `qmm_accum` relies on this
78|  (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/block-1.metal:203-205`).
79|- **Data:** `n_reads=(16·32)/64=8`: each of the 64 threads loads 1
80|  scale + 1 bias (threads pair up on 32 distinct `bi` rows, so
81|  scales are fetched 2× — negligible), reads 8 consecutive packed
82|  bytes, and writes 16 dequantized bfloat into `Ws`
83|  (`:686-734`). Per K-iteration per group: a full 32×32 tile,
84|  1,024 elements from 512 B packed + 128 B scales/biases.
85|  `next()` advances scales by `group_stride=BROWS·src_ld/group_size`
86|  per K tile (`:772-790`) — exactly one scale group per (K tile,
87|  N tile), matching the `[E,K,N/32]` layout.
88|- **Neighbours:** weights stream per (row tile, N tile, K tile)
89|  visit; NOTHING is reused across visits — each extra row tile of
90|  an expert re-reads and re-dequantizes its full 184,320 B
91|  (147,456 weights + 36,864 scales/biases; round 2 §C). Dequant
92|  element-ops per product per layer = `T·K·N` = 17.7M / 88.5M /
93|  159.2M (round 2 §D). At ~10 ALU ops each (and/shift, mul, add,
94|  round, tg store) that is ≈0.18/0.89/1.59 GOP per product,
95|  ≈0.5/2.7/4.8 GOP per layer — under 10% of the measured time even
96|  at scalar rates, so dequant ALU is a real but minor share; the
97|  design win is AMORTIZATION (one dequant serves ≤16 rows) plus
98|  coalescing, not ALU savings.
99|- **Cost:** weight bytes per layer = `3·T·184,320` = 33.2 / 165.9 /
100|  298.6 MB → floors at 200 GB/s (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:10`) of 166 /
101|  829 / 1,493 µs (§S5). Coalescing: `BlockLoader`-style row runs —
102|  thread pairs `(2i,2i+1)` share K-row `bi` and read bytes 0–7 and
103|  8–15 of it (consecutive, one 16 B line), pairs stride by
104|  `N/2=192/384 B` per K-row (`:727-734`) — the standard tiled-GEMM
105|  pattern, full lines, no `qvm`-style 192 B-stride scalar loads
106|  (contrast round-1 §A / round-2 §F).
107|- **Invariants:** the bfloat16 rounding into `Ws` is rounding point
108|  1 (round 2 §D) — a fast branch must reproduce these exact rounded
109|  weights (same `s·q+b` float value, same cast), whatever its
110|  grouping.

112|### S3. Activation (x) dataflow — re-read per N-tile (new)
113|
114|- **Callers:** `BlockLoader<bfloat16,BM=16,BK=32,dst_ld=40,
115|  reduction_dim=1,tgp_size=64>` (`quantized.h:2611-2612`).
116|- **Callees:** `load_unsafe` (`steel/gemm/loader.h:74-80`) copies
117|  verbatim bfloat16→bfloat16 (exact, no rounding); partial row
118|  tiles (`tgp_bm<16`) take `load_safe` (`loader.h:83-128`), which
119|  zero-pads via a per-element `tmp_idx/tmp_val` bound-check dance —
120|  strictly slower loads on every partial tile.
121|- **Data:** `n_reads=512/64=8, TCOLS=4, TROWS=16`: threads `(4i..4i+3)`
122|  own x-row `bi=i`, each reading 8 consecutive bfloat (one 16 B
123|  vector) — a full coalesced 16×32 tile per K-iteration, 1 KB per
124|  group per iteration. But EVERY (row tile, N tile) group loads its
125|  own copy of the same x rows: issued x bytes per product =
126|  `T·(N/32)·K_it·1KB` = T·12·24 KB (gate/up) = 17.3 / 86.4 /
127|  155.5 MB per product per layer — the x row-tile (24 KB) is
128|  re-read 12× (gate/up) or 24× (down), once per N-tile. Total
129|  issued x per layer ≈ 52 / 259 / 467 MB — EXCEEDS issued weight
130|  bytes (33/166/299 MB). Counterpart: the 12–24 sharing groups run
131|  concurrently on 24 KB of shared addresses, so all but the first
132|  read per row tile should hit in cache; distinct x per layer is
133|  only `B·(768+768+384)·2B` = 2.0 / 15.6 / 31.4 MB. DRAM x-traffic
134|  is therefore between 2/16/31 MB (all hits) and 52/259/467 MB
135|  (all miss) — unmeasured, and a replacement that loads each x
136|  row-tile once per N-slab (or once per row, qvm-style into
137|  registers) banks the difference for free.
138|- **Neighbours:** at 127 rows EVERY useful tile is partial
139|  (`cnt_e≈8.5<16`, all 60 tiles): 100% of useful work takes
140|  `gemm_loop_unaligned` + `load_safe` + `store_result_safe`. At
141|  1,016 ≈20% of tiles are partial (5th of 5 per expert), at 2,048
142|  ≈11% (9th of 9). The 127-row size thus pays the safe-path tax
143|  everywhere — a regrouped branch with full tiles (e.g. smaller or
144|  variable BM) avoids it.
145|- **Cost:** folded into §S5's mains range; the safe-path tax has no
146|  separate measured figure (no per-tile timing exists).
147|- **Invariants:** x values are exact through the loader (no rounding
148|  point) — regrouping never changes them.

151|
152|- **Callers:** `gemm_loop_aligned` (full tiles) /
153|  `gemm_loop_unaligned` (partial) (`quantized_utils.h:6-75`): per
154|  iteration, barrier → load x + dequant w → barrier → `mma()`.
155|  TWO threadgroup barriers per 32-K step, 48 per gate/up group, 24
156|  per down group — the kernel's latency skeleton.
157|- **Callees:** `BlockMMA<...,BM=16,BN=32,BK=32,WM=1,WN=2>`
158|  (`steel/gemm/mma.h:439-537`), `AccumType=float` default
159|  (`mma.h:451`). Per simdgroup: `TM=16/8=2`, `TN=32/16=2` frags;
160|  `mma()` steps `kk` over BK in 4 8-wide steps, each
161|  `tile_matmad` issuing 2·2·1=4 `simdgroup_matrix` 8×8×8
162|  multiply-accumulates (`mma.h:406-427,513-537`) with 3
163|  `simdgroup_barrier`s per step. Per group per K-iteration:
164|  2 simdgroups × 4 steps × 4 MMAs = 32 MMAs = 32,768 flops;
165|  per gate group total: 24 × 32,768 = 786K flops.
166|- **Data:** operands reload from threadgroup (`Ws` bfloat→float
167|  widen on load, `mma.h:57-67`); accumulators stay in float frag
168|  registers across the whole K loop; one float→bfloat16 store per
169|  output (`store_result`, `mma.h:540-592`) — rounding point 2's
170|  container (round 2 §E). Useful MMA per layer = `3·2·B·K·N`
171|  (K·N=294,912) = 0.90 / 7.19 / 14.50 GFLOP → floors at 5.2

177|  replacement is free to tile bigger (regrouping is free, §S1)
178|  but must keep the 8-wide frag accumulation order per row
179|  (round 2 §E invariant) — bigger tiles change WHICH rows share
180|  loads, never a row's own add order, as long as BK=32 frag
181|  stepping is kept.
182|- **Cost:** §S5.
183|- **Invariants:** per-output accumulation grouping (contiguous
184|  8-wide frag dots, sequential over BK=32 tiles, increasing K)

186|  (attempt-7 `block-1.metal:197-230`) — bit-exact today

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write faster MobileMoE-S kernels, for decoding and prompt processing
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|A request goes through two phases: **prompt processing** (the prefill), which runs its whole prompt through the model, and **decoding**, one step per generated token. An improvement must hold in both: faster in one, and no slower in the other ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A kernel that speeds up the decode step but slows the prefill is not an improvement.
12|
13|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
14|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
15|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
16|
17|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
18|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
19|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
20|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
21|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
22|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
23|
24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
95|
96|## Tools and limits
97|
98|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
99|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
100|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
101|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.
102|
103|## Rules of this session

107|- **Write only inside `muse-spark/`.** Never change `bench/`, `claude/`, `results/`, `tools/`, `third_party/`, or any other file. A copy of the grader you edit is never used.

180|## How each attempt is judged
181|
182|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.
183|
184|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
185|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
186|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
187|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.

{"content":"# attempt-2 (round 3): vectorized per-pair scalar prefill — one thread per weight word (builder-2-b)

First attempt in direction (b) for `hyp-2-experts-prefill` (slot
`experts`, baseline `none`). Starting point
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7` (fused single kernel,
512 threads/pair, G2 pass all six, prefill 15,220 / 119,154 /
240,681 µs/layer at 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows).

## The one main change

Only the `rows >= 60` prefill branch is rewritten; the fused decode
path is byte-identical (verified by diff: `block-0.metal` differs
from attempt-7 only in the header comment and the three `} else {`
prefill branches; `block-1.metal` decode helpers `qvm_block`,
`qvm_gate_up_pair`, `qvm_down_pair` byte-identical; `spec.json`
byte-identical — same kernel, same `rows*2048` grid, no `max_rows`).

- **Before:** one thread per output called scalar `qmm_accum`: 32
  threads per 32-output block, each walking all of K with one
  accumulator, each issuing its own W + S + B + x loads per k.
- **After:** one thread per weight word calls `qmm_accum8`
  (`block-1.metal`): 4 threads per block, each accumulating the
  word's 8 outputs into 8 independent accumulators (`p[0..7]` —
  the kernel-scope `p` reused in this disjoint phase, re-zeroed on
  entry, so no third thread array and the same 512-thread pipeline
  budget as attempt-7). One W/S/B/x load per k feeds all 8
  outputs: 8× fewer issues, 8 accumulators overlapping in flight.
- **Packing:** 8 blocks per simdgroup (`block = simd*8 +
  (lane>>2)`, `word = lane&3`): gate/up 12 blocks in one wave of
  2 simdgroups (48 active threads, 16 lanes idle in the second),
  down 24 blocks in one wave of 3 simdgroups (96 active, none
  idle) — replacing gate/up's 384-thread phases and down's 2
  waves.
- **Bits:** each output keeps the scalar branch's exact per-output
  sequence — same contiguous `BK=32` tile order, same
  `q = (w >> shift) & 0xf` extraction, same
  `wq = s*q + b` / `acc += x*(bfloat)wq` terms (S/B/x loaded once
  per k hold the same values every output would load itself), same
  `(bfloat)` store. Bit-exact by the same G2-proven coincidence
  the scalar branch relies on.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

`ineff-baseline-experts-1` (round 3, confirmed): the serial scalar
prefill chain at ~29.5 µs/pair and 18.8 GB/s (9.4% of peak). This
attempt removes its first two causes inside each pair — the
single-accumulator serial chain (now 8 overlapping accumulators)
and the 12.8× redundant scalar loads (now 8× fewer W/S/B/x issues:
per k per block 32 threads × 4 loads → 4 threads × 4 loads) —
while keeping every output's accumulation order. It deliberately
keeps the third cause (no cross-row reuse: per-pair grid, 553 KB
unique per pair) — that is direction (c)'s prize.

## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)

512 threads/group ≤ 1,024. Threadgroup memory unchanged: 3,840 B.
Distinct thread arrays unchanged: two 32-float accumulators (`p`,
shared `q`) — prefill reuses `p[0..7]`, adding none, so the
pipeline's `maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` should still admit 512

Done. Attempt folder: `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-2/`.

What I built: direction (b) — rewrote only the `rows >= 60` prefill branch so one thread computes a weight word's 8 outputs via a new `qmm_accum8` helper (8 accumulators in reused kernel-scope `p[0..7]`, one W/S/B/x load per k, each output keeping the scalar branch's contiguous BK=32 bfloat16-rounded order). Fused decode path, decode helpers, dispatch, grid, and `spec.json` verified byte-identical to round-2 attempt-7 by diff; no `max_rows`.

Verdict (`grade.json`): G1 pass, G2 pass all six sizes with differ 0. Decode 152.8/173.3/634.1 (`slower`/`faster`/`faster`, same verdicts as starting point). Prefill 20,444/156,416/303,543 (`slower` at all three, 0 wins); `beats_compiled` false. Prediction (3,000/24,000/49,000) refuted ~6.5×.

Why it failed: each k step's 8 FMAs depend on that step's loads with no k-unrolling, so serial depth stayed 768 while active threads fell 384→48/group — the widening removed cross-thread latency hiding without shortening any chain. (Caveat: this run's machine was much slower than the basis run's — byte-identical decode code also slowed — so within-run vs-compiled ratios 18.4/23.1/18.6× vs 15.8/27.7/20.1× are the signal: no speedup.)

Recorded: verdict + miss analysis in attempt `notes.md`, builder-2-b section in `hyp-2-experts-prefill.md`, note on `ineff-baseline-experts-1.md`, log lines.

One change I'd make next: keep the word-packing but unroll 4 k-steps × 8 outputs into `p[0..31]` (4 loads outstanding per thread, same G1 budget); if that fails, direction (b) is exhausted.

1|# Territory: quantized-kernels (round 3 — prefill SPEED)
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-quantized-kernels
4|- **Status:** done
5|- **Version:** 2
6|- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T17:41:57Z
7|- **Next:** none — rhs speed anatomy mapped (§S1–§S7), 2 inefficiencies posted, note left on `territory-baseline-experts`
8|
9|## What it does
10|
11|This territory is MLX 0.32.4's `mx.gather_qmm` Metal kernels behind the
12|`experts` slot (`quantized.h`, `quantized_utils.h`). Round 1 mapped the
13|decode kernel (`affine_gather_qvm`) and round 2 mapped the prefill
14|kernel's ROUNDING (`affine_gather_qmm_rhs`: bfloat-rounded dequant +
15|8-wide frag accumulation, and why a size branch at rows ≥ 60 is
16|required) —
17|[`muse-spark/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md`](../../exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md)
18|and
19|[`muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md`](../round-2/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md)
20|(both frozen; cited, not rewritten). Round 3 needs its SPEED: the
21|compiled prefill runs at 960.8 / 4306.0 / 11998.9 µs per layer at
22|127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows
23|(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`),
24|15–28× faster than the starting point's scalar prefill branch, and any
25|fast exact prefill branch — or `max_rows` hand-off that skips one —
26|must match or avoid what is mapped here. This entry writes only what is
27|new: tiling, occupancy, dequant/x/MMA dataflow, rate analysis, and the
28|match-or-avoid list. Rounding facts are round 2's (§D/§E/§F there).
29|
30|## The checklist
31|
32|### S1. Tiling and grid — what `gather_qmm_rhs` launches (speed view)
33|
34|- **Callers:** same dispatch as round 2 §A (frozen): `M==1 && B>=16 &&
35|  right_sorted_ && B/E>=4`, i.e. rows ≥ 60. Legacy tiles `bm=16, bn=32,
36|  bk=32`, `wm=1, wn=2` (round 2 §B; NAX never runs on this GPU).
37|- **Callees:** `affine_gather_qmm_rhs<bfloat16,32,4,BM=16,BN=32,BK=32,
38|  WM=1,WN=2,transpose=false>` (`quantized.h:2570-2593`) with
39|  `group_dims=(32,2,1)=64` threads and `grid_dims=((N+31)/32,
40|  min(B,ceil(B/16)+E-1),1)` (round 2 §B; host formula at
41|  `quantized.cpp:1817-1819`). Per call:
42|
43|  | prefill rows | B | grid_y | gate/up groups (12×gy) | down groups (24×gy) | per layer (3 prods) |
44|  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
45|  | 127 | 508 | 91 | 1,092 | 2,184 | 4,368 dispatched (2,880 useful + 1,488 empty) |
46|  | 1,016 | 4,064 | 313 | 3,756 | 7,512 | 15,024 dispatched (14,400 + 624) |
47|  | 2,048 | 8,192 | 571 | 6,852 | 13,704 | 27,408 dispatched (25,920 + 1,488) |
48|
49|  Useful counts use balanced-expert `T=60/300/540` row tiles (round 2
50|  §C); empty counts are round-2 `ineff-quantized-kernels-1`'s table ×
51|  48 N-tiles per layer. Each group runs `K_it=K/32` loop iterations
52|  (24 gate/up, 12 down) over §S2–§S4's dataflow, then one
53|  `store_result(_safe)`.
54|- **Data:** threadgroup `Xs[16×40]+Ws[32×40]` bfloat16 = 1,280+2,560 =
55|  3,840 B per group (round 2 §C; `BK_padded=BN_padded=40`,
56|  `quantized.h:2596-2597`). 64 threads × 3.84 KB is a small, cheap
57|  group — the opposite of the decode `qvm` grid's occupancy problem.
58|- **Neighbours:** 3 offsets kernels + sort/unsort + `swiglu` share the
59|  chained slot time (§S5); the mains dominate by byte floors (§S5).
60|- **Cost:** no per-kernel prefill timing exists (grader times the
61|  chained slot only); §S5 prices the mains from the chained totals.
62|- **Invariants:** regrouping rows is free (round 2 §C invariant):
63|  padded rows never mix into valid rows (`store_result_safe`,
64|  `:2694`), so a replacement may use any BM, variable tiles, or no
65|  tiles, as long as each row's own accumulation matches round 2
66|  §D+§E. Grid over-provisioning (≤59 y-tiles) is pure waste (§S6).
67|
68|### S2. Dequant dataflow — `QuantizedBlockLoader`, per-K-tile (new)
69|
70|- **Callers:** the rhs kernel instantiates the loader with
71|  `BROWS=BK=32, BCOLS=BN=32, tgp_size=64` (`quantized.h:2613-2621`).
72|- **Callees:** `load_unsafe` (`quantized.h:736-747`) → `dequantize`
73|  bits=4 (`:617-623`): per packed byte, `w[2i]=(bfloat)(s·(b&0x0f)+b)`,
74|  `w[2i+1]=(bfloat)((s/16)·(b&0xf0)+b)`, with `s,b` the float-upcast
75|  scale/bias. The `s/16` high-nibble form equals `s·(b>>4)+b` as a
76|  float (power-of-two scaling is exact), so both forms round
77|  identically — attempt-7's `qmm_accum` relies on this
78|  (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/block-1.metal:203-205`).
79|- **Data:** `n_reads=(16·32)/64=8`: each of the 64 threads loads 1
80|  scale + 1 bias (threads pair up on 32 distinct `bi` rows, so
81|  scales are fetched 2× — negligible), reads 8 consecutive packed
82|  bytes, and writes 16 dequantized bfloat into `Ws`
83|  (`:686-734`). Per K-iteration per group: a full 32×32 tile,
84|  1,024 elements from 512 B packed + 128 B scales/biases.
85|  `next()` advances scales by `group_stride=BROWS·src_ld/group_size`
86|  per K tile (`:772-790`) — exactly one scale group per (K tile,
87|  N tile), matching the `[E,K,N/32]` layout.
88|- **Neighbours:** weights stream per (row tile, N tile, K tile)
89|  visit; NOTHING is reused across visits — each extra row tile of
90|  an expert re-reads and re-dequantizes its full 184,320 B
91|  (147,456 weights + 36,864 scales/biases; round 2 §C). Dequant
92|  element-ops per product per layer = `T·K·N` = 17.7M / 88.5M /
93|  159.2M (round 2 §D). At ~10 ALU ops each (and/shift, mul, add,
94|  round, tg store) that is ≈0.18/0.89/1.59 GOP per product,
95|  ≈0.5/2.7/4.8 GOP per layer — under 10% of the measured time even
96|  at scalar rates, so dequant ALU is a real but minor share; the
97|  design win is AMORTIZATION (one dequant serves ≤16 rows) plus
98|  coalescing, not ALU savings.
99|- **Cost:** weight bytes per layer = `3·T·184,320` = 33.2 / 165.9 /
100|  298.6 MB → floors at 200 GB/s (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:10`) of 166 /
101|  829 / 1,493 µs (§S5). Coalescing: `BlockLoader`-style row runs —
102|  thread pairs `(2i,2i+1)` share K-row `bi` and read bytes 0–7 and
103|  8–15 of it (consecutive, one 16 B line), pairs stride by
104|  `N/2=192/384 B` per K-row (`:727-734`) — the standard tiled-GEMM
105|  pattern, full lines, no `qvm`-style 192 B-stride scalar loads
106|  (contrast round-1 §A / round-2 §F).
107|- **Invariants:** the bfloat16 rounding into `Ws` is rounding point
108|  1 (round 2 §D) — a fast branch must reproduce these exact rounded
109|  weights (same `s·q+b` float value, same cast), whatever its
110|  grouping.
111|
112|### S3. Activation (x) dataflow — re-read per N-tile (new)
113|
114|- **Callers:** `BlockLoader<bfloat16,BM=16,BK=32,dst_ld=40,
115|  reduction_dim=1,tgp_size=64>` (`quantized.h:2611-2612`).
116|- **Callees:** `load_unsafe` (`steel/gemm/loader.h:74-80`) copies
117|  verbatim bfloat16→bfloat16 (exact, no rounding); partial row
118|  tiles (`tgp_bm<16`) take `load_safe` (`loader.h:83-128`), which
119|  zero-pads via a per-element `tmp_idx/tmp_val` bound-check dance —
120|  strictly slower loads on every partial tile.
121|- **Data:** `n_reads=512/64=8, TCOLS=4, TROWS=16`: threads `(4i..4i+3)`
122|  own x-row `bi=i`, each reading 8 consecutive bfloat (one 16 B
123|  vector) — a full coalesced 16×32 tile per K-iteration, 1 KB per
124|  group per iteration. But EVERY (row tile, N tile) group loads its
125|  own copy of the same x rows: issued x bytes per product =
126|  `T·(N/32)·K_it·1KB` = T·12·24 KB (gate/up) = 17.3 / 86.4 /
127|  155.5 MB per product per layer — the x row-tile (24 KB) is
128|  re-read 12× (gate/up) or 24× (down), once per N-tile. Total
129|  issued x per layer ≈ 52 / 259 / 467 MB — EXCEEDS issued weight
130|  bytes (33/166/299 MB). Counterpart: the 12–24 sharing groups run
131|  concurrently on 24 KB of shared addresses, so all but the first
132|  read per row tile should hit in cache; distinct x per layer is
133|  only `B·(768+768+384)·2B` = 2.0 / 15.6 / 31.4 MB. DRAM x-traffic
134|  is therefore between 2/16/31 MB (all hits) and 52/259/467 MB
135|  (all miss) — unmeasured, and a replacement that loads each x
136|  row-tile once per N-slab (or once per row, qvm-style into
137|  registers) banks the difference for free.
138|- **Neighbours:** at 127 rows EVERY useful tile is partial

150|### S4. MMA structure — what each K-iteration does (new)
151|
152|- **Callers:** `gemm_loop_aligned` (full tiles) /
153|  `gemm_loop_unaligned` (partial) (`quantized_utils.h:6-75`): per
154|  iteration, barrier → load x + dequant w → barrier → `mma()`.
155|  TWO threadgroup barriers per 32-K step, 48 per gate/up group, 24
156|  per down group — the kernel's latency skeleton.
157|- **Callees:** `BlockMMA<...,BM=16,BN=32,BK=32,WM=1,WN=2>`
158|  (`steel/gemm/mma.h:439-537`), `AccumType=float` default
159|  (`mma.h:451`). Per simdgroup: `TM=16/8=2`, `TN=32/16=2` frags;
160|  `mma()` steps `kk` over BK in 4 8-wide steps, each
161|  `tile_matmad` issuing 2·2·1=4 `simdgroup_matrix` 8×8×8
162|  multiply-accumulates (`mma.h:406-427,513-537`) with 3
163|  `simdgroup_barrier`s per step. Per group per K-iteration:
164|  2 simdgroups × 4 steps × 4 MMAs = 32 MMAs = 32,768 flops;
165|  per gate group total: 24 × 32,768 = 786K flops.
166|- **Data:** operands reload from threadgroup (`Ws` bfloat→float
167|  widen on load, `mma.h:57-67`); accumulators stay in float frag
168|  registers across the whole K loop; one float→bfloat16 store per
169|  output (`store_result`, `mma.h:540-592`) — rounding point 2's
170|  container (round 2 §E). Useful MMA per layer = `3·2·B·K·N`
171|  (K·N=294,912) = 0.90 / 7.19 / 14.50 GFLOP → floors at 5.2
172|  TFLOPS (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:14`) of 173 / 1,383 / 2,788 µs.
173|- **Neighbours:** BM=16 means only TM=2 M-frags per simdgroup —
174|  half the M-reuse of a BM=32 tile; the NAX variant MLX uses on
175|  M3-class GPUs runs `bm=32/64, bn=bk=64` (round 2 §H), i.e. MLX
176|  itself buys 4–8× bigger tiles where the hardware allows. A
177|  replacement is free to tile bigger (regrouping is free, §S1)
178|  but must keep the 8-wide frag accumulation order per row
179|  (round 2 §E invariant) — bigger tiles change WHICH rows share
180|  loads, never a row's own add order, as long as BK=32 frag
181|  stepping is kept.
182|- **Cost:** §S5.
183|- **Invariants:** per-output accumulation grouping (contiguous
184|  8-wide frag dots, sequential over BK=32 tiles, increasing K)

237|
238|Attempt-7's `rows>=60` branch (`qmm_accum`, `block-1.metal:206-230`,
239|called per output per pair, `block-0.metal:59-72,103-112`) is bit-exact

241|961/4306/11999 µs/layer). Three compounding causes, all in the gap

24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.

68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.

72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
