{"content":"# Round-3 attempt 2 — builder-3-b, hyp-3-routing-prefill direction (b)

Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4` (the slot's
starting point: G1+G2 pass, decode `faster` x3, prefill `slower` x3).
Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the compiled reference
in both phases.

## The one main change

A second kernel with a GEMM shape for prefill sizes, sharing each
`w_router` K-chunk across 16 rows, behind a size branch that keeps decode
on the winning staged path:

- Kernel 0 (`block-0.metal` + `block-1.metal` header) is attempt-4
  verbatim — same GEMV branch at `rows == 1`, same split-K staging,
  same sigmoid, same top-4 — plus `if (rows > 32) return;` at the top.
  Its outputs are renamed `inds0`/`weights0`. Grid `rows*256`,
  threadgroup 256, threadgroup memory unchanged at 28,080 B.
- Kernel 1 (`block-2.metal`) is new. Grid `rows*60`, threadgroup 960:
  one threadgroup spans 16 rows with one thread per (row, expert); 60
  divides 960 so every group covers whole rows and no bounds check is
  needed (round-1 attempt-2's grid precedent). Each of the 12 staged
  groups stages 4 K-chunks of `w_router` once per 16 rows with
  attempt-4's exact coalesced `float4` mapping into `wsh[4096]`, plus
  the 64 current d-values per row into `xst[1024]`; each thread
  accumulates its (row, expert) score into per-partition partials in
  registers, each partial a serial scalar sum in increasing d, folded
  in partition order — the exact rows-branched per-row orders, so G2
  follows attempt-4's proof (feeding changes without order changes).
  Sigmoid, strictly-greater top-4 and the left-fold normalise are
  verbatim copies, run by one thread per row. At `rows <= 32` it only
  copies kernel 0's outputs. Threadgroup memory
  (4096+1024+1024)*4 = 24,576 B of 32 KB; 25 barriers per group of 16
  rows (12x2 + 1), i.e. ~1.6 per row against attempt-4's 24.

Against round-1 attempt-2's failure (slower everywhere): that kernel
staged with serial per-thread loops (60 threads x 64 serial loads),
2 launches with two [rows,60] intermediates, and strided device reads.
This one stages cooperatively (960 threads share 960 vector loads),
keeps one [rows,4] hand-off, and reuses attempt-4's proven coalesced
mapping — but the proof is the chained timing below, not the contrast.

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-routing-1` (per-row `w_router` re-read) and
`ineff-baseline-routing-2` (per-row shape cost) together: `w_router`
device traffic falls from rows x 184,320 B to ceil(rows/16) x 184,320 B
(16x at full groups), barriers from 24/row to ~1.6/row amortised, duty
from 23% to 100% in the single-partition regime (every thread owns one
expert of its row through all 12 groups), footprint from 28,080 B to
24,576 B.

## Predicted us per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 / 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows

Anchor: the round-3 re-grade of attempt-4
(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`):
ref / compiled / candidate = 68.4/65.1/49.8 at 1 row,
169.2/135.7/113.5 at 8, 159.3/145.2/121.3 at 32,
102.3/87.3/227.1 at 127, 231.3/221.1/1298.8 at 1,016,
310.0/290.4/2513.0 at 2,048. Decode margins: 15.3/22.2/23.9.

- Decode (1/8/32): kernel 0 is attempt-4 plus a never-taken branch
  (~0); kernel 1 adds one copy launch (grid rows*60 threads, rows*4
  elements x 8 B copied). Allowance 3 us: **53 / 117 / 124** vs
  compiled 65.1/135.7/145.2 — still `faster`, spending ~3 of 15-24 us
  of margin.
- Prefill traffic floors at 200 GB/s (w staged once per 16 rows):
  - 127 rows: 8 groups x 184,320 B (w) + 127 x 1,536 B (x) + 127 x 32 B
    (out) = 1,673,696 B -> 8.4 us. + 25 barriers x 0.5 us = 12.5 +
    idle kernel-0 launch 4 + chained fixed cost 25 -> **~50** vs
    compiled 87.3.
  - 1,016 rows: 64 x 184,320 + 1,016 x 1,536 + 1,016 x 32 = 13.4 MB ->
    67 us. 64 groups / 16 cores = 4 waves x 25 x 0.5 = 50 + idle
    launch 6 + fixed 25 -> **~148** vs compiled 221.1.
  - 2,048 rows: 128 x 184,320 + 2,048 x 1,536 + 2,048 x 32 = 26.7 MB ->
    134 us. 8 waves x 25 x 0.5 = 100 + idle launch 8 + fixed 25 ->
    **~267** vs compiled 290.4 — thin: if barriers cost 1 us not 0.5,
    this is ~367 and `slower`. The barrier cost is a guess; the
    chained timing decides.

Prediction: **53 / 117 / 124 / 50 / 148 / 267 us**. G2 prediction: pass
at all six sizes — every accumulation order is copied op-for-op from
attempt-4, which passes G2 at all six (it fails on speed, not bits).

No `max_rows`: the hand-off is direction (a)'s fix; this attempt must
prove the GEMM kernel same-or-better at prefill on its own merits.

9-31 (kernel-0 staged path, same code as graded 8/32 but other
partition groupings); 33-126 (kernel-1 split-K path with 16/8
partitions, exercised in kind but not in verdict); 129-767 and 769+
(kernel-1 paths past the 129/257/768 transitions); above 2,048 rows;
prefill past the first chunk; whole-request composition (ready check);
the 24,576 B threadgroup sum (unchecked by slots.build); unwritten
threadgroup reads and thread-timing dependence (one equality run per
layer cannot expose them).

Read text file `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/notes.md`.
1|# Round-2 attempt 4 — builder-2-d, hardening of hyp-2-routing-exact
2|
3|Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-3` (scalar
4|full-G2; chained 46.9/300.0/297.2 µs/layer vs compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9 —
5|latency-bound from uncoalesced device loads + `xsh` bank conflicts).
6|Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the compiled reference.
7|
8|## The one main change
9|
10|Stage each K-chunk's `w_router` block into threadgroup memory with
11|coalesced vector loads and sum from threadgroup with a padded `x`
12|layout, nothing else:
13|
14|- Staging: chunks are staged 4 at a time (12 groups cover all 48
15|  BK=16 chunks). Each staged chunk is 60×16 floats, loaded as 240
16|  `float4` loads (consecutive threads cover one expert's 4 vectors,
17|  then the next expert) and stored transposed in `wsh[slot][k][expert]`
18|  with expert stride 64.
19|- Padded `x`: chunk `c` of `x` sits at `xpad[c*17 + k]` (one pad float
20|  per chunk), replacing attempt-3's flat `xsh[768]`.
21|- Scalar chain: expert-parallel lanes read `wsh` at consecutive expert
22|  banks (conflict-free) and `xpad` uniformly per `k` (broadcast).
23|  Partials live transposed in `parts[partition][expert]` (stride 64)
24|  and are resumed product-by-product in increasing `d` across staged
25|  groups, so each (expert, partition) partial is still one serial
26|  scalar sum in increasing `d`; partials are then summed sequentially
27|  in partition order. 24 barriers on the scalar path (2 per group).
28|- Threadgroup memory: (816 + 60 + 2048 + 4096) × 4 B = 28,080 B of
29|  32 KB. Same grid (`rows*256`), threadgroup (256) and one-kernel layout.
30|
31|Kept verbatim from attempt-3: the regime branch on `rows` (GEMV only
32|at `rows == 1`; split-K while `rows <= 768`; regular above — the GEMV
33|branch is unchanged apart from reading the padded `x` layout), the
34|split-K partition formula (32 partitions at 8/32 rows, 8 of 96 at 127,
35|2 at 257–768, single partition above 768, last partition absorbing the
36|remainder chunks), the GEMV lane order and shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1,
37|MLX's verbatim sigmoid (`1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`),
38|the strictly-greater insertion top-4 (earliest index wins ties), and
39|`((w0+w1)+w2)+w3 + 1e-20`, divide, ×2.5 on unbiased scores.
40|
41|## Inefficiency removed
42|
43|`ineff-baseline-routing-1` stays removed (same orders as attempt-3).
44|The target is attempt-3's diagnosed feeding cost (its notes: the
45|scalar chains read `w_router` uncoalesced — warp lanes 64 B apart,
46|16 cache lines per step — and `xsh[p*16+k]` with 16-way bank
47|conflicts on every product). Staging turns the device reads into
48|coalesced `float4` loads and the dependent chain's reads into
49|conflict-free threadgroup reads. The per-row `w_router` re-read
50|(`ineff-baseline-routing-4`) and the serial thread-0 scan are
51|untouched.
52|
53|## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write faster MobileMoE-S kernels, for decoding and prompt processing
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|A request goes through two phases: **prompt processing** (the prefill), which runs its whole prompt through the model, and **decoding**, one step per generated token. An improvement must hold in both: faster in one, and no slower in the other ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A kernel that speeds up the decode step but slows the prefill is not an improvement.
12|
13|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
14|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
15|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
16|
17|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
18|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
19|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
20|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
21|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
22|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
23|
24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
95|
96|## Tools and limits
97|
98|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
99|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
100|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
101|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.
102|
103|## Rules of this session
104|
105|These keep your work apart from everyone else's. Git hooks and an audit script enforce them, and a commit that breaks them is refused.
106|
107|- **Write only inside `muse-spark/`.** Never change `bench/`, `claude/`, `results/`, `tools/`, `third_party/`, or any other file. A copy of the grader you edit is never used.
108|- **Commit only on `muse-agent`,** with the co-author trailer your settings add: `Co-Authored-By: Muse Spark (Meta Model API) <muse-spark@meta-model-api.invalid>`. Start each subject with `Muse Spark:`. No other co-author.
109|- **Never push, merge, rebase, change git config, or skip hooks.**
110|- **Don't read `.env`** or any credentials file.

112|

118|  kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>/

120|    spec.json                                the launch spec

124|

129|```
130|

132|

137|  "targets": [
138|    {"slot": "routing+combine", "why": "...", "expected_saving_ms": {"rows_1": 0.0, "rows_32": 0.0}, "design": "..."}
139|  ]

142|

144|
145|**The launch spec** (`spec.json`):
146|
147|```json
148|{

150|    {
151|      "name": "fused_routing",
152|      "source_block": 0,
153|      "header_block": null,
154|      "inputs": ["x", "w_router", "bias"],
155|      "outputs": [
156|        {"name": "inds", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "uint32"},
157|        {"name": "weights", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "float32"}

169|
170|- **`source_block` and `header_block`** are the numbers of your `block-N.metal` files.
171|- **Kernels run in list order.** A kernel's `inputs` may name slot inputs or outputs of earlier kernels.
172|- **`slot_outputs`** maps each output of the slot to the kernel output that provides it.
173|- **`max_rows`** (optional, an integer of at least 1): inputs with more rows than this skip your kernels and run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. Use it to keep prefill-sized inputs on MLX's own code when your kernels are built for decode sizes; MLX switches its own experts kernel at 60 rows. The hand-off is graded like the rest: bit-exact, and timed at the prefill sizes.
174|- **For `routing+combine`,** `spec.json` holds two specs, each in the format above for its own slot, `max_rows` included: `{"routing": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}, "combine": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}}`. The original experts and shared expert run between the two parts. The grader tests each part on its own, and the combine part receives the reference routing weights.
175|- **Shape and grid entries** are integers, or products of integers and the names `rows`, `D`, `E`, `K` and `H`, such as `"rows*32"`. Nothing else is evaluated.
176|- **dtypes** are `float32`, `bfloat16`, `float16`, `uint32` or `int32`.
177|- **Template values** are one of those dtypes, an integer or a boolean.
178|- **`grid`** counts threads, not threadgroups, as in `mx.fast.metal_kernel`.
179|
180|## How each attempt is judged
181|
182|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.
183|
184|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
185|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
186|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
187|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
188|
189|   At every size:
190|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
191|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
192|
193|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
194|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
195|3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
196|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
197|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
198|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
199|
200|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
201|
202|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).
203|
204|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
205|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
206|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
207|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same` or `slower`); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.
208|
209|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
210|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
211|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
212|- **Per phase:** decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) are each `faster` when every size is, `slower` when any size is, and `not slower` otherwise.
213|- **`beats_compiled`** is true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
214|
215|It is a guide; the ready check in the round, and Claude's G3 after it, decide.
216|
217|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, or after 5 attempts. Name your final attempt per slot in `muse-spark/summary.md`; it goes to the end-to-end and G3 checks, which surucuonur's team runs after merging your branch.

## The one main change

Split the staged path at the regime boundary `rows = 768` into two
kernels so the single-partition regime (partitions == 1, i.e. exactly
rows > 768) drops the 2,048-float `parts` array:

- Kernel-A (`block-0.metal`): attempt-4 verbatim plus a uniform

- Kernel-B (`block-2.metal`): at rows <= 768 copies kernel-A's outputs
  through (bit-exact, 4 threads/row); at rows > 768 runs the
  single-partition path with each expert's whole 768-product chain in
  one thread-private accumulator across the 12 staged groups — no
  `parts`, so threadgroup is (816 + 60 + 4,096) x 4 B = 19,888 B
  (60.7% of 32 KB) instead of 28,080 B (85.7%).

Two kernels are required because threadgroup arrays are statically
sized: one kernel would still declare `parts` for its general path.
Each kernel's outputs are fresh buffers (`bench/grader/slots.py:343-356`,
`env.update` overwrites per kernel), so same-name sharing is impossible
and the copy-through is the wiring.

Kept verbatim: the `rows`-branched regimes (the split is at the
regime boundary, never at graded values), staging layout/stride,
product order within every (expert, partition) chain (kernel-B's
register chain visits chunks/groups in the same increasing order the
`parts` path resumes them in), the 24 in-loop barriers, sigmoid,
strictly-greater top-4, and the weights fold. G2 prediction: pass at
all six sizes — storage changes only (register vs threadgroup vs copy),
no order changes.

Design alternatives ruled out while writing (for the failure ledger /
inefficiency notes): register-held partials in ONE kernel cannot shed
`parts`, because the final ordered partition-sum needs all
partitions x 60 partials simultaneously visible (a gather scratch of up
to 1,920 floats ~= `parts` itself); 8-chunks/group needs 8,192 floats
of `wsh` alone (> 32 KB) and 6-chunks/group needs 36,272 B with `parts`
(34,224 B even at stride 60) — both infeasible, so attempt-4's notes'
"stage 8, halve the barriers" suggestion does not fit; sharding one
expert's K across threads would reorder its serial chain and fail G2.

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-routing-2` (shape), partially: the 28 KB residency cap
at the two single-partition prefill sizes (1,016/2,048 rows), where the
running kernel's footprint falls 29% (28,080 -> 19,888 B). Barriers
(24), single-partition duty (60/256) and all of `ineff-baseline-routing-1`
(traffic) are untouched — so prefill stays `slower` (the traffic floor
alone exceeds compiled total 1.35x/4.3x/6.6x); this attempt buys only a
slice of the 142.7/336.8 us/layer shape residual at 1,016/2,048 rows.

## Predicted us per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 / 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows

Anchors (different runs, drift caveat per builder-1-b): decode
47.5/69.1/72.9 vs compiled 60.7/84.9/89.5 (round-2 grade run);
prefill measured 227.1/1298.8/2513.0 vs compiled 87.3/221.1/290.4
(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`).

from (reference - attempt-4)/11 kernels in the round-2 run:
(71.1-47.5)/11 = 2.1, (102.9-69.1)/11 = 3.1, (104.9-72.9)/11 = 2.9
us/layer at 1/8/32 rows -> ~2-3 us/layer for the empty/copy kernel
(copy traffic is rows x 64 B, negligible).

- 1 row: 47.5 + ~2.5 = **50** (compiled ~60.7, faster, margin ~10 us).
- 8 rows: 69.1 + ~3 = **72** (compiled ~84.9, faster).
- 32 rows: 72.9 + ~3 = **76** (compiled ~89.5, faster).
- 127 rows: 227.1 + ~3 (copy kernel) = **230** (compiled ~87.3, slower).
- 1,016 rows: 1298.8 + ~2.5 (empty kernel-A) - residency saving.
  Residency is an unmeasured mechanism (entry-2 verdict), so the saving
  is a guess: ~10% of the 354.7 residual ~= **-35 -> ~1266**

- 2,048 rows: 2513.0 + ~2.5 - ~10% of 609.8 ~= **-70 -> ~2446**

`beats_compiled` false. G1 pass, G2 pass (0 rows differing, all sizes).

No `max_rows`: direction (c) is a kernel fix; the hand-off is
direction (a)'s. Every size runs the kernels.

Ungraded row counts on the new dispatch: 769-1,015 (kernel-B compute
path in kind, untested), 33-767 (kernel-A + copy-through in kind),
2-7/9-31 (same), above 2,048; the residency mechanism itself (still
inferred, not measured); the empty/copy launch cost on other machine
states; exact 4th/5th ties (no graded row is one); prefill beyond the

- Prefill-big is encouraging: −15%/−17% vs anchor against a slower bar, consistent with removing most of the 355/610 µs shape residual — but cross-run and drift-confounded (the compiled bar swung ~2× between adjacent runs that hour).

4|direction (a): the `max_rows` hand-off. Starting point
5|`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4` (staged scalar path;

7|every prefill size: 2.6/5.9/8.7x compiled).

9|## The one main change
10|
11|`block-0.metal` and `block-1.metal` are byte copies of the starting
12|point's (verified: `diff` against
13|`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/` is empty).
14|`spec.json` is the starting point's plus one key: `"max_rows": 32`.
15|
16|Rows 1-32 run the candidate kernels; rows above 32 run the slot's
17|reference under `mx.compile` through the attempt's own dispatch
18|(`bench/grader/slots.py:327-337`). The regime branch on `rows`
19|(GEMV at `rows == 1`, split-K while `rows <= 768`), the
20|`rows`-only split-K partition formula, the verbatim sigmoid, the
21|strictly-greater top-4 scan, the weights fold, grids, and the
22|28,080 B threadgroup layout are untouched. The split-K branch for
23|33-768 rows and the single-accumulator branch above 768 are now
24|dead code at every graded size (all graded sizes above 32 hand
25|off), kept verbatim so the kernels stay valid if `max_rows` is
26|ever raised.
27|
28|## Which inefficiency it removes, and how
29|
30|`ineff-baseline-routing-1` (confirmed, traffic: per-row `w_router`
31|re-read, excess 116.1/935.4/1886.5 us/layer at 127/1,016/2,048
32|rows) and `ineff-baseline-routing-2` (confirmed, shape: 24
33|barriers, 28 KB residency cap, 23% single-partition duty, residual
34|24.1/142.7/336.8 us/layer) together. This attempt removes the
35|whole staged path from the graded prefill sizes: every prefill
36|size hands to the compiled reference, so prefill times `same` as
37|compiled by construction and the full prefill gap (measured -
38|compiled = 139.8/1077.7/2222.6 us/layer) is banked without
39|touching a line of kernel code. Decode is untouched, so the
40|starting point's decode wins are kept.
41|
42|## max_rows: 32, and why
43|
44|The boundary's hand-off window is 32 <= `max_rows` <= 126: every
45|decode step (1-32 rows, `claude/muse-agent-brief.md:26`) must stay
46|on the staged scalar path that already wins there (`max_rows >=
47|32`), while any `max_rows <= 126` hands all three graded prefill
48|sizes (127/1,016/2,048) to compiled. Routing has no MLX kernel
49|switch at 60 rows (that is the experts slot's); its reference
50|regimes change at `rows = 1` and `rows = 768` only.
51|
52|32 is the bottom of the window, picked because there is no
53|measured win to preserve above it: the staged path's traffic
54|floor alone exceeds the compiled reference's whole measured time
55|from 127 rows on (1.35x/4.3x/6.6x), so unlike the experts hand-off
56|(where 33-59 share the `qvm` decode path the kernels win), keeping
57|33-126 on the candidate could only slow real serving. 32 also
58|empties the boundary's can't-see band 33-126 (kernel-visible
59|counts in chunked-prefill serving with no piece verdict) and
60|dead-ends the regular-GEMM branch wherever the kernels run: below
61|the hand-off the kernels face only the GEMV (`rows == 1`) and
62|split-K (1 < rows <= 32) roundings, both already G2-passing and
63|winning. Sizes above `max_rows` exercise the compiled reference
64|through this attempt's own dispatch, and the compiled reference
65|was bit-exact with the reference at all six sizes on 2026-11-04
66|(`bench/micro/compiled_exact.py`).

103|  verdict exists there.

109|  exercise the compiled reference, whose exactness above

111|- Sizes above 2,048 (item 3), prefill beyond the first
112|  seeded-random chunk (item 4), whole-request noise at 1 request
113|  (item 6), other prompts / later decode steps / layers' drift /
114|  unseen exact 4th/5th ties (no graded row is one), score
115|  magnitudes saturating the sigmoid differently, threadgroup
116|  memory (item 8, unchecked by `slots.build`), unwritten
117|  threadgroup reads and thread-timing dependence.

119|  by this builder -- boundary tooling, not a gate.

121|## Verdict
122|
123|Graded 2026-11-04T18:14Z, one grader run

125|no `--baseline`: baseline `none`). Verdict kept in `grade.json`.

127|G1 pass. **G2 pass at all six sizes** (`rows_differ` 0,
128|`rows_other_experts` 0, `max_rel_err` 0.0 at 1/8/32 and
129|127/1,016/2,048 -- no differing row anywhere, so no first
130|difference to cite).

132|Chained us/layer, reference / compiled / candidate (`grade.json`,
133|medians of 30 paired repeats):
134|
135|| size | reference | compiled | candidate | wins | verdict |
136||---|---|---|---|---|---|
137|| rows 1 | 251.3 | 139.4 | 103.6 | 25 | `faster` |
138|| rows 8 | 154.7 | 157.2 | 129.9 | 28 | `faster` |
139|| rows 32 | 173.7 | 149.7 | 126.5 | 25 | `faster` |

141|| prefill 1,016 | 260.1 | 228.4 | 229.3 | 18 | `same` |
142|| prefill 2,048 | 322.2 | 291.7 | 299.7 | 8 | `slower` |
143|
144|`phases_vs_compiled`: decode `faster`, prefill `slower`.
145|**`beats_compiled` false** -- on the 2,048-row prefill size alone,
146|where the candidate *is* the compiled reference.
147|
148|## Why the attempt failed, and why 1-row decode missed by >20%
149|
150|Two findings, both machine/verdict-level: the kernels are
151|byte-identical to the starting point, so no kernel change can
152|explain either.
153|
154|1. **The 2,048-row `slower` is paired noise on identical code,
155|   not a slowdown.** Above `max_rows` the candidate runs
156|   `mx.compile(REFERENCE[slot])` built in `slots.build`
157|   (`bench/grader/slots.py:331-337`); the bar is a second
158|   `mx.compile` of the same reference built at timing time
159|   (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py:361`). Same function, same
160|   shapes, same `chained` wrapper, 3 warmup calls each, order
161|   balanced across the 30 repeats (2 functions alternate,
162|   `check_candidate.py:231-232`). The three prefill outcomes are
163|   18/18/8 candidate wins with medians 4.0% under, 0.4% over and
164|   2.7% over compiled -- all inside the brief's own "the same
165|   kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%" band
166|   (`claude/muse-agent-brief.md:211`). A systematic handicap in
167|   the candidate-side compile instance would lose at all three
168|   sizes; instead 127/1,016 split for the candidate and only the
169|   last-timed size (hottest machine) hit exactly the 22-loss
170|   `slower` threshold. P(<=8/30 | fair coin) ~= 0.008 -- a rare
171|   verdict-level event over 30 correlated repeats, and the prize

173|   median gap anywhere above the hand-off is 2.7%.
174|2. **The 1-row decode absolute missed because this run's machine
175|   was ~2x slower at small sizes.** Predicted 49.8, measured
176|   103.6 (+108%); but compiled moved 65.1 -> 139.4 (+114%) and the
177|   plain reference measured 251.3 in the same run. 8 rows:
178|   predicted 113.5, measured 129.9 (+14%); 32 rows: 121.3 ->
179|   126.5 (+4%). The relative wins hold and match the prediction
180|   (`faster` x 3, ahead 35.8/27.3/23.2 us/layer, 25/28/25 wins):
181|   chained absolutes drift with machine state (same observation
182|   as builder-1-b's and builder-2-b's notes this round), most
183|   where fixed overhead dominates. Nothing in the kernels changed,
184|   so the drift is the whole story.

151|## Rules for every agent
152|
153|- **Writes go only to this round's folder, in the files your role names.** Earlier rounds' folders, everything else in the worktree, and everything outside it are read-only.

A run of `time_candidates.py`, `breakdown.py` or any other timing script made directly is evidence of nothing.

157|  - **measured, piece:** the grader verdict that timed exactly that slot, `grade.json` in its attempt folder;
158|  - **measured, whole request:** the `ready-verdict.json` that timed exactly that slot or combination;
159|  - **prediction:** anything else. It counts only the candidate's own measured effect, shows its arithmetic, and stands beside the measured value once there is one.

163|- **The API-stage kernels** in the history before the tag `agent-era` are from an earlier, removed stage (PROVENANCE.md) and stay unread.

1|# Round-3 attempt 2 — builder-3-b, hyp-3-routing-prefill direction (b)
2|
3|Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4` (the slot's
4|starting point: G1+G2 pass, decode `faster` x3, prefill `slower` x3).
5|Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the compiled reference
6|in both phases.
7|
8|## The one main change
9|
10|A second kernel with a GEMM shape for prefill sizes, sharing each
11|`w_router` K-chunk across 16 rows, behind a size branch that keeps decode
12|on the winning staged path:
13|
14|- Kernel 0 (`block-0.metal` + `block-1.metal` header) is attempt-4
15|  verbatim — same GEMV branch at `rows == 1`, same split-K staging,
16|  same sigmoid, same top-4 — plus `if (rows > 32) return;` at the top.
17|  Its outputs are renamed `inds0`/`weights0`. Grid `rows*256`,
18|  threadgroup 256, threadgroup memory unchanged at 28,080 B.
19|- Kernel 1 (`block-2.metal`) is new. Grid `rows*60`, threadgroup 960:
20|  one threadgroup spans 16 rows with one thread per (row, expert); 60
21|  divides 960 so every group covers whole rows and no bounds check is
22|  needed (round-1 attempt-2's grid precedent). Each of the 12 staged
23|  groups stages 4 K-chunks of `w_router` once per 16 rows with
24|  attempt-4's exact coalesced `float4` mapping into `wsh[4096]`, plus
25|  the 64 current d-values per row into `xst[1024]`; each thread
26|  accumulates its (row, expert) score into per-partition partials in
27|  registers, each partial a serial scalar sum in increasing d, folded
28|  in partition order — the exact rows-branched per-row orders, so G2
29|  follows attempt-4's proof (feeding changes without order changes).
30|  Sigmoid, strictly-greater top-4 and the left-fold normalise are
31|  verbatim copies, run by one thread per row. At `rows <= 32` it only
32|  copies kernel 0's outputs. Threadgroup memory
33|  (4096+1024+1024)*4 = 24,576 B of 32 KB; 25 barriers per group of 16
34|  rows (12x2 + 1), i.e. ~1.6 per row against attempt-4's 24.
35|
36|Against round-1 attempt-2's failure (slower everywhere): that kernel
37|staged with serial per-thread loops (60 threads x 64 serial loads),
38|2 launches with two [rows,60] intermediates, and strided device reads.
39|This one stages cooperatively (960 threads share 960 vector loads),
40|keeps one [rows,4] hand-off, and reuses attempt-4's proven coalesced
41|mapping — but the proof is the chained timing below, not the contrast.
42|
43|## Inefficiency removed
44|
45|`ineff-baseline-routing-1` (per-row `w_router` re-read) and
46|`ineff-baseline-routing-2` (per-row shape cost) together: `w_router`
47|device traffic falls from rows x 184,320 B to ceil(rows/16) x 184,320 B
48|(16x at full groups), barriers from 24/row to ~1.6/row amortised, duty
49|from 23% to 100% in the single-partition regime (every thread owns one
50|expert of its row through all 12 groups), footprint from 28,080 B to
51|24,576 B.
52|
53|## Predicted us per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 / 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows
54|
55|Anchor: the round-3 re-grade of attempt-4
56|(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`):
57|ref / compiled / candidate = 68.4/65.1/49.8 at 1 row,
58|169.2/135.7/113.5 at 8, 159.3/145.2/121.3 at 32,
59|102.3/87.3/227.1 at 127, 231.3/221.1/1298.8 at 1,016,
60|310.0/290.4/2513.0 at 2,048. Decode margins: 15.3/22.2/23.9.
61|
62|- Decode (1/8/32): kernel 0 is attempt-4 plus a never-taken branch
63|  (~0); kernel 1 adds one copy launch (grid rows*60 threads, rows*4
64|  elements x 8 B copied). Allowance 3 us: **53 / 117 / 124** vs
65|  compiled 65.1/135.7/145.2 — still `faster`, spending ~3 of 15-24 us
66|  of margin.
67|- Prefill traffic floors at 200 GB/s (w staged once per 16 rows):
68|  - 127 rows: 8 groups x 184,320 B (w) + 127 x 1,536 B (x) + 127 x 32 B
69|    (out) = 1,673,696 B -> 8.4 us. + 25 barriers x 0.5 us = 12.5 +
70|    idle kernel-0 launch 4 + chained fixed cost 25 -> **~50** vs
71|    compiled 87.3.
72|  - 1,016 rows: 64 x 184,320 + 1,016 x 1,536 + 1,016 x 32 = 13.4 MB ->
73|    67 us. 64 groups / 16 cores = 4 waves x 25 x 0.5 = 50 + idle
74|    launch 6 + fixed 25 -> **~148** vs compiled 221.1.
75|  - 2,048 rows: 128 x 184,320 + 2,048 x 1,536 + 2,048 x 32 = 26.7 MB ->
76|    134 us. 8 waves x 25 x 0.5 = 100 + idle launch 8 + fixed 25 ->
77|    **~267** vs compiled 290.4 — thin: if barriers cost 1 us not 0.5,
78|    this is ~367 and `slower`. The barrier cost is a guess; the
79|    chained timing decides.
80|
81|Prediction: **53 / 117 / 124 / 50 / 148 / 267 us**. G2 prediction: pass
82|at all six sizes — every accumulation order is copied op-for-op from
83|attempt-4, which passes G2 at all six (it fails on speed, not bits).
84|
85|No `max_rows`: the hand-off is direction (a)'s fix; this attempt must
86|prove the GEMM kernel same-or-better at prefill on its own merits.
87|
88|## What this attempt leaves unmeasured
89|
90|For the hypothesis entry's Unverified list: ungraded row counts 2-7 /
91|9-31 (kernel-0 staged path, same code as graded 8/32 but other
92|partition groupings); 33-126 (kernel-1 split-K path with 16/8
93|partitions, exercised in kind but not in verdict); 129-767 and 769+
94|(kernel-1 paths past the 129/257/768 transitions); above 2,048 rows;
95|prefill past the first chunk; whole-request composition (ready check);
96|the 24,576 B threadgroup sum (unchecked by slots.build); unwritten
97|threadgroup reads and thread-timing dependence (one equality run per
98|layer cannot expose them).
99|
100|## Verdict
101|
102|G1 fail, no G2, no timing (`grade.json`): `ValueError: Thread group size
103|(960) is greater than the maximum allowed threads per threadgroup (640).`
104|One grader run, one attempt — recorded as graded; the fix is a copied new
105|attempt (see below).
106|
107|## Why G1 failed
108|
109|The brief's 1,024-thread cap (brief:100) is the device max; Metal derives
110|each pipeline's actual `maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` from the kernel's
111|own resource use — here 640, against my 960-thread (16 rows x 60 experts)
112|threadgroup. The likely binder is registers (the `part[16]` partial array
113|plus staging temporaries per thread), with 24,576 B of threadgroup memory
114|as the other candidate; either way the number to design under is 640, not
115|1,024. Round-1 attempt-2's 480-thread groups passed G1, consistent with a
116|cap in the 480-960 band. Nothing about the GEMM direction is refuted: no
117|correctness or timing evidence exists (the kernel never ran), and the
118|predicted 53/117/124/50/148/267 us stands uncompared — a >20% analysis is
119|not applicable with no measurement.
120|
121|Next change (one, in a copied new attempt): 10 rows per threadgroup
122|(600 threads, `xst`/`sc` to 10x64, `Rg` cap and row stride 16->10, grid
123|stays `rows*60`). 600 < 640 under either binding constraint, and 60 still
124|divides 600 so groups stay row-aligned with no bounds checks. Re-derived
125|prefill traffic floors at 200 GB/s: 127 rows: 13 x 184,320 + 127 x 1,536
126|= 2.6 MB -> ~13 us; 1,016 rows: 102 x 184,320 + 1,016 x 1,536 = 20.4 MB
127|-> ~102 us; 2,048 rows: 205 x 184,320 + 2,048 x 1,536 = 40.9 MB ->
128|~205 us (thin vs compiled 290.4 — the chained timing decides). If that
129|attempt passes G1, the open question is unchanged: whether barriers and
130|waves fit the remaining headroom.

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write faster MobileMoE-S kernels, for decoding and prompt processing
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|A request goes through two phases: **prompt processing** (the prefill), which runs its whole prompt through the model, and **decoding**, one step per generated token. An improvement must hold in both: faster in one, and no slower in the other ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A kernel that speeds up the decode step but slows the prefill is not an improvement.
12|
13|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
14|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
15|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
16|
17|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
18|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
19|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
20|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
21|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
22|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
23|
24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
95|
96|## Tools and limits
97|
98|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
99|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
100|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
101|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.
102|
103|## Rules of this session
104|
105|These keep your work apart from everyone else's. Git hooks and an audit script enforce them, and a commit that breaks them is refused.
106|
107|- **Write only inside `muse-spark/`.** Never change `bench/`, `claude/`, `results/`, `tools/`, `third_party/`, or any other file. A copy of the grader you edit is never used.
108|- **Commit only on `muse-agent`,** with the co-author trailer your settings add: `Co-Authored-By: Muse Spark (Meta Model API) <muse-spark@meta-model-api.invalid>`. Start each subject with `Muse Spark:`. No other co-author.
109|- **Never push, merge, rebase, change git config, or skip hooks.**
110|- **Don't read `.env`** or any credentials file.
111|- One commit per attempt, after you've run the grader on it, so the history shows every attempt in order.
112|
113|## Your files
114|
115|```
116|muse-spark/
117|  strategy.md                                your choice and design, ending with the targets JSON
118|  kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>/
119|    block-0.metal, block-1.metal, ...        Metal kernel bodies (and headers), numbered from 0
120|    spec.json                                the launch spec
121|    notes.md                                 optional: what you tried and why
122|  summary.md                                 your final attempt per slot
123|```
124|
125|`<slot-folder>` is `routing`, `combine`, `routing-combine` or `experts`. Grade an attempt with:
126|
127|```bash
128|.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_candidate.py muse-spark/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N> <slot>
129|```
130|
131|where `<slot>` is `routing`, `combine`, `routing+combine` or `experts`.
132|
133|**The targets JSON** at the end of `strategy.md`:
134|
135|```json
136|{
137|  "targets": [
138|    {"slot": "routing+combine", "why": "...", "expected_saving_ms": {"rows_1": 0.0, "rows_32": 0.0}, "design": "..."}
139|  ]
140|}
141|```
142|
143|List one or two targets, in the order you work on them.
144|
145|**The launch spec** (`spec.json`):
146|
147|```json
148|{
149|  "kernels": [
150|    {
151|      "name": "fused_routing",
152|      "source_block": 0,
153|      "header_block": null,
154|      "inputs": ["x", "w_router", "bias"],
155|      "outputs": [
156|        {"name": "inds", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "uint32"},
157|        {"name": "weights", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "float32"}
158|      ],
159|      "grid": ["rows*32", 1, 1],
160|      "threadgroup": [32, 1, 1],
161|      "template": {"T": "bfloat16"},
162|      "init_value": null,
163|      "atomic_outputs": false
164|    }
165|  ],
166|  "slot_outputs": {"inds": "inds", "weights": "weights"}
167|}
168|```
169|
170|- **`source_block` and `header_block`** are the numbers of your `block-N.metal` files.
171|- **Kernels run in list order.** A kernel's `inputs` may name slot inputs or outputs of earlier kernels.
172|- **`slot_outputs`** maps each output of the slot to the kernel output that provides it.
173|- **`max_rows`** (optional, an integer of at least 1): inputs with more rows than this skip your kernels and run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. Use it to keep prefill-sized inputs on MLX's own code when your kernels are built for decode sizes; MLX switches its own experts kernel at 60 rows. The hand-off is graded like the rest: bit-exact, and timed at the prefill sizes.
174|- **For `routing+combine`,** `spec.json` holds two specs, each in the format above for its own slot, `max_rows` included: `{"routing": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}, "combine": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}}`. The original experts and shared expert run between the two parts. The grader tests each part on its own, and the combine part receives the reference routing weights.
175|- **Shape and grid entries** are integers, or products of integers and the names `rows`, `D`, `E`, `K` and `H`, such as `"rows*32"`. Nothing else is evaluated.
176|- **dtypes** are `float32`, `bfloat16`, `float16`, `uint32` or `int32`.
177|- **Template values** are one of those dtypes, an integer or a boolean.
178|- **`grid`** counts threads, not threadgroups, as in `mx.fast.metal_kernel`.
179|
180|## How each attempt is judged
181|
182|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.
183|
184|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
185|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
186|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
187|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
188|
189|   At every size:
190|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
191|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
192|
193|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
194|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
195|3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
196|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
197|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
198|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
199|
200|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
201|
202|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).
203|
204|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
205|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
206|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
207|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same` or `slower`); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.
208|
209|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
210|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
211|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
212|- **Per phase:** decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) are each `faster` when every size is, `slower` when any size is, and `not slower` otherwise.
213|- **`beats_compiled`** is true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
214|
215|It is a guide; the ready check in the round, and Claude's G3 after it, decide.
216|
217|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, or after 5 attempts. 1|# Round-3 attempt 3 — builder-3-c, hyp-3-routing-prefill direction (c)
2|
3|Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4` (the slot's
4|starting point: G1+G2 pass, decode `faster` x3, prefill `slower` x3 at
5|2.6/5.9/8.7x compiled). Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar
6|is the compiled reference.
7|
8|## The one main change
9|
10|Split the staged path at the regime boundary `rows = 768` into two
11|kernels so the single-partition regime (partitions == 1, i.e. exactly
12|rows > 768) drops the 2,048-float `parts` array:
13|
14|- Kernel-A (`block-0.metal`): attempt-4 verbatim plus a uniform
15|  `if (rows > 768) return;` first and outputs renamed to
16|  `inds_a`/`weights_a`. Serves rows <= 768 (GEMV + split-K).
17|- Kernel-B (`block-2.metal`): at rows <= 768 copies kernel-A's outputs
18|  through (bit-exact, 4 threads/row); at rows > 768 runs the
19|  single-partition path with each expert's whole 768-product chain in
20|  one thread-private accumulator across the 12 staged groups — no
21|  `parts`, so threadgroup is (816 + 60 + 4,096) x 4 B = 19,888 B
22|  (60.7% of 32 KB) instead of 28,080 B (85.7%).
23|
24|Two kernels are required because threadgroup arrays are statically
25|sized: one kernel would still declare `parts` for its general path.
26|Each kernel's outputs are fresh buffers (`bench/grader/slots.py:343-356`,
27|`env.update` overwrites per kernel), so same-name sharing is impossible
28|and the copy-through is the wiring.
29|
30|Kept verbatim: the `rows`-branched regimes (the split is at the
31|regime boundary, never at graded values), staging layout/stride,
32|product order within every (expert, partition) chain (kernel-B's
33|register chain visits chunks/groups in the same increasing order the
34|`parts` path resumes them in), the 24 in-loop barriers, sigmoid,
35|strictly-greater top-4, and the weights fold. G2 prediction: pass at
36|all six sizes — storage changes only (register vs threadgroup vs copy),
37|no order changes.
38|
39|Design alternatives ruled out while writing (for the failure ledger /
40|inefficiency notes): register-held partials in ONE kernel cannot shed
41|`parts`, because the final ordered partition-sum needs all
42|partitions x 60 partials simultaneously visible (a gather scratch of up
43|to 1,920 floats ~= `parts` itself); 8-chunks/group needs 8,192 floats
44|of `wsh` alone (> 32 KB) and 6-chunks/group needs 36,272 B with `parts`
45|(34,224 B even at stride 60) — both infeasible, so attempt-4's notes'
46|"stage 8, halve the barriers" suggestion does not fit; sharding one
47|expert's K across threads would reorder its serial chain and fail G2.
48|
49|## Inefficiency removed
50|
51|`ineff-baseline-routing-2` (shape), partially: the 28 KB residency cap
52|at the two single-partition prefill sizes (1,016/2,048 rows), where the
53|running kernel's footprint falls 29% (28,080 -> 19,888 B). Barriers
54|(24), single-partition duty (60/256) and all of `ineff-baseline-routing-1`
55|(traffic) are untouched — so prefill stays `slower` (the traffic floor
56|alone exceeds compiled total 1.35x/4.3x/6.6x); this attempt buys only a
57|slice of the 142.7/336.8 us/layer shape residual at 1,016/2,048 rows.
58|
59|## Predicted us per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 / 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows
60|
61|Anchors (different runs, drift caveat per builder-1-b): decode
62|47.5/69.1/72.9 vs compiled 60.7/84.9/89.5 (round-2 grade run);
63|prefill measured 227.1/1298.8/2513.0 vs compiled 87.3/221.1/290.4
64|(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`).
65|Extra cost: one more kernel launch per layer. Launch cost estimated
66|from (reference - attempt-4)/11 kernels in the round-2 run:
67|(71.1-47.5)/11 = 2.1, (102.9-69.1)/11 = 3.1, (104.9-72.9)/11 = 2.9
68|us/layer at 1/8/32 rows -> ~2-3 us/layer for the empty/copy kernel
69|(copy traffic is rows x 64 B, negligible).
70|
71|- 1 row: 47.5 + ~2.5 = **50** (compiled ~60.7, faster, margin ~10 us).
72|- 8 rows: 69.1 + ~3 = **72** (compiled ~84.9, faster).
73|- 32 rows: 72.9 + ~3 = **76** (compiled ~89.5, faster).
74|- 127 rows: 227.1 + ~3 (copy kernel) = **230** (compiled ~87.3, slower).
75|- 1,016 rows: 1298.8 + ~2.5 (empty kernel-A) - residency saving.
76|  Residency is an unmeasured mechanism (entry-2 verdict), so the saving
77|  is a guess: ~10% of the 354.7 residual ~= **-35 -> ~1266**
78|  (compiled ~221, slower).
79|- 2,048 rows: 2513.0 + ~2.5 - ~10% of 609.8 ~= **-70 -> ~2446**
80|  (compiled ~290, slower).
81|
82|Prediction: decode faster x3 (wins kept), prefill slower x3,
83|`beats_compiled` false. G1 pass, G2 pass (0 rows differing, all sizes).
84|
85|No `max_rows`: direction (c) is a kernel fix; the hand-off is
86|direction (a)'s. Every size runs the kernels.
87|
88|## What this leaves unmeasured (for the hypothesis entry's Unverified)
89|
90|Ungraded row counts on the new dispatch: 769-1,015 (kernel-B compute
91|path in kind, untested), 33-767 (kernel-A + copy-through in kind),
92|2-7/9-31 (same), above 2,048; the residency mechanism itself (still
93|inferred, not measured); the empty/copy launch cost on other machine
94|states; exact 4th/5th ties (no graded row is one); prefill beyond the
95|first seeded chunk.
96|
97|## Verdict (2026-11-04T18:18:49Z, one grader run)
98|
99|G1 pass, **G2 pass at all six sizes** (rows_differ 0,
100|rows_other_experts 0, max_rel_err 0.0). Chained us/layer
101|(ref / compiled / candidate, `grade.json`): 1 row 77.9 / 64.7 /
102|**66.1** (14 wins, `same`); 8 rows 109.8 / 95.4 / **96.1** (15,
103|`same`); 32 rows 117.4 / 103.9 / **109.5** (9, `same`); 127 rows
104|108.7 / 96.9 / **266.0** (0, `slower`); 1,016 rows 242.2 / 235.3 /
105|**1098.3** (2, `slower`); 2,048 rows 324.8 / 299.7 / **2097.3** (0,
106|`slower`). `phases_vs_compiled`: decode `not slower`, prefill
107|`slower`; **`beats_compiled` false**. Baseline none, no
108|`beats_baseline`.
109|
110|## Why the decode timing missed the prediction by >20%
111|
112|Predicted 50/72/76/230/1266/2446, measured 66.1/96.1/109.5/266.0/
113|1098.3/2097.3: decode +32/+33/+44%, 127 rows +16%, prefill-big
114|-13%/-14% (better than predicted). Two causes, in order:
115|
116|1. **Machine-state drift (dominant).** The anchor mixed two runs
117|   already; this run's compiled bar (64.7/95.4/103.9) sits above the
118|   round-2 anchor (60.7/84.9/89.5), while sibling attempt-1, graded
119|   minutes earlier, saw compiled at 139.4/157.2/149.7 — a ~2x swing
120|   of the bar between adjacent runs. Attempt-4's own decode margin
121|   compressed from -13/-16/-17 us to ~+/-few us of coin-flip races
122|   (14/15/9 wins). Same lesson as builder-1-b's and builder-3-a's:
123|   chained absolutes drift; only paired verdicts in one run count.
124|2. **The real wiring cost (~2-3 us, as predicted).** Kernel-A on the
125|   decode path is attempt-4 plus a uniform branch (free) plus the
126|   copy-through launch. In a compressed-margin state that small real
127|   cost flips `faster` to `same` — attempt-1's identical decode
128|   kernel without the copy won `faster` x3 in its (higher-margin)
129|   run. The cost exists; the verdict flip is drift meeting it.
130|
131|Prefill-big reads the other way and is the encouraging half:
132|candidate 1098/2097 vs the 1299/2513 anchor (-15%/-17%) against a
133|compiled headwind (+6%/+3% slower bar) — consistent with removing

138|expected (same kernel-A work + copy) and the +17% against a +11%
139|bar move is noise/drift on a small absolute.

141|Next change (one): copy this attempt byte-identically to a new
142|attempt number and re-grade WITH `--baseline
143|muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4`, so one run isolates

1|# Inefficiency: `w_router` re-read once per row costs 116/935/1887 µs per layer at prefill sizes
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
4|- **Status:** confirmed
5|- **Version:** 2
6|- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T17:41:11Z
7|- **Next:** done — confirmed by verifier (see Verdict); builders may use the excess bounds
8|
9|## Slot
10|
11|`routing`
12|
13|## What happens
14|
15|Every row's threadgroup stages its own full copy of the router weight from
16|device memory. In the GEMV branch (`rows == 1`) each lane reads `w_router`
17|straight from device (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/block-0.metal:41-45`,
18|frozen); on the staged scalar path (`rows > 1`) all 256 threads cooperatively
19|load all 48 K-chunks × 60 experts as `float4`s into `wsh` across the 12 groups
20|(block-0:81-93) — coalesced, but still a private full copy per row. Nothing is
21|shared across rows: per layer the kernel reads rows × 60×768×4 B = rows ×
22|184,320 B of `w_router`, plus rows × 1,536 B of `x` (bfloat16).
23|
24|The reference's GEMM/GEMV reads `w_router` once per layer and reuses each tile
25|across all rows in the tile (round-2 `territory-baseline-routing.md`
26|section 3.1, frozen). This entry is the prefill side of round-2
27|`ineff-baseline-routing-4` (frozen, confirmed), which ranked the same re-read
28|0/0.13/0.57 ms/step at decode sizes and 0 at prefill because prefill was
29|untimed (ADR 0010:42). Under two-phase judgment (ADR 0011) the prefill side
30|is the slot's largest measured cost.
31|
32|## Cost
33|

37||---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

39|| 8 | 1.47 MB | 0.01 MB | 1.49 MB | 7.4 µs | 113.5 µs | 135.7 µs |
40|| 32 | 5.90 MB | 0.05 MB | 5.95 MB | 29.7 µs | 121.3 µs | 145.2 µs |
41|| 127 | 23.41 MB | 0.20 MB | 23.60 MB | 118.0 µs | 227.1 µs | 87.3 µs |

43|| 2,048 | 377.49 MB | 3.15 MB | 380.63 MB | 1903.2 µs | 2513.0 µs | 290.4 µs |
44|
45|Measured/compiled: chained µs/layer from
46|`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`
47|(frozen). The compiled reference's traffic per layer is ~184 KB once plus
48|rows×1.5 KB of `x` (≈0.4/1.7/3.3 MB at prefill sizes, i.e. ≈2/9/17 µs
49|floors) — the re-read excess is (rows−1)×184,320 B per layer:

51|- decode: 0 / 6.5 / 28.6 µs/layer at 1/8/32 rows (as round-2 entry 4);

20|   `threadgroup_barrier`s (stage-then-compute, compute-then-overwrite,
21|   block-0:94,119), plus 3 outside the loop (lines 33,129,137). Every
22|   barrier stalls the whole 256-thread threadgroup.

24|   `parts[2048]` + `wsh[4096]` floats, block-0:15-25) — 85.7% of the
25|   32 KB limit. Only ~1 such threadgroup fits a core's allocation at a
26|   time, so as row counts grow into the hundreds the waves of threadgroups
27|   serialise and barrier/staging latency that overlapped at decode sizes
28|   is exposed. Attempt-4's own notes measured the decode side of this:
29|   flat 69→73 µs from 8 to 32 rows because staging and barriers overlapped
30|   other resident threadgroups' compute (`notes.md:88-103`) — that overlap
31|   is what the residency cap takes away as rows scale.

33|   phase runs `dparts*60` of 256 threads (block-0:99-101), where `dparts`
34|   is the partitions the group's 4 chunks touch. From the partition
35|   formula (block-0:57-75; audited in round-2 hyp-2, frozen): at 8/32 rows

40|   and the final sequential partial sum runs 60/256 at every size
41|   (block-0:121-127). The per-row FMA count is fixed (60×768 = 46,080),
42|   but above 768 rows it issues through one quarter of the lanes in
43|   serial dependent chains.

{"content":"# Round-3 attempt 4 — builder-3-d, hyp-3-routing-prefill direction (b)

Builds on `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-2` (direction (b),
G1 fail: kernel 1 asks 960 threads/group against the pipeline max 640;
no G2, no timing). Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the
compiled reference in both phases.

## The one main change

10 rows per threadgroup instead of 16 in kernel 1 (the GEMM-shaped
prefill kernel), exactly the fix attempt-2's notes prescribe — nothing else:

- `spec.json`: kernel 1 `threadgroup` 960 → 600; grid stays `rows*60`.
  60 still divides 600, so every threadgroup covers whole rows (the last
  possibly fewer than 10) and no bounds checks are needed — edge groups
  clip to whole rows exactly as in attempt-2's 16-row design.
- `block-2.metal`: `xst`/`sc` 1024 → 640 floats (10 rows × 64 stride);
  `wsh[4096]` unchanged (4 K-chunks × 16 k × 64-expert stride is
  row-count independent); row stride `g * 16u` → `g * 10u` in `r`, `Rg`
  and `rr`; `Rg` cap 16 → 10. The `w`-staging loop bound stays 960
  (4 slots × 240 elements of total work, independent of rows/group);
  every remaining `16u` is K-chunk geometry (16 d-values per chunk,
  `part[16]`), correctly untouched.
- `block-0.metal`, `block-1.metal`: byte-identical to attempt-2
  (`diff` empty) — decode path untouched.

Threadgroup: (4096 + 640 + 640) × 4 B = 21,504 B of 32 KB (was 24,576 B).
600 threads < 640 pipeline cap under either binding constraint
(registers or threadgroup memory — both shrank), so G1 should pass.

## Inefficiency removed

Same as attempt-2: `ineff-baseline-routing-1` (per-row `w_router`
re-read) and `ineff-baseline-routing-2` (per-row shape cost) together.
`w_router` device traffic falls from rows × 184,320 B to
ceil(rows/10) × 184,320 B (~10× at full groups, was 16×), barriers from
24/row to 25 per group of 10 rows (~2.5/row amortised, was ~1.6),
duty from 23% to 100% in the single-partition regime, footprint from
28,080 B to 21,504 B.

## Predicted us per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 / 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows

Anchor: the round-3 re-grade of attempt-4
(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`):
ref / compiled / candidate = 68.4/65.1/49.8 at 1 row,
169.2/135.7/113.5 at 8, 159.3/145.2/121.3 at 32,
102.3/87.3/227.1 at 127, 231.3/221.1/1298.8 at 1,016,
310.0/290.4/2513.0 at 2,048. Decode margins: 15.3/22.2/23.9.

- Decode (1/8/32): kernel 0 is attempt-4 plus a never-taken branch
  (~0); kernel 1 adds one copy launch (grid rows*60 threads, rows*4
  elements × 8 B copied). Allowance 3 us: **53 / 117 / 124** vs
  compiled 65.1/135.7/145.2 — still `faster`, spending ~3 of 15–24 us
  of margin. Unchanged from attempt-2 (decode code is byte-identical).
- Prefill traffic floors at 200 GB/s (`w` staged once per 10 rows):
  - 127 rows: 13 groups × 184,320 B (w) + 127 × 1,536 B (x) + 127 × 32 B
    (out) = 2,595,296 B → 13.0 us. 13 groups fit 16 cores → 1 wave ×
    25 barriers × 0.5 us = 12.5 + idle kernel-0 launch 4 + chained
    fixed cost 25 → **~55** vs compiled 87.3 (`faster`).
  - 1,016 rows: 102 × 184,320 + 1,016 × 1,536 + 1,016 × 32 =
    20,393,728 B → 102 us. ceil(102/16) = 7 waves × 12.5 = 87.5 +
    idle launch 6 + fixed 25 → **~220** vs compiled 221.1 — tied;
    the chained timing decides.
  - 2,048 rows: 205 × 184,320 + 2,048 × 1,536 + 2,048 × 32 =
    40,996,864 B → 205 us. ceil(205/16) = 13 waves × 12.5 = 162.5 +
    idle launch 8 + fixed 25 → **~400** vs compiled 290.4 —
    `slower` under this barrier model.

Prediction: **53 / 117 / 124 / 55 / 220 / 400 us**. G1 prediction: pass
(600 < 640; 21,504 B < 32 KB; grid divisible along whole rows). G2
prediction: pass at all six sizes — every accumulation order is copied
op-for-op from attempt-4 (via attempt-2, which this copies), and only
the grouping changed, never any row's order. `beats_compiled`
prediction: false under the 0.5-us/barrier guess (2,048 rows slower,
1,016 tied) — but the barrier cost is a guess, and barriers may
overlap across resident groups; the chained timing decides whether
prefill-big is `same`-or-better. The decode `faster` × 3 is the firm
half of the prediction.

No `max_rows`: the hand-off is direction (a)'s fix; this attempt must
prove the GEMM kernel same-or-better at prefill on its own merits.

## What this attempt leaves unmeasured

For the hypothesis entry's Unverified list: ungraded row counts 2–7 /
9–31 (kernel-0 staged path, same code as graded 8/32 but other
partition groupings); 33–126 (kernel-1 split-K path with 16/8
partitions, exercised in kind but not in verdict); 129–767 and 769+
(kernel-1 paths past the 129/257/768 transitions); above 2,048 rows;
prefill past the first chunk; whole-request composition (ready check);
the 21,504 B threadgroup sum (unchecked by slots.build); unwritten
threadgroup reads and thread-timing dependence (one equality run per
layer cannot expose them).
